title: India’s Ringg gets backing from Peak XV as it pushes voice AI past the phone call
snippet: Ringg has raised $10 million from Peak XV as a part of its Series A extension.
fullText:
More than 76% of consumers in India prefer talking to businesses over a phone call, according to a recent study from Truecaller. Since voice is still consumers’ preferred way to communicate, that leaves a big opportunity to automate support and outreach calls using voice AI in the country. Voice AI startup Ringg, which already processes 20 million call attempts a month, is betting that volume keeps climbing over the coming months, and it just raised more money on that belief.

The company said today it has landed $10 million from Peak XV Partners as an extension of its Series A. It had previously raised $5.5 million in a Series A round earlier this year, bringing the round’s total to $15.5 million.

Ringg started life as a text-to-speech startup called DesiVocal, but training its own speech models proved expensive, so the founders moved up the stack — building voice AI agents for enterprises instead. Indian fintech Cred became its first customer, and Ringg has since signed Indian startups like Flipkart, Practo, Groww, and Policybazaar.

“At the start, we were doing high-volume, low-complexity use cases like outbound calling, lead qualification, loan collection, and more. We quickly realized these are not sticky use cases, and so it’s always going to be a price game,” the startup’s co-founder Siddharth Tripathi told TechCrunch.

Ringg still serves some of those simpler use cases, but it has set its sights on more complex workflows: appointment booking for healthcare clinics, abandoned-cart recovery for e-commerce sites, and onboarding/KYC (“know your customer”) checks for fintech apps.

Tripathi said Ringg’s voice agent now runs across 1,200 clinics for the healthcare app Practo, helping patients book visits or follow up on next steps post-visit.

Voice calls still make up over 70% of Ringg’s business, but the startup has started branching into other channels, including chat and WhatsApp. For some clients like Shell, it’s also automating browser-based support requests.

“We are trying to position ourselves as a platform for agents that bring outcomes or get things done rather than voice agents for enterprises,” Tripathi said.

Most of Ringg’s customers are based in India, with a handful in the Middle East and the U.S. But the startup isn’t trying to sell directly to U.S. companies; instead, it wants to partner with global capability centers in India — the offshore hubs multinationals increasingly lean on for back-office and support work — to sell automation capacity alongside human support.

Tripathi said the company builds its own speech recognition and generation models and would eventually like to own the full voice stack, including infrastructure and deployment. For now, though, that remains too costly, so the product works as an orchestration layer, routing tasks to different models depending on the use case.

Rishen Kapoor, a principal at Peak XV, said that because Ringg started as a research lab building its own models, that technical depth shows up in the complex use cases it’s now tackling.

“Because of the technical capabilities, they can actually do these hard-won enterprise workflows end to end. They can complete these higher-value tasks like merchant onboarding, like L1 and L2 support, with quality and with consistency,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Voice AI in India is a crowded field. Model makers, including Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Cartesia, and local players like Sarvam and Smallest.ai, are all jockeying for pole position. Orchestration-focused startups like Bolna and Blue Machines are chasing the same layer Ringg occupies, while sector-focused players like Gnani and Arrowhead concentrate heavily on finance.

That layered stack — model makers, orchestrators, and application-layer players all trying to lock in enterprise workflows — is itself the story. The money and the defensibility increasingly sit with whoever owns the customer relationship and the outcome.

Ringg currently has 40 employees, with more than 15 hired in the last three months. The startup is hiring for forward-deployed engineer roles that combine technical chops with product management skills, along with researchers focused on bringing down the cost of running its models.

title: Ring Gave Itself a Security Makeover Called TAKE. Here’s What’s Actually Changing
snippet: Amazon Ring has a new policy for its encryption practices and what they mean for your security videos or AI use. Customers are getting more choices, too.
fullText:
Starting this September, Amazon’s Ring security brand is clarifying how it encrypts customer data on cameras, including security video data used for AI analysis, like turning it into video descriptions on your phone. This begins with a unique Ring standard called Throw Away the Key Encryption.

Previously, Ring’s cloud practices were a bit of a black box. We knew the sort of encryption used, but not how easily or frequently Ring could access videos for analysis. Privacy concerns quickly followed, especially as Ring has come under scrutiny — and lawsuits — for features like its AI familiar face technology.

Now Ring has redefined the process and outlined several encryption practices made to give customers more protection or at least more information. Here’s how TAKE works.

A tale of two keys

Ring’s cloud storage is typically necessary to save videos and use intelligence features.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

TAKE is a new approach and a significant jump in transparency for Ring. When TAKE is used and a Ring camera records a video, that video is encrypted with rotating encryption keys, which means the keys are periodically updated with new versions.

One copy of the key is held in the cloud by Ring, in what Ring describes as a “secure enclave,” which requires specific permissions and situations to access. If you have any Ring artificial intelligence features enabled for your Ring device, like video descriptions and summaries, familiar face detection, advanced object recognition and so on, then Ring takes the key out of its vault and uses it — once — to analyze your video footage.

After Ring uses its copy of the key to analyze your video and use the data gathered, it deletes the key and can no longer access that video for any purpose. The company says, “Ring can only receive access to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account,” but I’m not sure if that includes analysis for Ring’s own purposes, like AI training, too. Either way, it seems like it can only happen for one instance.

Meanwhile, you keep the master key for your Ring video, so you can access your cloud storage clips whenever and how often you want, until the cloud storage limit runs out. (Ring’s storage starts at 180 days.) If you have Shared Users on your Ring account who you’ve enabled to access videos, they’ll have this master key, too.

Jamie Siminoff, founder and chief inventor at Ring, told CNET, “We wanted to provide E2EE-like security while allowing customers to continue using all the features they expect from their Ring devices.”

What about end-to-end encryption?

Ring has excellent cameras, but you may want to turn off certain features.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

In the past, Ring has offered an end-to-end encryption mode for users to enable with a password. The video is automatically encrypted and can only be viewed by those who have the password. This option will remain with TAKE, offering the highest level of privacy for Ring security videos — but at a cost.

With the end-to-end encryption mode on, most of Ring’s cloud-based features won’t work. That includes all its AI features. However, you’ll still be able to use live view, access videos in cloud storage and share videos as long as you have your password. It’s a give and take that benefits anyone worried about Ring’s AI or analysis and wants to skip that part of the cameras altogether.

What if I don’t have a Ring subscription at all?

You can get local storage on Ring devices, but it will disable a lot of features.Julie Snyder/CNET

Without a Ring subscription, you can’t store videos in the cloud, so none of this really applies. There are ways to get local storage with Ring, notably using a Ring security hub, that can act as a local storage device if you add a microSD card. But much like end-to-end encryption, you won’t get any of Ring’s extra cloud features.

Getting Ring’s TAKE standard

The new TAKE approach is free for users, although you’ll have to pay a Ring subscription in the first place to access any of this cloud storage. Ring subscriptions start around $5 for a single camera, but you’ll need a $20 subscription to start accessing more advanced AI features and 24/7 professional monitoring.

Ring told me the TAKE standard will start rolling out in September, but the company didn’t give me any indication of how long it would take to update for all users. When it comes to your camera, TAKE will be turned on by default. I’ll keep an eye on my Ring app and let you know if I notice significant differences, although most of this update is behind the scenes.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

With degrees in Business Management, Literature and Technical Writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. title: The Google Pixel 11 Pro Still Has the Best Display for Gaming, but Other Troubles Emerge
snippet: An underpowered Tensor chip and odd game glitches keep the Pixel 11 Pro from nabbing the top spot on our gaming phone rankings.
fullText:
In 2025, I lauded the Google Pixel 10 Pro for its bright, vibrant display that was great to game on. Now, its successor has arrived, and although it looks identical — with some slight hardware changes — the luster has worn off. The Google Pixel 11 Pro feels underpowered when it comes to gaming, and odd glitches that emerged while playing make it harder to recommend for gaming on the go.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro is unquestionably the best phone Google has ever released, with its AI-powering Tensor G6 chip, a trio of great cameras with refined photo software and an expansive list of generative AI features. With all these advantages, the 11 Pro is one of the best phones out there for taking pictures. But its hardware and software edge doesn’t extend as much to gaming as other phones do, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 and its Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

In practice, the Pixel 11 Pro struggles with higher graphics settings within games, and will pop up warnings about overheating and battery drain when I pump it up above the lowest resolution, frame rate and detailing. It’s a bit surprising given the phone’s premium price.

Unfortunately, that price has gone up, though in a roundabout way. Google got rid of the 128GB entry option for its entire lineup, so the $1,099 starting price for the Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage is the same price as last year at that storage level — you just can’t pick up a lower-storage configuration for under $1,000 anymore. That’s especially limiting for mobile gamers, since installing multiple titles can quickly eat through the available storage. The action RPG Genshin Impact alone takes up 55GB.

When reached for comment, Google confirmed that the raised storage and price reflects the impact of the RAM shortage, driven by AI, which has made components more expensive across consumer tech. But it bites the Pixel 11 Pro phones in another way: That new entry model comes with only 12GB of RAM. You’ll still get 16GB with the 512GB and 1TB storage options ($1,219 and $1,499 respectively, $50 higher than last year’s prices), but it’s a bummer after last year’s 10 Pro series all shipped with 16GB.

Google says that this reduction in RAM doesn’t matter as much, since its 11 Pro phones are faster and smoother than last year’s thanks to optimizations in silicon and software. I wasn’t able to test this claim, as the Pixel 11 Pro review unit Google sent me had 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM, but it’s worth keeping in mind.

With those considerations, the Pixel 11 Pro starts off with compromises, which progressed as I spent more time gaming on the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s svelte design made it easy to handle while gaming, though not everyone may be comfortable with the sizable camera block on the back side.David Lumb/CNET

What it’s like to play games on the Pixel 11 Pro

As with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro, the new Pixel 11 Pro stands out among other phones with its 6.3-inch OLED display. Details are crisp with its 2,856×1,280-pixel resolution and colors are vivid with HDR10 Plus support. 

Once again, the 3,600-nit maximum brightness sets the Pixel 11 Pro’s screen apart from competitors, allowing me to play in direct sunlight and brightening up dark rooms. Other phones are catching up, with screens on this year’s Samsung Galaxy S26 at 2,600 nits and the iPhone 17 Pro Max at 3,000 nits. But the Pixel 11 Pro keeps its lead, showing a stunning array of colors and details from games of all genres.

The phone itself is comfortable enough to hold and play. While it’s physically identical to the Pixel 10 Pro from last year, the metal frame ringing the sides feels slightly more polished, leading my fingers to slip on it while gaming — perhaps the tiniest nitpick I’ve ever had with a phone. The wide camera bump on the back of the Pixel 11 Pro rises up enough to make for a decent finger hold, though unavoidably touching the bump’s metal rim and glass becomes a problem when the handset heats up during high-graphics gaming (more on that later). 

The dual speakers at the top and bottom of the device pump out admirable sound. Like a lot of phones, the speaker on the bottom edge of the phone can be easily covered by a finger when holding the handset sideways to play games, which cuts off half the audio — unfortunate, but not uncommon. 

What is extremely rare in gaming are the sound issues I ran into while playing the action RPG Diablo Immortal, in which the audio occasionally switched into an echoing, garbled mess. I’d never experienced this before.

Most games have touchscreen controls in the form of parts of the screen converted to digital buttons, which are suitable, if clunky, necessities when playing on an all-glass display. The Pixel 11 Pro had suitably responsive touch controls, and the only trouble was with my own fat thumbs incorrectly pressing one part of the display instead of another. A physical wrap-around controller is a big upgrade for most games, and I relished using my Backbone One to play Dead Cells and others that rely on fast responses with a range of options to dodge or attack.

Unlike some other premium Android phones, the Pixel 11 Pro has magnets embedded in its rear cover (playfully called Pixelsnap) that makes it compatible with a lot of accessories, including wireless chargers. I was able to snap on an official Apple MagSafe charger and play while juicing it back up, which was convenient — and helpful. The phone’s 4,850-mAh battery lasted awhile through gaming, but its wired charging maxes out at 30 watts, which is slower than other phones, but I worry about the heat buildup if it were any faster. Its Qi2.2-supporting wireless charging tops out at 25 watts. Being able to top up in the middle of a play session was nice, even if it doesn’t match the faster 45-watt ability of a phone such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus or even the 60-watt charging of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. 

The Pixel 11 Pro is truly plug-and-play with the Backbone One after the Backbone app is installed — slide it in, pull it out and the game continues either way.David Lumb/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro’s gaming problems are in the present Tensor

While the Pixel series’ Tensor chips power superior AI features such as Magic Eraser and live translation, they’ve been underpowered compared to other silicon in benchmark testing, with Pixel phones routinely coming in lower than devices running Snapdragon chips such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 series. Silicon makes a huge difference in graphically intensive tasks, like gaming. 

It stands to reason that the Pixel 11 Pro’s Tensor G6 chip is what keeps it from mustering the higher-tier graphics capabilities that other premium phones achieve. When I loaded up Diablo Immortal, the game defaulted to the lowest graphical setting possible, and even just ratcheting that up to medium with a faster framerate, a pop-up warned me that I was risking overheating and battery drain. 

Typical play, even with higher graphics settings, got the phone warm but not toasty, only reaching dangerous levels of heat when I had it plugged in to recharge and was downloading more game content. The camera block on the back of the phone became uncomfortable to touch with its metal rim and glass atop the cameras. Most games didn’t do this, and it was only in specific circumstances that the heat hit concerning levels, but it still leads me to conclude that the phone’s heat management isn’t quite as good as other premium phones during graphically heavy tasks.

It’s worth mentioning that, with heat management concerns, I removed Google’s official case off the phone to ensure heat could escape off the back and sides. This made the warm metal on the sides of the phone less comfortable to hold, but hopefully would keep it from cooking within the case.

Supposedly, this is Genshin Impact. Things still happened on-screen, but I couldn’t see what was going on.David Lumb/CNET

Then there’s the field of pink. I loaded up Genshin Impact, an older Hoyoverse game that’s presumably more optimized than more recently released titles such as Wuthering Waves. Yet when I booted up Genshin (after downloading the aforementioned 55GB of content), I loaded into the game’s world to find it awash in pink, a layer of obfuscating color that made it impossible to tell what was going on. Clearly, it was a graphical glitch, but one I reproduced over and over. Perhaps this will be ironed out in a patch, but I’ve never had a major mobile game become unplayable just when dropping in.

Combined with the odd audio issues on Diablo Immortal (again, something that hasn’t happened when loading the game on other phones), I’m unsure whether this is just post-launch glitching that’ll be fixed in immediate patches or a deeper issue with the phone’s hardware. It’s bothersome for sure, though thankfully the only bizarre issues I ran into across the half-dozen games I played.

Overall, the Pixel 11 Pro remains a good gaming phone for its fantastic display, which also shines when you’re taking photos and watching films and TV shows. Other concerns keep it from being a top recommendation for playing games, but if it’s a secondary or tertiary priority above photography and AI, the Pixel 11 Pro would serve you well — and hopefully those glitches won’t affect the games you want to play.

Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. title: NASA Astronaut Christina Koch’s Secret Trick to Decompress After Artemis II
snippet: The Artemis II astronaut told CNET how she adjusts to life back on Earth. She also spoke about AI, engineering and support for STEM students.
fullText:
How do you recover from 10 days of traveling through outer space and around the moon? If you’re astronaut Christina Koch, you disconnect from being online and just journal.

“I spent that first week journaling about the mission without looking at any photos from the mission,” Koch told CNET on Monday during a visit to her alma mater, North Carolina State University, where an engineering building was being named after her. “I knew that, one day, the photos might define my memories, but initially, it was important to remember things as they were [with] fresh memories.”

Koch’s latest mission was NASA’s Artemis II, which sent her, commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover and Canadian mission specialist Jeremy Hansen on a 10-day voyage in early April beyond the far side of the moon and back, becoming the first astronauts to go that distance in more than 50 years.

The NASA astronaut said she really “kept the blinders on” for the first two weeks. “The biggest fear I had when I landed was that I would forget it all so quickly.”

“The process of coming home is such an important one, whether you’ve done 328 days or nine days,” Koch said. She compared it to a kind of military deployment. “Reentering to Earth is a process, physical and mental. You’re coming back and, in some cases, coming into a routine [that] has gone ahead without you.”

Koch said she also came home to “quite a few” text messages, all congratulatory. But any emails she got from April 1 to April 10 are still unread; “I think people understand why,” she said with a laugh.

After a few weeks, Koch did look at the photos, and by then, the snaps were already world-famous. The photos the Artemis II team took — on off-the-shelf iPhones and Nikon cameras — came to be how the world experienced Artemis II. More than 18 million people tuned in to watch the crew’s takeoff, and their photos and live TV appearances spread in what became known as “Moon Joy.”

The Artemis II crew — (clockwise from left) Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen, Reid Wiseman, and Victor Glover — take time out for a group hug inside the Orion spacecraft on their way home.

NASA

It was a record-breaking trip. As a whole, the Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for the furthest space travel, traveling over 700,000 miles total. Koch became the first woman to go beyond low Earth orbit; Glover, the first Black person; and Hansen, the first Canadian. 

Koch also holds the record for the longest-ever single spaceflight by a woman from her 2019 stint on the International Space Station, as well as taking part in the first all-female space walk.

One of the most popular photos from the trip is of Koch looking out the Orion spacecraft window, the planet Earth a bright sea of blue and green, her hair braided and iconic curls lit up. The image quickly went viral and became a rallying cry for women interested in science, technology, engineering and math, known as STEM.

Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch looks out the window at Earth.

NASA

Launching an aerospace career

Being a role model isn’t new to Koch, and she considers it a big part of her job now, especially for women and girls.

“I had an experience meeting Sally Ride once,” Koch said, referring to the astronaut who became the first woman in space in 1983. “And in one moment, shaking my hand and her looking into my eyes, I felt like she said so much. She said, ‘Your dreams are valid. I see you. I believe in you.’ And I think that that’s really the job that’s before me, is to just look at people that might be looking after me, to tell them I see them, to tell them that their dream matters.”

A big part of Koch’s hometown visit was highlighting how her education was a launchpad for her aerospace career. Koch is a three-time NCSU grad, earning her Bachelor of Science degrees in electrical engineering and physics and a Master of Science in electrical engineering in the early aughts. 

But it wasn’t just the technical know-how that aided her on the moon mission. Koch said her time working for NCSU’s student newspaper, the Technician, sharpened her photography skills. She recalled learning how every photo should tell a story, something she thinks about “every single time I raise a camera to my eye,” whether the subject is the moon or her friends. 

The young engineers and space enthusiasts who turned out in droves to see Koch this week have more reason than ever to aim for the stars, literally. In many ways, Artemis II kicked off what space enthusiasts hope will be the beginning of a new space age. 

Four Artemis missions are slated to run before the end of the decade; Koch’s team was the first crewed mission. They stress-tested the new Orion spacecraft (which they named “Integrity”) and the Space Launch System that will be foundational to other missions.

North Carolina State University, led by Chancellor Kevin Howell (left), renamed one of its engineering buildings in honor of its alum, Christina Koch. Koch is making the university’s “Wolfpack” hand symbol.Katelyn Chedraoui/Rene Ramos/CNET

Artemis III is the next mission, slated for 2027. It plans to test docking procedures in a low Earth orbit, with NASA commander Randy Bresnik, mission specialists Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and European Space Agency pilot Luca Parmitano. Astronauts won’t step foot on the moon’s surface until Artemis IV in early 2028. 

Koch said she won’t be part of Artemis IV but will cheer on her friends who are. She spoke briefly about the “revolutionary” role of new technology in powering these future explorations and discoveries, specifically generative AI. But she also called out the need to address fundamental issues with the tech.

“I think the biggest challenge with AI is still preserving truth in our world,” Koch said. “If you find the thing that you can do the longest, for the slowest, and still love every day, you’re doing the right thing, no matter what people predict about AI or what it may do or not do.”

The upcoming Artemis missions have already stirred controversy. The all-male Artemis III crew sparked outrage and criticism, particularly after so many women and girls watched Koch break new records with Artemis II. The name “Artemis” even comes from the Greek goddess of hunting. NASA’s 2025 astronaut class also had, for the first time ever, more women than men (six versus four).

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in an X post in June that staffing decisions “tak[e] into account many factors, including the background and expertise of the astronauts,” and that the Artemis III astronauts are “experienced, qualified and deserve to be celebrated.”

Koch remains steadfastly optimistic that there will be room for many young people as we invest in future aerospace missions and science, both at NASA and with “commercial ventures” like Blue Origin and SpaceX. She hopes to be an active role model for students, ones like she was at NCSU and beyond — in her self-described “ripped jeans [and] pink hair” with an “inexplicable love of rockets.”

“For the students in the fourth row who think they’re the only ones in the room who don’t understand, and maybe haven’t been told yet, that’s not a disqualification,” Koch said. “Students of every kind, walking by and into this building, are my ‘why.’ Because it’s not the record for miles you travel away that really matters. It’s the impact you make, we make, right here at home.”

title: Before Splurging on a $500 Vitamix, Consider This Cheaper Model. It Works Just as Well
snippet: If you’re in the market for a Vitamix blender, you don’t need to shell out $500 to get the best model.
fullText:
CNET’s key takeaways 

If you want a great Vitamix blender, you don’t have to spend $500 for a great model. Go for the VX1 instead and save yourself $120.

The VX1 has self-cleaning and pulse modes, a sleek, modern design and doesn’t compromise on power.

The VX1 is a larger blender at 64 ounces. If you don’t need that much blending space, opt for a personal blender, such as the $130 Ninja BlendBoss, instead. 

Certain brands have become synonymous with the products they create. Think Kleenex, Sharpie, Band-Aid and even Vitamix. That notoriety can make it easier for consumers to know which brands to turn to for quality tissues, permanent markers, adhesive bandages or blenders. But choosing becomes tricky when you realize these brands offer multiple versions of their most popular products. So which model should you buy?

In the case of Vitamix, when testing the VX1 and 5200, two of its most popular blenders, for CNET’s best blenders list, I learned that more expensive doesn’t always mean better. Here’s why. 

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Blenders: Picks for Smoothies, Dips, Soup and More					

							

		

My experience with the Vitamix VX1

Launched as a replacement for the discontinued and beloved Explorian, the VX1 is now one of Vitamix’s most affordable blenders at $380. It’s also CNET’s pick for the best overall blender, since it excelled during our hands-on testing.

Vitamix VX1 vs. 5200 

Both the 5200 and VX1 have a 64-ounce capacity, cord storage underneath and 10 speeds, but neither is dishwasher-safe. However, the VX1 has a few extra features, including a pulse mode, a self-cleaning program and 0.2 more horsepower. It also has a slightly smaller footprint than the 5200. 

The VX1 (right) measures 9.5×7.8×19.6 inches, compared to the 5200’s 20.5×8.75×7.25 inches.Anna Gragert/CNET

During testing, the 1440-watt VX1 outperformed 10 other models at blending raw almonds into almond butter, taking only 1 minute and 13 seconds. It also excelled at turning chickpeas into hummus in less than a minute. 

As for the 1380-watt 5200, it took 1 minute and 51 seconds to blend almond butter and 1 minute and 41 seconds to blend hummus. It also took 12 seconds longer than the VX1 to blend a green smoothie.

Where the 5200 impressed

Although I preferred the VX1’s operation, the 5200 still performed well in two specific tests: blending cubed ice and butternut squash soup. It blended the former in 24 seconds to create snow-like ice, leaving just two medium cubes, while the VX1 took 26 seconds and left several large cubes. When blending the soup, the 5200 required only 12 seconds, which was five seconds less than the VX1. 

The 5200 was also a smidge quieter than the VX1 when mixing a green smoothie on high speed, with a max of 93 A-weighted decibels. The VX1 was 95.1 dBA on high. Despite these wins, I don’t think the 5200 justifies such a steep price increase.

While it doesn’t have a pulse mode, the 5200 does have a “high” speed switch, which is nice if you often blend challenging ingredients that require more power and don’t want to fiddle with a speed dial. 

I prefer the more modern look of the VX1.Anna Gragert/CNET

The one I’d keep on my countertop

Numbers aside, I prefer the VX1 over the 5200 in terms of design. It has a more modern look and is visually less angular and bulky. I also like that there are three different ways to safely stop blending: an on/off switch under the base, a start/pause switch on its front and a standby mode on the speed dial.

3.5 feet of cord storage. Not too shabby. Anna Gragert/CNET

Vitamix’s 5200 costs $500, $120 more than the $380 VX1. While both models have a limited warranty, you get seven years with the 5200, two years more than the VX1’s five-year warranty.

title: Robotics startup Generalist reaches $3B valuation, sources say
snippet: The $200 million extension comes just months after the physical AI startup reached a $2 billion valuation.
fullText:
Generalist, a robotics startup, is now valued at $3 billion after raising additional capital led by 8VC, according to two people with knowledge of the funding. 

The fresh capital totals nearly $200 million according to a regulatory filing. That additional capital is an extension of a $400 million Series B led by Radical Ventures that the company announced in June at a $2 billion valuation, the people said. The new capital brings the round’s total funding to $600 million.

Generalist and 8VC didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Generalist was founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind researchers Pete Florence and Andy Zeng, along with former Boston Dynamics engineer Andrew Barry. It received early backing from 8VC and Radical Ventures as well as Nvidia, Union Square Ventures, Bezos Expeditions, and AI researcher Fei-Fei Li.

Until recently, the startup operated quietly and with little publicity. 

Generalist is developing an AI foundation model that can work with various robots. It claims its newly released Gen 1.5 model enables robots to master new tasks from video demonstrations as short as 3 to 12 seconds long.

The startup is working with a handful of customers, using their feedback to tailor the model for specific use cases, according to one source.

Generalist isn’t alone in its pursuit of building a brain for a broad range of robots. Other competitors include Physical Intelligence, which is reportedly valued at $11 billion, and SoftBank-backed Skild AI, valued at $14 billion, as well as Genesis AI, which was in talks as of last month to raise capital at a $3 billion valuation.

The funding surge reflects a bet from some investors that robotics may soon reach its own “ChatGPT moment,” meaning that robots will be able to perform general tasks without being explicitly trained for each one. However, because robots cannot be trained on the entirety of the internet’s data the way LLMs can, some VCs warn that a truly general robotics model may still be years away.

title: Garmin’s Fenix 9 Pro Goes All In on Titanium and Off-Grid Connectivity
snippet: A stronger build, more storage, and a battery life that just won’t quit. Here’s what a $1,000-plus sports watch will get you.
fullText:
Garmin’s high-end, all-out sports watch just stepped it up. The company unveiled the Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro, along with a solar-powered version of the Pro. The latter gets the first titanium case on a Fenix, pushing Garmin’s flagship even further into luxury sports watch territory.

The Fenix 9 also gets more memory and storage, better offline maps, new training tools and LTE, while the smaller 43mm Pro model gets satellite connectivity. And despite brighter displays and more horsepower, Garmin is still promising the kind of weeks-long battery life that’s become one of the Fenix’s biggest selling points.

Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro pricing and availability

The Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro are available to order starting Aug. 28. The Fenix 9 starts at $1,000, while the Fenix 9 Pro starts at $1,100, both with AMOLED displays. There’s also a solar-powered Fenix 9 Pro in 47mm and 51mm sizes, starting at $1,200.

The LTE versions of the Pro with satellite connectivity require an active subscription to inReach, Garmin’s satellite connectivity service. Its entry-level plan costs $8 a month and includes a 30-day free trial, but emergency SOS messaging remains free for up to 12 months after the trial ends. Other satellite messages may incur additional per-use charges depending on the plan.

Garmin

A brighter screen and a titanium makeover

The Fenix 9 doesn’t look dramatically different from its predecessor, but there are some important hardware upgrades, particularly to the Pro line. Both models get a brighter AMOLED display that tops out at 3,000 nits (twice as bright as the Fenix 8), and a sapphire lens for better scratch resistance. 

The Pro has also traded in its polymer-based case for Garmin’s first titanium watch case, which the company says makes it thinner and lighter without sacrificing durability or screen real estate.

The 51mm Fenix 9 Pro now has a 1.5-inch AMOLED display that’s 15% larger than the Fenix 8’s while keeping the same dimensions. The Pro also adds a new green flashlight – joining the existing white and red options – to help with night vision. They all come in 43mm, 47mm and 51mm sizing options, while the solar version (which swaps the AMOLED display for a lower-power MIP display) comes in 47mm and 51mm.

Notably absent this year is the 4,500-nit MicroLED display Garmin introduced on the Fenix 8 Pro. At the time, it was the brightest screen of any sports watch (the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 has since dethroned it), but it also pushed the price to $2,000 and dropped smartwatch battery life to around 10 days.

Garmin

Battery life is still the Fenix superpower

Despite the brighter displays, Garmin hasn’t sacrificed the monster battery life that helps distinguish the Fenix from most mainstream smartwatches.

The largest 51mm Fenix 9 gets up to 29 days in smartwatch mode (raise to wake), while the 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED stretches that to 31 days, per Garmin’s claims. The 51mm solar model is rated for up to 30 days without help from the sun or as much as 57 days with enough solar exposure. Garmin bases that latter claim on three hours per day outside in bright sun.

Those aren’t huge gains over the previous generation, but Garmin isn’t exactly starting from a weak position and it’s now operating with a brighter screen. Having a battery measured in weeks rather than hours becomes particularly valuable when paired with the Pro’s off-grid emergency features. 

And satellite SOS now comes in a smaller package.

Garmin debuted LTE and satellite connectivity on the Fenix 8 Pro last year, but the feature was limited to its larger 47mm and 51mm sizes. The Fenix 9 Pro extends that option across to the 43mm model, meaning people with smaller wrists (like me) no longer have to sacrifice comfort for access to Garmin’s safety features.

You can send text or voice messages, share your location and trigger an SOS even when you’re off the grid without your phone in tow (or running on empty). In an emergency, the SOS connects you with Garmin Response, the company’s coordination center. It’s staffed 24/7, and it can communicate with you, contact local rescue services and keep designated family members informed. You can even get weather forecasts through satellite. 

The caveat is that the satellite features require an unobstructed view of the sky and won’t work if you’re below the tree line. 

And when you’re back in LTE range, you can also make and receive calls, send voice messages and share LiveTrack information. Garmin is adding Garmin Locate, which lets loved ones request your location through Garmin Messenger.

More power, storage and faster maps

Garmin also beefed up the hardware behind its maps. The Fenix 9 gets 50% more RAM than the Fenix 8, along with a more powerful map engine that Garmin says makes panning up to 30% faster.

Storage doubles to 64GB, giving you room for twice as many downloadable maps compared with the Fenix 8 and up to 7,000 songs for offline listening.

Built-in routable maps also get a new perspective view to give you a better sense of what’s coming by zooming in or out of your route.

New stamina, rowing and rucking tools

Garmin is adding new tools called Stamina Zones and Stamina Curve to its long list of training features which can show how your endurance changes over time and can help you pace yourself during activities.

Indoor rowing also gets more detailed, with VO2 max metrics and a power curve when paired with a compatible power-meter-equipped rowing machine.

Rucking (hiking with added weight) gets an upgrade too. Whether it’s a weighted vest, a loaded pack or, in my case, a small child on your back, you can now change your pack weight during an activity, follow workouts directly from the watch and set targets such as calories burned with up to 100 kilograms (220 pounds) of additional weight.

Garmin is also launching a new feature called Garmin Epic, which groups multiple activities into one shareable story via its Garmin Connect app. A multiday backpacking trip, cycling tour or even a months-long training plan can be bundled together with health and performance data and photos to share (or boast) on your feed.

Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro: Bottom line

Garmin has refined the things that make the Fenix stand out: never-ending battery life, serious navigation tools and a potential lifeline for people venturing off the grid. Whether that’s worth four figures will come down to how much you value that extra endurance and independence.

At $1,000 and up, it’s still a serious splurge, especially when there are so many other more affordable and capable options in Garmin’s line-up. And if prices on the Fenix 8 Pro start to drop, it could become the better deal for people who still want weeks of battery life and satellite connectivity but don’t need the brighter screen, titanium case, faster maps or 43mm option.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Vanessa Hand Orellana

She joined the brand first as an on-camera reporter for CNET's Spanish-language site, then moved on to the English side to host and produce some of CNET's videos and YouTube series. When she's not testing out the latest health tech, you can catch her on a hike or trail run with her family.

title: OpenAI loses a top data center exec as stream of high-profile departures continues
snippet: In a statement to TechCrunch about Malone's departure, OpenAI said it had "recently reorganized" its "infrastructure organization to support the scale and pace of our work."
fullText:
OpenAI has lost yet another executive, and the timing of this one stands out in particular given this individual oversaw the execution of the company’s data center strategy.

Chris Malone, OpenAI’s former head of data centers, left the company last week, the Wall Street Journal has reported. Malone, who spent nearly five years at Meta and more than a decade at Google before that, joined OpenAI in March of last year, making his tenure relatively short.

Malone joined the company not long after the launch of the Stargate Project, a $500 million data center initiative championed by the Trump administration that has sought to develop data centers in the U.S. OpenAI, along with Oracle, Nvidia, SoftBank, and Microsoft, is considered a key partner in the effort.

Why is Malone leaving? It isn’t entirely clear. With the AI infrastructure buildout frenzy in full swing across the industry, data center strategy has become one of the most closely watched roles at any AI lab, which makes turnover in that seat especially surprising.

In a statement to TechCrunch about Malone’s departure, OpenAI said it had “recently reorganized” its “infrastructure organization to support the scale and pace of our work.” It added: “We have a strong, deeply experienced data center team in place, with clear leadership and the technical expertise to execute our plans.”

As part of that reorganization, per the WSJ, Malone stopped reporting directly to OpenAI president Greg Brockman and began reporting to OpenAI vice president Sachin Katti, who took over leadership of the group.

Several other executives are said to be currently overseeing OpenAI’s data center strategy, including Uday Ruddarraju, who leads the company’s data center team; Brent Mayo, who leads the data center build and delivery program; and Spas Lazarov, a veteran of the data center and energy industries, who leads all data center engineering.

Whatever the reason for Malone’s departure, he isn’t alone. His exit adds to a string of more than a dozen executive departures this year. Business Insider recently tallied the total 2026 departure count at 13, with several leaving in just the last month. And these aren’t junior employees walking out the door — they’re some of the company’s most senior seats.

Two weeks ago, the company replaced its chief revenue officer, Denise Dresser, after Dresser had only been with the company for some eight months. Two days prior to Dresser’s announced departure, the company also lost Brad Lightcap, one of its longest-serving executives, who spent years as the company’s chief operating officer. Lightcap said he would be “starting something new” but hasn’t given details on what that new project entails.

Approximately a month before those departures, the company also lost Fidji Simo, the company’s de facto second-in-command (Simo served as product and business chief and reported directly to CEO Sam Altman). She stepped down from her position to recover from a “chronic illness.” Simo remains with the company in an advisory role.

OpenAI’s safety and ethics teams have seen notable departures, too. In July, the company lost its “head of ethics,” Chloé Bakalar, and, last week, it was reported that OpenAI had disbanded its preparedness team, a unit dedicated to assessing whether the company’s AI models could result in catastrophic risks.

Other team leaders, like Bill Peebles, the former head of OpenAI’s now defunct AI image generator Sora, have left because their projects were shut down. In April, the company also lost its chief marketing officer, Kate Rouch, who — like Simo — reportedly left for health reasons.

The company’s remaining talent has tried hard to minimize the significance of the ongoing talent flight, with co-founder Greg Brockman recently lamenting that the intense “spotlight” on his company means that “every departure gets scrutinized in a way that it doesn’t otherwise.”

But the churn has naturally raised questions, especially as it preps for an IPO. OpenAI’s public listing, originally expected this year, is now reportedly pushed to 2027, and the company is undergoing a kind of reputational vetting that comes with any looming listing. Concerns have arisen that the company may be overvalued and that its profitability doesn’t match the gargantuan investments being made in the lab.

Suffice it to say, the flood of outgoing executives certainly hasn’t quieted those doubts.

title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa

fullText:
In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers — which, according to The Associated Press, would be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

More than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term, it’s become clear that the only way Trump can get the deportation numbers he wants is by stripping legal immigrants of status. Beyond having ICE arrest, detain, and deport immigrants, the administration is pressuring noncitizens to “self-deport,” in some cases imposing civil fines on them and threatening to seize their assets. It’s creating legal hurdles not only for new legal immigrants but for those already in the country, and in the process, likely hurting businesses and social services nationwide.

H-1B visas are often seen as synonymous with Big Tech, in no small part because Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are the three biggest employers of H-1B workers. A federal judge struck down Trump’s previous attempt to raise the cost of these high-skilled employment visas in June, but not until over 70 employers paid the $100,000 fee. Now Trump wants to raise the cost to $103,265. Advocates and business leaders are worried Trump will soon come after the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which DHS hinted may soon carry a $100,000 fee of its own. OPT lets international students work in their field of study for 12 months, with extensions of up to 24 months for some STEM students and additional extensions for holders of certain graduate degrees.

“Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board.”

“This is clearly unlawful,” said Todd Schulte, the president of FWD.us, an immigration reform organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and other tech executives in 2013. “We don’t have to guess what this is for. This is to get rid of the OPT and H-1B program, which will have upstream and downstream devastating consequences: companies will be started elsewhere, people will be hired elsewhere.”

This won’t just hurt the tech industry. The previous fee hike exacerbated labor shortages at rural hospitals across the country and Alaska public schools, both of which have increasingly turned to high-skilled immigrant workers in the wake of local population decline. If the $100,000 fee was an inconvenience for Amazon and Meta, it was utterly catastrophic for rural communities already having trouble attracting qualified candidates.

Foreign workers aren’t the only legal immigrants Trump is targeting. According to the AP, which broke the news, the State Department will rescind up to 200,000 business and travel visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to people who applied for asylum after arriving in the US. Beyond limiting their ability to travel outside the country, this move won’t change much for asylum seekers who came to the US on nonimmigrant visas — at least not for now. But Schulte said the visa revocations are part of Trump’s efforts to gut the humanitarian immigration system. “Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board,” he said. “It’s an all-of-government approach.”

The administration is framing this change as a way of closing a loophole in the asylum system: people coming to the country on nonimmigrant visas, ostensibly for work or pleasure, only to ask for asylum upon setting foot in the country.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the AP.

But the people who applied for asylum this way didn’t break any laws. In fact, a person needs to be present on US soil to apply for asylum; there’s no way to apply from outside the country. And Trump has closed most other avenues for humanitarian migration. There’s an effective “asylum ban” in place at the US-Mexico border. Refugee admissions have dropped to record lows, and the administration is now prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans and denying almost everyone else.

In his second term, Trump has shown that the only immigrants he wants are those who look a certain way — or who can pay a small fortune for the privilege of working in America.

title: X sends cease-and-desist to open source project Nitter over alleged scraping
snippet: X has sent cease-and-desist letters to Nitter, the open source project behind privacy-friendly X front ends, demanding its instances and code repository be taken down over alleged scraping.
fullText:
Nitter, an open source project that allowed people to read X posts without logging into or even opening the X app, has received cease-and-desist letters from X demanding that it shut down. The news was shared via a brief message posted to the project’s website, and follows X’s earlier attempts to knock Nitter offline by technical means. 

The service also powers a number of other sites, including XCancel, that allow people to view X posts directly.

This isn’t X’s first attempt to shut down Nitter. In 2024, Nitter’s flagship instance, Nitter.net, went dark temporarily after X rolled out new API restrictions. Nitter worked by fetching public X posts and then stripping out the ads, tracking cookies, and JavaScript, giving people a clean, clutter-free way to read posts without an account or the app.

After that crackdown, those who wanted to host a Nitter instance had to connect it to a real X account, according to the project’s GitHub page. Despite the restrictions, development picked back up and Nitter instances came back online.

This time, X is working to shut down Nitter and its instances via legal means. Nitter’s website states that the Nitter.net project is offline while its creator seeks legal advice after receiving a cease-and-desist letter. That creator, a developer who goes by the handle Zedeus, told TechCrunch by email that other Nitter instances received similar letters.

On Nitter’s website, the message currently reads:

On 24 August 2026 cease and desist letters have been sent by X Corp. demanding a permanent takedown of Nitter instances and the project’s repository.

nitter.net is offline and development has stopped for the time being. I’m seeking legal advice and won’t be commenting further on the specifics for now.

Thank you to everyone who used, hosted, packaged, donated and contributed to Nitter over the past seven years.

The letter from X, which TechCrunch has viewed, accuses Nitter of an “unlawful use and circumvention of X’s Application Programming Interface (API) and associated data,” through its service, saying that X has evidence that Nitter scraped X data and accessed X accounts and session tokens in violation of X’s rules.

Lawyers for X said the actions are in violation of “various state and federal laws, including, but not limited to, the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act (§ 143.001 and § 33.02) and the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 1114, 1125).” The letter gave Nitter until 5 p.m. EST on August 25 to shut down.

X is hardly alone in policing alleged scrapers. Meta has taken numerous scrapers to court, and most larger social networks today restrict the use of third-party readers, forcing users to log in and access the site’s content through the official app, where they can be tracked and shown personalized ads.

It’s an unfortunate development for lurkers, given that Nitter and its instances offered a handy way to keep up with certain people’s posts on X without an account. Now those people will either need to give up that access or, as X likely hopes, create an account and log in.

Remastered will be a free upgrade for players who own the base game on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X / S. With the launch of Remastered, The Witcher 3 will also be coming to the Nintendo Switch 2.

CDPR is set to launch a brand new Witcher 3 expansion, titled Songs of the Past, in 2027, and it’s aiming to release its next mainline Witcher game, The Witcher 4, in 2028.

title: Stability AI, maker of image generator Stable Diffusion, raises $76 million in fresh funding
snippet: The company's new fundraising total now stands at $232 million.
fullText:
Stability AI, the startup behind AI image generation model Stable Diffusion, has raised $76 million in Series B funding. The new haul brings the company’s fundraising total to $232 million.

The company announced the round Tuesday, saying the new capital comes partly from a number of prominent entertainment industry organizations, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music Group, Warner Music Group, and gaming giant Electronic Arts (EA). Two investment firms, AMD Ventures and Pacific Alliance Ventures, also took part.

It’s an unusual roster and a less typical venture round than a lineup of the companies Stability now depends on for content licensing and distribution deals.

Stability AI CEO Prem Akkaraju, who joined the company in 2024, called the funding “an affirmation of our vision where generative AI empowers every producer, musician, and storyteller.”

The company says it plans to use the money from its latest funding round to continue building out its “creative production” product suite while also expanding its professional services arm. Currently, Stability offers a variety of AI models that are designed for the purposes of AI music, video, and image generation.

Stability, founded in 2019, has spent the past year signing deals to weave generative AI into entertainment companies’ creative workflows. It struck partnerships with Universal Music and EA last October and with Warner Music last November, each giving those companies a hand in co-developing Stability’s AI tools rather than just licensing the output..

Stability has also had a mostly winning stretch in court. The company largely prevailed in a copyright lawsuit brought by Getty Images in the United Kingdom, which had accused the company of infringing upon IP rights by using the company’s images in the training of its image generation model. A judge ruled largely in Stability’s favor in that case, but a similar lawsuit from Getty in the U.S. is still working its way through the courts.

Stability was also sued in 2023 by the company’s co-founder, Cyrus Hodes, who claimed that he was tricked by the other co-founder, Emad Mostaque, into selling his share in the company.

title: SpaceX will build a second, $100B ‘Starbase’ spaceport in Louisiana
snippet: The company says it will start construction in 2027 and that a Starship rocket could take flight as soon as 2029.
fullText:
SpaceX has announced it will build a second spaceport for future launches of its Starship mega-rocket at a former Exxon property in Louisiana, ending what the company says was a seven-year search for a suitable location.

The new launch site will sit along the Gulf Coast in Vermilion Parish, west of New Orleans and roughly 10 hours from the company’s existing Starbase complex in South Texas. SpaceX says it is investing $100 billion, with construction starting in 2027. SpaceX claims the first Starship launch will take place in 2029. 

Louisiana Economic Development (LED), the state agency that oversees business development, offers a slightly more conservative timeline. It says construction will start by the end of 2027 with “initial operations expected to come online in 2030.”

Before any of that happens, SpaceX is still trying to prove that it can fly Starship into low-Earth orbit and make the rocket reusable, like its existing Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets. SpaceX has performed 13 test flights of Starship since 2023, and while the company has ticked off a lot of development boxes, it still has a lot of work to do.

An upcoming 14th test flight could see SpaceX send Starship’s upper stage to orbit for the first time. But the company has yet to return both the booster and the upper stage to the launch pad on a single flight, a basic necessity if Starship is to become truly reusable. Even then, SpaceX must show that it can bring the vehicle back and refurbish it quickly enough to reach its own aggressive goal of sending up multiple Starships per week.

That isn’t stopping SpaceX from betting almost everything on Starship. This past week, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said he will retire the Falcon rockets once Starship is flying multiple times per week. His comments confirmed earlier reporting from Bloomberg News that the company was already telling prospective customers about the impending end of the Falcon program.

SpaceX has spent more than $8 billion developing Starship, according to filings submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The rocket — which is the largest and most powerful ever built — is crucial to maintaining and growing the only profitable part of SpaceX’s business, its Starlink satellite internet service. SpaceX is also planning to build an entire network of satellites dedicated to AI processing, which it needs Starship to launch.

The new Starbase site will create 3,000 direct new jobs over 10 years, with an average annual salary of $92,600, according to LED. More than 30,000 construction jobs are expected at the peak of the buildout.

It’s not immediately clear if SpaceX intends to create a company town around the new Starbase site, like the one it has architected in Texas. The Texas municipality, once called Boca Chica and renamed Starbase, has its own ZIP code and volunteer fire station, and is building its own police force and community library. It is run by a local government filled with SpaceX employees (or family members of SpaceX employees).

SpaceX did say in its announcement that it wants to make the new site a “self-sustaining spaceport” with “propellant production, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities, vehicle processing facilities, and an airport.”

As a mix of a launch complex and active construction zone, the Starbase site in Texas has also seen extremely high injury rates over the last decade. It’s the most dangerous site SpaceX operates and the company has reported hundreds of injuries to the Occupational Health and Safety Administration. In May, a construction worker employed by a third-party contractor fell to his death at Starbase.

“We are very excited to be in this position to receive one of the best opportunities of a lifetime which will bring not only a variety of jobs to our Parish but will offer opportunities to our grandchildren allowing them to stay home for employment,” Vermilion Parish Police Jury President Chad Vallo said in a statement. 

SpaceX, which has for years faced criticism for — and fought legal battles over — how it treats the local ecosystem around its Texas site, has “already engaged the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries, Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority and other appropriate state agencies to proactively address potential impacts to wildlife, fisheries and their supporting habitats,” according to LED. 

The company also says it is “partnering with state and federal agencies to expand Louisiana’s Coastal Master Plan and Coastal Wetlands Planning, Protection and Restoration Act projects, including Gulf shoreline protection breakwaters designed to reduce wave energy” and reduce shoreline erosion in the area.

title: Your vote matters! Decide which Audience Choice sessions will make it to TechCrunch Founder Summit
snippet: Each year, we get a huge influx of applicants to speak at TechCrunch’s events, and this year’s Founder Summit in Boston on November 4 will be no different!
fullText:
Each year, we get a huge influx of applicants to speak at TechCrunch’s events, and this year’s Founder Summit in Boston on November 4 will be no different! We want to thank everyone who applied to take part in our programming and to help share their expertise with the startup community.

After careful review, we have 11 finalists who are vying for four slots within this year’s event agenda, and each one showcases the kind of practical, essential insights that can only be delivered by those who have built, iterated, and succeeded.

You can vote via this link to weigh in on which sessions ultimately make the cut. Submissions will close on September 4. If you’re voting and haven’t already gotten your Founder Summit tickets this year, what are you waiting for?

On November 4 in Boston, you’ll get the chance to learn directly from the experts in intimate, exclusive sessions that can put you ahead of the competition or set you up to play a pivotal role in developing the next era of innovators. We still have discounts running on tickets that can save you up to $100 right here!

With that said, let’s dive into our Disrupt Audience Choice nominees, and remember: The voting takes place via this form, so take a look and then submit your vote!

How to Build Events Strategy Before You Can Afford a Full-Time Events Team 

Alexandra Ames: Founder and Chief Event Strategist, Blueprint Lab 

Early-stage founders approach events one of two ways: say yes to every opportunity, or avoid them entirely because the ROI feels impossible to justify. Neither is smart. Events can build your audience and credibility before product-market fit but only if you’re strategic about which ones deserve your time and budget. We’ll discuss how to think strategically when resources are tight, including how to maximize ROI from founder events like this one. You’ll leave with frameworks for prioritizing stage-appropriate event investments, tactics for proving value without complex tools, and clarity on when events make sense and when they don’t.

How to Build a “Made in the USA” Hardware Company and Actually Scale It 

Hannan Happi: CEO and Co-Founder, Exowatt 

Domestic manufacturing is back in the spotlight, but building hardware in the U.S. is still widely seen as too expensive to scale. This session explores how founders can design hardware companies that make “Made in the USA” economically viable from day one. We’ll break down supply chain strategy, cost structure, factory partnerships, and how policy tailwinds like the IRA and CHIPS Act change the equation. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for evaluating when domestic manufacturing can become a competitive advantage — not just a branding decision.

Build Something We Don’t Have a Word for Yet

Andy Tang: Partner, Draper Associates 

Pitches that change industries rarely fit existing categories — and most investors will pass on them for exactly that reason. This talk explores why the most fundable startups are often the hardest ones to describe, and what that means for how you build and position yours. Founders will leave with a clearer sense of the difference between a market insight and a market-creating idea, and what it actually takes to get a pattern-matching investor to bet on something genuinely new — before the rest of the world has a name for it.

GraphRAG in Action: Stop Hallucinations with Knowledge Graphs

Shishir Tewari: Head of Enterprise Data Engineering, Procore Technologies 

Are messy data sources causing your LLMs to hallucinate? Relational databases struggle to bridge the semantic gap for AI. Learn to build a production-ready GraphRAG pipeline that turns chaotic data into actionable insights. Actionable takeaways: Build an offline pipeline to resolve disjointed datasets into “golden records.” Translate flat records into an interconnected Neo4j knowledge graph. Deploy a secure, local LLM (Ollama) to translate natural language into validated Cypher queries. Give your AI the foundational data structure it needs!

The Enterprise AI Playbook: How to Close L’Oreal and Vodafone Before You Raise a Series A 

Merve Kitapci: Managing Partner and CGO, ADIN.AI 

Most founders chase product-market fit before landing enterprise clients. We did the opposite. This roundtable covers the exact motion for closing global enterprise accounts at pre-Series A: how to structure the first conversation with a Fortune 500 CMO; why agency partnerships accelerate enterprise sales; how to price with no brand recognition; and what zero organic churn means for your fundraising story. Attendees leave with a repeatable enterprise sales framework, an early-stage AI pricing model, and the three things that make a CMO say yes before legal sees the contract.

Lessons from 20 Years of Bootstrapping an Open Source Business to $50M+

Peter Farkas: CEO, Percona 

Building a successful open source company without venture capital is rare — scaling it past $50 million in revenue is even rarer. This talk shares two decades of lessons from growing a commercial open source business from zero to global scale. We’ll cover product-market fit, monetizing open source while keeping the core free, building distributed teams before remote work was mainstream, and creating a repeatable go-to-market engine without outside funding. We’ll also discuss failures, hard lessons, and how to compete against well-funded alternatives while staying bootstrapped. Attendees will leave with practical strategies for scaling sustainably.

Small but Mighty: How AI Lets Lean Teams Outship the Giants

Linden Tibbets: CEO and Co-Founder, IFTTT 

The playbook has flipped, and we have lived it firsthand. A five-person team can now outbuild, outship, and outmaneuver companies with 500 engineers. This roundtable gets into the tactical reality of running a lean, AI-powered team: which tools are actually worth your time, how to build workflows that compound instead of bloat, and where most teams are burning cycles on AI that goes nowhere. Walk away knowing how to audit your current stack for speed gaps, which AI-driven growth motions are converting right now, and how to use your small size as an advantage, not an excuse.

The Demo Trap: Why Impressive AI Doesn’t Always Build Real Companies

Jeff Mahler: Co-Founder and CTO, Ambi Robotics 

In today’s AI boom, impressive demos can generate headlines, funding, and early excitement, but they rarely prove a real business by themselves. This session explores the gap between prototype performance and real-world deployment, and why many promising AI startups stall before reaching scale. Founders and investors will learn how to evaluate whether AI systems are truly ready for production, the operational and reliability metrics that matter most, and how to build companies that can move beyond hype to durable, real-world impact.

From CentOS to Rocky Linux: Building Movements That Outlast You 

Gregory Kurtzer: CEO and Founder, CIQ 

Greg Kurtzer helped create CentOS, one of the world’s most widely used operating systems, then founded CIQ and launched Rocky Linux when Red Hat discontinued CentOS. In this session, he shares hard-won lessons from building open source movements and a startup from scratch: why founders must leave ego at the door, then navigate the transition from hiring versatile generalists early, then moving to a team of specialists as you scale. He explains the mistake he almost made by dismissing the value of culture and core values, and what it really takes to build something durable.

The Healthcare AI Companies That Will Actually Matter 

Vikram Chaudhery, PhD: CEO and Founder, Genoa Ventures 

Most AI healthcare demos look incredible and ship nothing. The companies that will matter in 2026 aren’t the ones with the best models. They’re the ones that get decisions to clinicians in an actionable window and change what doctors actually do for the patient in real clinical workflows. This roundtable digs into what separates investable healthcare AI from expensive science fairs, where agentic systems are creating real value beyond copilots, what founders consistently get wrong before their Series A, and the bar that anyone funding, founding, or joining a healthcare AI company should apply.

How Technical AI Founders Get Into YC, a16z Speedrun, and Raise from Top-Tier VCs

George Bandarian: Founder and General Partner, Untapped Ventures 

The best technical founders building in AI and robotics aren’t failing because of their product — they’re failing because they don’t understand what top investors are actually looking for. In this roundtable, early-stage technical founders will work through what YC, a16z speedrun, and top-tier VCs evaluate beyond the deck: founder-market fit signals, why most technical founders need a business counterpart earlier than they think, how to position an autonomous economy company for a lead investor, and what the fundraising process actually looks like before you have traction.

title: Claude Cowork finally remembers what you told the app in chat
snippet: Anthropic is giving Claude a shared memory across chat and Cowork, so users no longer have to repeatedly brief the AI on projects, preferences, and other context.
fullText:
A change to Claude’s memory system will eliminate one of the most annoying things about using agents — the constant need to rebrief the AI on things it already knows. On Tuesday, Anthropic announced it’s merging the memory system used by chat and Claude Cowork, which means that Claude will always remember what it learned in one area, even when you’re engaging with it in another.

Anthropic is also exposing what Claude has retained in its memory, allowing users to read, edit, or delete information on any topic.

Image Credits:Anthropic

The update will improve the experience for Claude’s users as it will allow them to more seamlessly move between the research phase and taking action. 

Before, you may have developed ideas for projects over time while chatting with Claude, but when it came time to actually enact the changes, you’d have to start over by telling Cowork all the details. This was incredibly frustrating. The update makes Claude now feel like one continuous assistant, rather than two separate products under one roof.

Anthropic offers an example of someone needing to draft an update for their manager or an agenda for a conference, where Cowork would already understand the references because of the past conversations about the matter at hand. For instance, it would know the headcount, city, and speakers at the conference, so you wouldn’t have to re-input that information. 

Image Credits:Anthropic

In addition, Claude will now add topics to its memory as you chat, instead of summarizing a conversation when it ends. That makes it easier to move back and forth between chat and Cowork, as the new memories are more quickly updated and shared between the two experiences, even if the chat is ongoing.

Anthropic says that, by default, Claude won’t store personal or sensitive information like your health data, race, ethnicity, religious beliefs, politics, gender identity, and more. However, users can opt to enable these things by toggling on “include sensitive topics in memory” if they prefer. The app will also notify users whenever a sensitive topic is saved in memory.

However, the company says that Claude won’t ever save certain things, like government-issued ID and Social Security numbers, criminal history, immigration status, or other things that violate its acceptable use policy.

The memory feature is enabled by default on Free, Pro, and Max plans across web, desktop, and mobile. On iOS and Android, users will need to update their app to the latest version.

title: Waymo robotaxis are headed to Munich
snippet: Germany's autonomous vehicle regulations have made it a hotspot for autonomous vehicle testing and eventual commercial robotaxi deployment.
fullText:
Waymo said Tuesday it plans to launch a robotaxi service in Munich, months after the Alphabet-owned autonomous vehicle company set up an entity in Germany. 

The company still must weave its way through mapping and testing, as well as clear regulatory hurdles before it can launch commercial operations. 

Waymo will begin, as it has in the other 11 cities where it has commercial robotaxi operations, by first manually driving its vehicles to map the streets of Munich. It will then test its autonomous vehicles with human safety drivers behind the wheel, before removing them. Waymo typically allows its employees, media, and other invited guests to ride in its driverless vehicles at this stage.

The company will eventually open its robotaxis to limited service, and eventually to all riders once it receives the regulatory approval required to operate commercially. Waymo said in a blog post on Tuesday that it is working with Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), state authorities, and local officials, and expects to open commercial ride-hailing to the public toward the end of 2027.

Waymo’s entry into Germany comes more than five years after the country’s lawmakers adopted legislation to allow driverless vehicles on public roads, and in that process making it the first country in the European Union to create a legal framework for Level 4 autonomous driving. Level 4 autonomy is a designation by the Society of Automobile Engineers (SAE) that means the self-driving system handles all the driving, with no expectation of a human taking over, in certain conditions or environments.

This legal framework has made Germany a hotspot for autonomous vehicle testing. Today, several companies, including Mobileye and Volkswagen, hold permits to test their autonomous vehicles in the country, according to the KBA’s latest data. Waymo does not currently have any permits.

However, the vast majority, including U.K. self-driving startup Wayve, and Israel-based Autobrains, hold Level 3 permits. Level 3, or conditional automated driving, is a system that can handle all the driving within specific operating conditions, such as low speeds on highways, but the driver must be able to take over when needed.

Germany isn’t the only overseas hotspot for AV developers. The U.K., especially London, is shaping up as another robotaxi battleground. Waymo has said it plans to launch a commercial service in London in 2026, which will pit it against Wayve and its partner Uber. Chinese tech giant Baidu has also started testing autonomous vehicles in the city as part of its partnership with Lyft and Freenow.

title: Ads have landed in Apple Maps, and they are as bad as expected
snippet: When we ran a poll last month, the overwhelming majority of 9to5Mac readers agreed that Apple should exit the ad business. Ads have now landed in Apple Maps in the US and Canada, and my view is that they are every bit as bad as expected …
fullText:
When we ran a poll last month, the overwhelming majority of 9to5Mac readers agreed that Apple should exit the ad business. 

Ads have now landed in Apple Maps in the US and Canada, and my view is that they are every bit as bad as expected …

Apple warned us back in March that we would begin seeing ads in the company’s Maps app at some point in the summer. We first spotted them ourselves yesterday, and the company confirmed that the rollout began in the last few days. Within a few weeks, everyone in the US and Canada will be seeing them.

Before searching: Suggested Places in the search screen will feature an ad.

After searching: Ads will appear in search results when relevant.

The company says that privacy is a major focus.

The new Maps ads build on Apple’s existing privacy-first approach to advertising. A user’s location and the ads they see and interact with in Maps are not associated with their Apple Account. Personal data stays on the user’s device, is not collected or stored by Apple, and is not shared with advertisers or other third parties.

I’m sure all of that is true, but I still think it’s a terrible look for two reasons.

First, while Apple isn’t doing any kind of tracking in order to deliver personalized ads, almost every other app and website is. Most people are going to assume the iPhone maker is doing the same, and – however unfair the perception might be – that damages the company’s reputation for protecting our privacy.

Second, it simply looks cheap. Ads are a necessary evil in both the app and web publishing ecosystems: they are what keep the lights on when an app or website is free to use. But Apple doesn’t need ad revenue to pay its bills: it already charges a premium price for premium hardware. Ads simply don’t fit with the company’s image.

I think it was John Gruber who likened ads in Apple apps to those awful Intel Inside stickers you got on cheap Windows laptops. Sure, we understand that companies aiming to provide budget laptops need every revenue stream they can find, but we would never have expected Apple to cheapen the look of a MacBook by adding them. Why, then, should we see ads in the stock apps on our Apple devices?

My view very much remains that Apple has no business being in the ad business.
