title: Life360 expands pet tracking with new $8 scannable tags and zoomie alerts
snippet: Life360’s new $7.99 scannable pet tags alert families when a lost pet is found and share its last known location, while new care-tracking features help households keep tabs on feeding, walks, medication, and more.
fullText:
Family location-sharing and safety app Life360 is expanding its pet-tracking capabilities on Tuesday with the launch of a new product line of $7.99 scannable pet tags and other pet-care features that tap into its tracking network technology.

Life360 expanded into pet tech last year with the launch of GPS pet trackers that leverage the lost-item-finding capabilities that the company integrated into its platform after its 2021 acquisition of AirTag rival Tile. With Tile, the company now offers not just location-sharing features for families, but also the ability for members to track other things of importance — like keys, handbags, luggage, and pets.

Since then, families on the service have added more than 8 million pets to their accounts, the company says.

However, the team found that not everyone wants to attach a bulky tracker to their pet’s collar, and not everyone needs access to location-tracking features or other advanced options like geofences and escape alerts.

In many cases, pet owners just want to put their contact information on a pet’s tag, which is what the new scannable pet tags support.

Image Credits:Life360

But there’s a twist. Instead of just providing a pet owner’s phone number when someone scans the QR code printed on the new pet tags, the scan also alerts the family through the Life360 app installed on the family’s smartphones. (The person who found the pet does not need to have the app for this to work.)

This helps in multiple ways — not only does it provide peace of mind to families searching for a lost pet, but it also provides the pet’s location details. That can be useful if the lost pet escapes from the finder’s control and runs off again, as the family will at least have the last known location recorded.

Families can update their contact details through the Life360 pet profile in the app. 

In addition, the company is rolling out several new pet-care features for families, including tools that let families schedule “care logs” to manage and track whether the pet has been fed, walked, given medication, or had its litter cleaned. Everyone in the family can see these care routines, so they will know if the pet needs their attention.

Image Credits:Life360

Another fun feature is “Zoomies Alerts” for GPS trackers, which track the bursts of energy a pet has at particular points during the day or evening. A new Weekly Roundup will recap other routines, like the distance walked or information about who in the family provided the pet with the most care during the week.

Image Credits:Life360

With the new features, the company is also making its pet trackers more affordable. Before, the Pet GPS trackers were only available with the higher-tier Platinum and Gold subscriptions, but now they’re included with the $99-per-year Silver bundles, too.

The new pet tags and GPS trackers are sold on both the company’s website and Amazon in the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.K.

title: Instagram can now create Reels automatically – but Meta doesn’t want to upset creators
snippet: Instagram now has a new iPhone-exclusive feature that can create reels automatically. You just select your video clips and it creates an edit with a single tap. However, Meta is being extremely careful not to upset creators by implying that the app can replace their manual editing skills …
fullText:
Instagram now has a new iPhone-exclusive feature that can create reels automatically. You just select your video clips and it creates an edit with a single tap.

However, Meta is being extremely careful not to upset creators by implying that the app can replace their manual editing skills … 

That caution even extends to the naming of the feature, which is known as First Draft, implying that it only provides a starting point for creative decisions.

Introducing First draft, a new way to create a Reel within the Instagram app. Simply select your clips, and with one tap, it cuts the pauses and trims down your clips, so you have a starting point to build from in seconds. Everything First draft does is reversible, you can adjust or reorder anything before moving on. It handles the early video trimming so you can focus less on technical production, and get to the creative part sooner.

The company shared an example of the process and the result in a Threads post.

There’s even an option to create a first draft edit immediately after filming.

There are 2 ways to access this feature:

1. Open Reels gallery → Select 1+ clips → Tap the “First draft” button at the bottom of your screen → Review edit → Proceed to full editor or publish.

2. Open camera in Instagram → Film your content → Tap the “First draft’ button + Review edit + Proceed to full editor to publish

Some creators are questioning why this is in the main Instagram app and not Edits, and the company has responded that it could make it available in both apps if desired. Right now, the feature is only available in the iPhone app, with the Android version likely to follow.

title: That fake Grand Theft Auto VI demo is actually just malware
snippet: Grand Theft Auto fans, eager for news about one of the most anticipated video games of all time, appear especially vulnerable to this new cyberattack.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

8:48 AM PDT · August 25, 2026

Image Credits:Leon Neal / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

In the long wait for the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, an open-world game about crime, some in the gaming community are being targeted by cybercriminals in the real world.

Fans are still waiting for the game more than a decade after the release of GTA 5, which sold more copies than any game ever, except for Minecraft. Now, after multiple GTA 6 delays and with some fans desperate for any scrap of news, hackers are using the cover as a perfect opportunity to target eager gamers.

Cybercriminals have created fake websites impersonating Rockstar, the developer behind GTA 6. These websites advertise a playable GTA 6 demo — but no legitimate demo exists. Once the unsuspecting gamer clicks the “Play Now” button, they download a file that looks like a game installer, but is actually malware, according to the cybersecurity company Malwarebytes.

The malware is an information stealer that is designed to find and take a victim’s passwords, cookies, and logged-in sessions stored in their web browser. These attacks can in some cases allow hackers to log in as if they were the account holder, even when protected by multi-factor authentication.

After multiple delays, GTA 6 is expected to release on November 19, 2026. On Thursday, Netflix will air an extended look at the game, which could perhaps answer some questions about the legitimacy of various leaks.

A relevant reminder as always: Don’t download stuff if you aren’t sure it comes from a reliable source.

title: 25% of US adults are interested in the iPhone Ultra – but won’t pay for it
snippet: Sometimes a headline is the complete inverse of the real news in the story, and that’s the case with a new survey measuring interest in the upcoming iPhone Ultra. The headline says 75% of US adults aren’t interested in a folding iPhone, while the real surprise is that as many as 25% are. Apple shouldn’t get too excited by the results, however, as willingness to pay was way, way less than the price we’re expecting the company to announce …
fullText:
Sometimes a headline is the complete inverse of the real news in the story, and that’s the case with a new survey measuring interest in the upcoming iPhone Ultra. The headline says 75% of US adults aren’t interested in a folding iPhone, while the real surprise is that as many as 25% are.

Apple shouldn’t get too excited by the results, however, as willingness to pay was way, way less than the price we’re expecting the company to announce …

CNET opens with that 75% stat.

Most US adults say they aren’t interested in buying a new foldable phone. A CNET survey that polled 2,605 US adults found that 75% aren’t interested in buying a foldable Apple device.

That most people aren’t interested is in no way surprising: the real news here is that a quarter of US adults do find the idea appealing.

Unsurprisingly, interest varies by generations:

Boomers: 13%

Gen X: 23%

Gen Z: 31%

Millennials: 32%

I would personally be surprised if the percentage of people who end up buying the first generation of Apple’s first foldable iPhone is more than very low single digits, and my view does seem to be vindicated by the price people are willing to pay.

Gen Z were willing to pay the most at $919, while the average across all US adults was $781. The actual price is likely to start no lower than $2,000.

Subsequent generations of Apple foldables may become somewhat more affordable as manufacturing costs fall, but it’s never going to get anywhere near the pricing respondents have indicated they want to pay. While people famously show they are willing to pay significantly more than claimed for shiny new Apple products once they launch, my own expectation is that it will always be a rather niche product through a combination of pricing and lack of pocketability.

title: There’s a $300 gotcha in an M5 Max Mac Studio upgrade
snippet: There was a pleasant surprise in yesterday’s announcement of the Mac Studio with M5 Max chip: the starting price is unchanged from that of the M4 Max Mac Studio, at $2,499. However, if you want to upgrade the GPU, there is a gotcha in the cost of doing so – it will cost you $300 more than Apple’s website initially indicates …
fullText:
There was a pleasant surprise in yesterday’s announcement of the Mac Studio with M5 Max chip: the starting price is unchanged from that of the M4 Max Mac Studio, at $2,499.

However, if you want to upgrade the GPU, there is a gotcha in the cost of doing so – it will cost you $300 more than Apple’s website initially indicates …

That hidden upgrade cost caught out John Gruber when he went to summarise the costs of each configuration of the new machines announced yesterday.

The base configuration of the machine is an 18-core CPU with a 32-core GPU. Apple then lists an upgrade to a 40-core GPU, which is very clearly displayed as costing an additional $300.

The gotcha is that selecting this option also changes the selected memory from 32GB to 48GB, which costs a further $300. Since you can’t upgrade the GPU cores without also upgrading to 48GB memory, then that upgrade actually costs twice as much as indicated, at $600.

Apple advises you of this in a slightly opaque way when you select the upgraded chip.

Based on your new selection, other parts of your configuration have been updated. Please review the changes.

title: Luffu’s New Health and Safety Wearable Isn’t Just for You. It’s for Your Entire Family
snippet: You can link your entire family together with Luffu’s new wearable and app ecosystem.
fullText:
Wearables like fitness trackers and smart rings traditionally focus on collecting health data at the individual level, but the AI-powered intelligent family care system Luffu is expanding that scope. 

Launched by Fitbit co-founders James Park and Eric Friedman in February, Luffu started out as an app where family members could log health information, including medications, diet, doctors’ appointments, vaccine records, symptoms and more. It’s currently in public beta.

Luffu announced on Tuesday that it now has its own screenless wearable, the Luffu Link, and it’s available for preorder in the US for people age 13 and up.

How Luffu links the entire family together

A press release described the Luffu Link as a health and safety band that operates over 4G LTE, meaning you don’t need to have your phone nearby to reach out to your contacts for help or use certain features, like voice logging for medications, meals, mood, symptoms, reminders and notes. It also has built-in GPS, so you can share your location or send a check-in to family members. 

When it comes to your personal health, Luffu Link can capture data around sleep, activity, heart rate variability, resting heart rate, calories burned and breathing rate. AI then uses this information to learn patterns and alert users to any changes. 

AI brings all your family’s health data into one app.Luffu

The band features a single button. When you press and hold the button, it allows for voice logging. Press twice to send a check-in to select family members. Any health information you log is organized by AI and then added to the family’s Luffu app, where you can also create a profile for your pet to log their medications, meals and vet visits. 

According to the press release, families decide what information gets shared and with whom. 

Coordinating care can be accomplished in the Luffu app for both family members and furry friends.Luffu

The Luffu timeline and cost

Luffu is designing its ecosystem around three locations: the phone, wrist and home. 

While the app is in public beta, broader US availability is planned for later this year.

As for Luffu Link, those in the US can now preorder it on the Luffu website for $250 and get beta access to the app along with a quick charger and large and small silicone bands. Available in halo gold, sterling blue and onyx black, Link is expected to start shipping in early 2027. After that, the expected price will be $300. 

Designed to be jewelry-like, Luffu Link has a slim metal core with a silicone band. Luffu

Water-resistant up to 50 meters, Luffu Link offers battery life of up to five days, a charging time of around 1 hour, a one-year limited warranty, and compatibility with Android 14 or later and iOS 18 or later.

LTE data service is included with no separate carrier plan needed. However, to use Luffu, a family plan is required. Sold separately and available later this year, the plan covering up to four people costs $20 per month or $200 per year, while the extended family plan for eight people is $30 per month.

Luffu is also developing an intelligent home device — expected to be announced later this year — that allows families to coordinate care across generations and households. In the meantime, the company sent over a preview photo of the device.

What Luffu’s home device will look like.Luffu

The intended audience

A Luffu representative told CNET that some are confusing Luffu Link as a device specifically for aging adults, but it’s intended for the entire family.

“That includes adults [ages] 35 to 60 managing kids, aging parents, pets and their own health; independent, active adults 65+ who want discreet health and safety support without a traditional emergency pendant; and younger or middle-aged adults who may start with health tracking or voice logging and also benefit from safety, location and shared care features,” the representative said.

Co-founders Park and Friedman said they were inspired by their own caregiving experiences to create Luffu and their goal is to give families a single place to easily track their loved ones’ health and safety.

title: WhatsApp Adds Security Measures to Help Prevent Accounts From Being Hacked
snippet: The world’s most widely used messaging app adds stronger two-step verification and allows for more than one passkey.
fullText:
WhatsApp announced Tuesday that it has two new security features to help prevent accounts from being hacked — upgrading PINs to passwords and allowing users to add more passkeys.

The Meta-owned app also announced that when you receive calls from someone outside your contact list, you’ll get more information and context about the caller, such as whether the phone number is originating from another country.

WhatsApp did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The security features come on the heels of other privacy-centered tools implemented in recent months, including a Scam Alert tool to flag incoming scam messages. In late June, the company said it would allow people to create usernames so their phone numbers would not be visible.

WhatsApp, launched in 2009, is by far the world’s most widely used messaging app, with more than 2 billion active users. Next on the list are Facebook Messenger, Snapchat and Telegram.

Opt for passwords over PINs

Since early 2017, WhatsApp users have used a six-digit PIN, either when installing the app on a new device or verifying their account phone numbers. Now, the company is letting you upgrade your PINs to passwords, which can consist of numbers, letters and special characters.

You can keep your old PINs if you want. If you prefer passwords instead, WhatsApp lays out the requirements on this web page: Passwords must be at least eight characters and include at least one number and one letter.

To create a password, go to your WhatsApp Settings, select Account, then Password.

Using a PIN or password is part of the app’s optional two-step verification process. When people log in to the app, they’ll get a text message code (first step) and then provide their PIN or password (second step) to open the app.

WhatsApp customers can add more passkeys and create stronger passwords.WhatsApp

Use multiple passkeys

WhatsApp said users can now have more than one passkey when using both Android and iOS devices.

Some people use passkeys instead of PINs or passwords to log in to WhatsApp or to register a new device. Passkeys consist of fingerprints, facial IDs and screen lock codes to keep the app secure and private. So, for example, you could use your face to unlock your iPhone’s WhatsApp, but use a fingerprint to unlock your Android tablet.

To add passkeys, navigate to Settings > Account > Passkeys on phones.

Know more about who’s calling

WhatsApp also announced that people using Android phones can now get more information about incoming calls from unknown numbers outside their contact list. You’ll see if the caller is from a different country and if you have any chat groups in common.

Getting more information about incoming callers is great for privacy, usability and security, says cybersecurity expert Joseph Steinberg, author of Cybersecurity for Dummies and a lecturer at Columbia University.

“If you get a call and someone says we’re in the same group together, how many people actually check to make sure it’s not a scammer? This helps prevent that kind of scamming,” Steinberg told CNET. “If you’re in the group, (the app) will say you’re in the same group.”

Steinberg said that WhatsApp’s new security measure “definitely improves things,” though it’s unknown if a breach or another event propelled the company to make the changes. Regardless of the motivation, Steinberg said: “It’s always better to have stronger security if there are no side effects.”

Avoid scams

Despite WhatsApp’s upgraded safety features, people normally don’t have their accounts hacked or taken over because others steal their PINs or SMS texts. Cybersecurity platform Keepnet Labs said the majority of hacks result from customers being tricked into giving sensitive information, enabling bad actors to access their accounts.

Meta doesn’t report how many WhatsApp users are hacked each year, but the Federal Trade Commission said an estimated $425 million was lost last year to scams originating on WhatsApp.

title: Witcher 3 Remastered Will Be Free in September With New Expansion Coming in 2027
snippet: Geralt’s story wraps up with new enemies, a mysterious region and a send-off before Ciri takes the spotlight in The Witcher 4.
fullText:
Gamescom 2026 kicked off on Tuesday with Opening Night Live, the trailer showcase for some of the games coming out later this year and next. Europe’s major gaming event of the year, based in Cologne, Germany, it showed off a bunch of new games, but it was the remaster and expansion for the 11-year-old The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt that stole the show.

Developer CD Projekt Red revealed during the show that The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered will launch on Sept. 29 as a free upgrade for anyone who owns the game on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. Along with this updated version of the game, next year, a new expansion called Songs of the Past will arrive as the swan song for the series protagonist, Geralt of Rivia. The Witcher 4 is expected in 2028, and will focus on his adopted daughter and fellow Witcher, Ciri.

The Witcher 3 Remastered will feature a slew of improvements to the 2015 game. They include smoother combat, UI enhancements, a revamped skill tree, an expanded photo mode, new finishing moves and plenty of graphic upgrades to the textures, lighting, ray tracing and more. The remastered game will also make its debut on the Nintendo Switch 2 and Battle.net the same day.

Not only will Witcher 3 owners get the free upgrade in September, but CD Projekt Red is also making the game’s two expansions free starting Tuesday. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine came out in the year following the release of The Witcher 3 and added new content, including a drawn-out story and a huge new region.

As for the new expansion, Songs of the Past will come out in 2027, and it will feature a new land for Geralt to explore. Letten is a region with its own identity that’s filled with questions, monsters and a dark secret. Players will fight off never-before-seen enemies and make use of new weapons in what could be the last adventure for Geralt.

The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt is out now on multiple platforms, but the free upgrade will only be available for PC, PS5 and Xbox Series consoles. Songs of the Past is currently slated for release only on PC and Xbox Series consoles, according to the game’s website, though this could change closer to release.

title: Sony Is Reminding Us (Again) That We Don’t Own Our PlayStation Games
snippet: The idea of ownership is becoming a relic of an earlier era.
fullText:
Some things are too bizarre to make up, and Sony’s inability to read the room is one of them. 

Over the last week or so, the media giant has sent emails to PlayStation users with its entire Terms of Service, which includes a reminder that their digital games are “licensed” and not “sold.” The communication comes as gamers continue to protest Sony’s removal of physical media from the PlayStation 6. 

As an isolated incident, Sony’s email isn’t really anything untoward. It lets the user know that they have recently accepted the most recent Terms of Service, Code of Conduct, End User License Agreement and Privacy Policy. The company even included full copies of each in the email. 

But the timing of Sony’s email appears intentional, not just unfortunate. PlayStation users are furious over the company’s decision to remove the physical disc drive from the PlayStation 6, as well as its announcement that it will stop producing game discs altogether as of January 2028. Sony announced the end of physical discs just a few days after removing several digitally purchased movies from users’ accounts. 

The email was spotted by The Verge’s Tom Warren, who posted about it on X over the weekend: “Sony emailing everyone about PlayStation terms of use during a backlash over the end of discs and a lack of digital ownership is certainly a choice.” 

The backlash has grown large enough to inspire a PlayStation boycott — starting Sunday — with players pledging not to buy, log in to or play games for a week to protest Sony’s abandonment of physical media for the console.

So, right in the middle of a protest centered on concerns about game ownership, Sony is reminding us we’re merely buying a license to use a game under the company’s terms.

The new normal: Lease, not own

HP printers throw tantrums if you try to use third-party ink cartridges.James Bricknell / CNET

A move like this from another multibillion-dollar company underscores the new normal in gaming and tech, where companies appear to be shifting further away from the idea of ownership. Instead, they ask consumers to retain access to products that may be revoked or restricted at the company’s discretion. These changes didn’t come in one dramatic wave, but in a steady stream of small consumer-facing microaggressions that have built up over time. 

Take the recent HP printer controversy, for example. HP programmed its printers to lock users out if third-party ink is detected. That means you can buy an HP printer and own it — but if you don’t fill it with the official (more expensive) ink cartridges, the printer can sass back like an angsty, spoiled teenager and refuse to work. 

There are subtler attempts to chip away at our agency (and purchasing power) as consumers. Apple raised MacBook prices this year, then started a program where the company will literally rent you one, presumably because you can’t afford it otherwise. You wouldn’t own the MacBook, so Apple could lock you out of your device if you missed a lease payment. 

When it comes to music and movies, streaming has been the norm for years — we’re dutifully reminded every so often that we’re renting the ability to listen or watch something rather than owning it. I’ll never forget a couple of years ago when the entire library from the rock band Coheed and Cambria’s was removed from YouTube Music due to a licensing dispute while I was in the middle of listening. 

Sony and other gaming companies are starting to adopt the same lending-access business model in software and digital entertainment: In this brave new world, mega corporations can own everything and make us “purchase” rentals entirely on their terms. That means they can change, restrict, discontinue or shut down access, but we can never keep, lend, sell or pass down a product. 

The shift is leaving older generations (millennials like myself included) increasingly nostalgic for a time when buying something meant taking home something tangible — something that belonged to us.

title: Apple Quietly Fixes iCloud Private Relay Vulnerability in iOS 26.6.1
snippet: The problem could leak your device’s IP address, even when the paid iCloud Plus feature was enabled.
fullText:
Apple’s iCloud Private Relay is back to private status, after an apparent fix in iOS 26.6.1 patched the vulnerability that would expose a person’s IP address even when the feature was enabled.

iCloud Private Relay is a paid feature available only to those with an iCloud Plus subscription. When it’s active, it routes web traffic through proxy servers to mask your physical location and web traffic. It’s specific to Apple’s Safari web browser and apps that use Apple’s WebKit framework, and is not the same as a VPN, which hides all internet traffic.

Earlier in August, developers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk noticed that Apple devices with iCloud Private Relay enabled could still leak their IP addresses in three circumstances. The developers set up a web page at leaks.psylo.app where you could check whether you’re vulnerable.

On Tuesday, Mysk posted on X that Apple’s iOS 26.2.1 release (and the 26.2.1 releases of Apple’s other operating systems) is where the fix appeared, even though it’s not noted in Apple’s security release notes. Now, if you go to that leaks page, it reports the masked IP address, not the actual address, of the device you’re running. You need to have iCloud Private Relay on in Settings > iCloud.

The Psylo leak checker website shows that none of the possible IP leaks reveal my device’s actual IP address.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Mysk also noted in a reply on X that, “It’s near to impossible Apple would have addressed this issue so quickly had we reported it to Apple first. As expected, they only fixed it for Safari.”

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Soon after its existence was revealed, the iCloud Private Relay vulnerability prompted a lawsuit by Clarkson Law Firm, the same outfit that negotiated a $250 million settlement with Apple over how the company advertised its Apple Intelligence features at launch. The firm has also recently sued smart ring maker Oura.

A Clarkson Law Firm representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

							Senior Writer

title: Add the AirPods 5, Beats 360 to Rumored Apple Headphones Coming Soon
snippet: There’s been a lot of chatter about new AirPods Pro buds with tiny IR cameras, but don’t sleep on the AirPods 5 and new Beats over-ear headphones.
fullText:
For months, we’ve been hearing that Apple had a new version of its AirPods Pro on the horizon, equipped with tiny IR cameras designed to power new Siri AI visual intelligence features and perhaps recognize hand gestures like Apple’s Vision Pro headset. 

Last week, a video found in the MacOS 26.7 release candidate allegedly showed the camera-equipped AirPods in action, supercharging rumors that new AirPods Ultra — or whatever Apple plans to name them — would turn up at this year’s iPhone event. But new rumors and leaks suggest new AirPods 5 open earbuds and new over-ear headphones from Apple-owned Beats are more likely to make their debut in the coming weeks.

AirPods 5 fresh rumors 

Citing unnamed sources, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said this year’s iPhone rollout “will include new AirPods 5, an update to Apple’s entry-level earbuds.” Meanwhile, Gurman maintains that the camera-equipped version of the AirPods “isn’t expected until next year.” And according to MacOS Rumors, AirPods 5 references were already discovered in MacOS 26.7 Release Candidate code. Released two years ago, the AirPods 4 are available with and without noise canceling, and AirPods 5 should also be available in two versions with similar list prices of $130 and $180, respectively.

The AirPods 5 could look similar to the AirPods 4 (shown) but feature performance upgrades.David Carnoy/CNET

It’s unclear whether the AirPods 5 will include any design changes, but one would expect them to offer performance upgrades, and it’s possible they may be the first AirPods to be powered by Apple’s rumored H3 chip.

The AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation are something of a technological marvel, as ANC is a rare feature for open earbuds because it typically doesn’t work with an open design. As I said in my review, while the AirPods 4’s ANC isn’t that great compared with what you get with the AirPods Pro 3 and other top noise-canceling earbuds from Bose and Sony,  that it works at all and is reasonably effective is kind of wild. Apple has had two years to make the ANC even more effective, so I’d expect the AirPods 5 to see some gains on that front, which would be impressive. 

Read more: Best Wireless Earbuds of 2026

Beats 360 headphones teases and leaks

Ahead of the World Cup in June, Spain’s star winger Lamine Yamal teased unreleased Beats headphones in an Instagram post. Since then, there’s been a steady trickle of leaks about the new Beats headphones, which are apparently called the Beats 360 and loosely share some design similarities with Apple’s AirPods Max headphones, though they look cheaper. Last week, MacOS Rumors reported that multiple Reddit users “found signs of the Beats 360 on UK websites like Amazon, though those listings have now been removed.”

The Beats 360 will come with replaceable mesh-covered earpads. Screenshot by David Carnoy/CNET

The Beats 360 have a sporty slant and are apparently sweat- and water-resistant, with an IPX4 rating. Also, their headband and earcups are replaceable with interchangeable cushion options. MacOs Rumors says the headphones will ship with Performance Knit cushions, but an UltraPlush option will also be available, and the headphones will come in pink, black, sky and cloud, with volt and navy cushion options available (it’s unclear if the headphones will also come in those colors). They are expected to cost around $300 in the US.

As I said, the Amazon listing for the headphones was removed, but a Reddit user did grab a screenshot of the product’s highlights. Notably missing is any mention of Apple’s H2 chip powering the headphones, which likely means they’ll have a custom Beats chip similar to the one found in the Beats Studio Pro headphones, only more powerful (Beats is touting “up to 1.75x more noise cancellation than Beats Studio Pro”).

From the Amazon listing:

The Beats 360 have interchangeable cushion options for both ear cups and headband, so you can have a fresh set ready after your workout or a new color just to switch up your look. These over-ear noise-canceling headphones are built for active lifestyles and all-day comfort.

Active Noise Canceling (ANC) blocks out unwanted noise to help you focus, after adapting to your environment and unique fit — with up to 1.75x more noise cancellation than Beats Studio Pro.

The bespoke, high-fidelity acoustic platform delivers powerful bass and pinpoint precision across the tonal range with ultralow distortion for the ultimate listening experience. Personalized spatial audio with dynamic head tracking delivers immersive surround sound.

Ear cushions are built from acoustically engineered memory foam and shaped to fit comfortably over your ears, forming an optimal seal for incredible sound.

Exceptional call quality powered by an advanced AI-trained algorithm and beam-forming mic system that filters out background noise.

Our first-ever sweat- and water-resistant over-ear headphones, with an IPX4 rating to ensure they’re built to go everywhere you do.

All-day battery life for extended playback even with ANC on.

Compatible with both Apple and Android for one-touch pairing and more. Easy-to-use controls are positioned on the back of each earcup, including a volume rocker, a multifunction button to control music and calls, a power button and a listening mode button.

Fold-flat design for extra comfort and convenience. Woven ripstop fabric case included.

What’s in the box: Beats 360 true wireless over-ear headphones with interchangeable performance knit cushions, woven ripstop fabric carrying case, warranty card and Quick Start Guide. Additional Beats 360 cushion kits, USB-C charging cable and power adapter sold separately.

The odds of the Beats 360 being released in the next few weeks seem close to 100%, and I always thought the AirPods 5 were likely to arrive this year, as Apple tends to have its AirPods models on a two-year refresh cycle. I don’t know quite what to believe as far as the camera-equipped AirPods Pro go, but either way, we should know soon enough.

title: These Cookies Are 3D-Printed and Made of Recycled Plastic
snippet: Scientists have engineered yeast that converts waste plastic and plant biomass into vanilla-flavored, 3D-printable protein cookies.
fullText:
Would you eat a cookie made from an upcycled water bottle? One group of scientists thinks that at least some people will in the near future. They’ve genetically engineered yeast to transform PET plastic and agricultural waste into a vanilla-flavored protein cookie that they think could be a solution to both plastic pollution and food shortages. Sounds delicious.

The project began as part of NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge — one of the agency’s Centennial Challenges — in which scientists and researchers were tasked with developing new technologies and approaches for the problem of feeding astronauts on long space voyages. For microbiologists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, the solution lay in converting plastic and plant waste into “edible, protein-rich supplements.”

Their concoction — snack-sized morsels called “µBites” (pronounced “microbites”) — didn’t end up winning the Deep Space Food Challenge. The grand prize went to Interstellar Lab of Merritt Island, Florida, and its autonomous, environment-controlled greenhouses that generate fresh vegetables, microgreens and insects (yes, insects) necessary for micronutrients. However, NASA pushed the team to keep working to bring its plastic-derived cookie to reality.

On Monday, at the American Chemical Society Expo in Chicago, the SIU Carbondale team, led by associate professor Lahiru Jayakody, presented new enhancements to the flavor, aroma and color of the cookies.

The process starts with one of the most common forms of single-use plastic, polyethylene terephthalate, or PET — what most single-use water and soda bottles are made of — which is mixed with plant waste biomass such as corn stalks and leaves. Hot, high-pressure water and oxygen break the mixture down into carbon-rich molecules, which are then fed to a mix of genetically reprogrammed, safe-to-eat yeast strains. 

Lahiru Jayakody, who led the project, holds one of the 3D-printed, plastic-derived cookies.Rusty Bailey/SIUC Media & Communication Resources

The feasting yeast converts plastics and agricultural waste into proteins, fats and flavor. An engineered strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae converts ferulic acid to vanillin, the compound responsible for vanilla flavor and aroma, while a modified strain of Rhodosporidium toruloides produces beta-carotene, a source of vitamin A. This result is further mixed with fiber, starch and sweetener to create an edible “slurry” that is passed through a 3D printer to form a familiar cookie disc, complete with the Greek letter “µ” branding.

At this point, the cookie is theoretically ready to eat. However, Jayakody told The Guardian that the team hasn’t yet actually tasted the cookies and is still “awaiting approval for testing on humans,” but that they “receive high marks on aroma.”

Though the project began as a moonshot food supply for long-distance space travel and disaster zones, Jayakody and team believe the concept could eventually find its legs as a “promising solution to address both food shortage and plastic pollution simultaneously.”

“Global food demand is expected to rise 35–56% by the year 2050, and about 30% of the world population will be at risk of hunger in the future,” Jayakody said in a statement. “The way to address that, I believe, is by using microbes.”

At this early stage, these cookies are also very expensive. Costing around $60 per kilogram (2.2 pounds) to produce, they’re far from an economical solution to world hunger. However, the SIU Carbondale researchers believe they can improve the yeast’s efficiency and, with scale, reduce costs. 

Personally, my curiosity is piqued; I want to know what they taste like. (I’m a fairly adventurous eater.) Convincing the public to accept and eat plastic-derived cookies made from trash, on the other hand, is a challenge that may take more than science to solve.

title: Anthropic Unifies Memory Across Claude and Cowork
snippet: You can also allow Claude to generate memory topics as you chat.
fullText:
Claude‘s memory capabilities are getting a significant upgrade. Now, when you switch from Claude to Cowork, the same memory from past chats with the AI tool stays with you. That way, you don’t have to readd context when you switch tools, saving you time and letting you focus on the project at hand.

With Cowork sharing Claude’s memory, all previous conversations are available for Cowork to dig into. It’ll remember your preferences on writing style and other projects you’ve worked on for reference. 

Anthropic has also added a series of new memory-related features, including options for what you want to store and easier ways to manage chat history. 

A helpful new addition for Claude is that you no longer have to tell it to remember something — it updates its memory as you chat with it. The real-time updates mean Claude can recall something specific without you having to tell it to. You can pause or reset your memory at any time by going to Settings > Memory. 

Anthropic is also making it easier to manage your memories. In the memory settings, you can view all the topics Claude has saved from your previous chats and edit or delete them right there, so you keep only what you want stored. 

You can now also have Claude save sensitive topics that would normally not be included in memory. Sensitive topics aren’t saved by default, but you can opt to have them stored in memory if you want. With the setting enabled, Anthropic says Claude will remember things like your gluten allergy when providing recipes for the week’s meal prep. 

For your privacy and safety, some sensitive information and topics, such as government ID numbers, criminal history, financial account numbers and immigration status, will not be stored in memory, even when the setting is enabled. Claude will notify you when it’s unable to save this type of information. 

By default, memory is enabled across free, Pro and Max plans on web, desktop and mobile. Sensitive topics are off by default and must be manually enabled. For mobile, Anthropic is updating the Claude app for iOS and Android to include the latest features.

title: Apple renews push for expedited discovery in OpenAI trade secret misappropriation lawsuit
snippet: Apple has submitted its response to OpenAI’s attempt to block expedited discovery in its ongoing trade secret lawsuit. Here are the details.
fullText:
Apple has submitted its response to OpenAI’s attempt to block expedited discovery in its ongoing trade secret lawsuit. Here are the details.

A bit of background

Earlier this month, Apple asked for an expedited discovery process in its lawsuit accusing former employees, OpenAI, and io Products of trade secret misappropriation.

That would include early production of documents and communications, forensic imaging of devices and accounts, and depositions of key witnesses.

Essentially, Apple wants substantive responses to its written discovery within 30 days and an OpenAI corporate deposition within 50 days, with both completed at the outset of the case rather than left to the broader fact-discovery process.

From Apple’s motion:

Apple needs expedited discovery to uncover dissipating facts outside its control to determine the full scope of how its proprietary information and trade secrets have been misappropriated.

Apple’s motion came one day after Apple filed for a preliminary injunction, seeking to stop OpenAI and the other defendants from accessing, using, or disclosing Apple’s alleged proprietary information while the case proceeds.

In essence, Apple argues that the longer OpenAI and the other defendants are allowed to use its alleged trade secrets, the harder it will be to reverse the alleged damage.

Here’s Apple:

The harm is happening now—every day that passes without an injunction allows OpenAI to embed their knowledge of Apple’s stolen information into its hardware development efforts, further damaging Apple and making it increasingly more difficult to unwind the harm.

Following Apple’s motion for expedited discovery, OpenAI and the other defendants filed an opposition, arguing that the request was unnecessary because much of the regular discovery process would overlap with Apple’s proposed expedited timeline. It also argued that Apple’s requests were “overbroad,” “burdensome,” and based on “improper purposes.”

From the opposition filing:

In any event, Apple fails to show the requisite good cause for expedited discovery, including because Apple’s discovery requests are untethered to the requested preliminary injunction, and instead appear aimed at gaining an improper peek at the corporate Defendants’ competitive product plans and strategies.

Which brings us to today.

Apple fires back

Apple today filed its reply to OpenAI’s opposition, arguing that not only did it establish “good cause for expedited discovery” in its initial filing, but also that its request isn’t moot, “even if expedited discovery overlaps with ordinary discovery.”

Apple also says the opposition brief “telegraphs the alternative: absent a court order, they will object, delay, and condition discovery into their misappropriation on tangential ‘reciprocal’ demands.”

From Apple’s new filing:

Defendants’ “mootness” position cannot be squared with court decisions in this district granting expedited discovery, even when ordinary discovery is set to open shortly. Moreover, this motion is now fully briefed, and resolving it promptly will inform the earliest stages of these proceedings. Even if expedited discovery overlaps with ordinary discovery, an order requiring some limited, urgent discovery to be completed at the outset will ensure that Defendants respond substantively in the first instance, rather than with boilerplate objections and promises to supplement over weeks and months.

In its response, Apple also narrows the timeframe of its document requests to August 1, 2023, and later, while poking at OpenAI’s objection that the requests lacked a date limit:

Defendants also argue that Apple’s [requests for production] are not limited to a specific timeframe. Defendants should not have Apple’s confidential information from any timeframe. However, to address Defendants’ concerns, Apple further specifies that it seeks Communications, Documents, and Things (as defined in the RFPs) dated on or after August 1, 2023 approximately six months before Mr. Tan left Apple to join OpenAI.

Finally, Apple reiterates that its urgency comes from concerns that OpenAI and the other defendants could keep using the alleged trade secrets while developing their own hardware, while Apple waits “months or years” to question key witnesses:

Defendants concede that Apple should be permitted to take its requested depositions but propose that they occur only once, presumably at the end of fact discovery. That proposal does not address the need to promptly discover the scope of Defendants’ misappropriation and deal with the actual or potential dissemination of Apple’s trade secrets. It would mean that Apple would have to wait months or years to ask a witness about that information. Meanwhile, OpenAI could continue to use Apple’s hardware trade secrets while racing to design and launch its own hardware device.

Apple’s expedited-discovery motion is scheduled for a hearing before Judge Edward Davila on October 1, although the judge could rule on the request before then.

title: What is the ‘Android Pulse’ app that just appeared in Google Play Store updates? [U]
snippet: On Saturday morning, you might have noticed an app called “Android Pulse” appearing in the list of available Google Play updates.
fullText:
On Saturday morning, you might have noticed an app called “Android Pulse” appearing in the list of available Google Play updates.

Update 8/25: In a statement today, Google explained that “Android Pulse is a Google system service.” 

Google system services updates make your Android devices more secure and reliable, and give you new and useful features.

—Google spokesperson

The app’s appearance in the Play Store was accidental, and Google has “pushed an update so users will now see it in their settings.” It now appears in the usual list alongside Google Play services and Android System Intelligence. On Pixel, go to Settings app > Google services > All services > Privacy & security > System services to check.

Original 8/22: Instead of an application icon, there’s just a blank square. Opening the Play Store listing does reveal it’s a first-party Google app meant for “Defining anomalies for debugging” rather than anything malicious.

	

com.google.android.apps.pulse

Google adds: “This app facilitates rule distribution for anomaly detection in critical system resource consumption by the Android operating system and installed applications.”

What does Android Pulse do?

That’s not a very user-friendly description, but our interpretation is that this service — which does not have an interface you can access — helps with software diagnostics for the OS itself and any installed apps. The “critical system resource consumption” could be a reference to battery, CPU, or memory usage.

This application is already installed on our Pixel devices, and it’s just referred to as “Pulse” in system Settings. The App info page also reveals a heart rate-inspired icon in green (as seen in the cover image above).

Let us know if you’re seeing this app or update on non-Pixel devices

	

According to APKMirror, this app has existed since March, with seven previous builds. The Play Store notes over 10 million downloads.

However, today is the first time it appears to have surfaced in the Play Store as an update you can manually install. It’s curious that Google did not use its dedicated System Services approach to update this kind of app.

In short, “Android Pulse” is a Google app that’s okay to have on your phone.

title: New M6 Mac Mini and Mac Studio With M5 Ultra Promise Needed Boost for AI and Graphics
snippet: At higher prices, naturally.
fullText:
As if a new range of iPhones expected in the coming weeks wasn’t enough, Apple broke from its usual announcement timing to debut new chips and configurations of its Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktops.

In addition to launching a Mac Mini with a new M6 chip and Mac Studio with a new M5 Ultra, Apple brings its desktops into line with its MacBook Pro offerings, adding M5 Pro configurations for the Mini and M5 Max models for the Studio. Both the Mini and the Studio are identical to their predecessors physically: The performance and capabilities of the updated chips are the only changes. 

That and the prices. With the exception of the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at the same $2,499, the prices for the base models of both systems have gone up. Prices have increased by $100 for the Mac Mini, which now starts at $899 for the M6 and $1,699 for the M5 Pro. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio has gone up by $200 to $5,499. Those are on top of the already significant bumps announced in June. 

	

			

Not that the price increases come as a surprise. We’ve been going through a huge price shock, oversimplistically dubbed “RAMageddon,”  thanks to ongoing component shortages. Semiconductor fab resources have been increasingly reallocated toward whatever’s ultimately the most profitable. Right now, that means anything critical to AI, notably data centers. And that pressure carries all the way down the supply chain, resulting in volatile prices for all other electronics. 

Preorders start today with a long lead, at least for Apple. They’re not slated to ship until Sept. 22, with the 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studio following about a month after that.

Apple/CNET

The Mini steps up with M6

The brand-new M6 brings some notable advances over the M5. It’s fabricated using a 2nm process — the first M series processor to downsize from the 3nm process. A smaller process allows for denser circuitry in the same size die, which lets you do things like increase the number of cores and clock speeds of an existing chip layout without requiring a significant design change to the system or (usually) the mainboard.

That means, for instance, it was possible to double the capacity of the Neural Engine, which goes from 16 cores to 32. The Neural Engine is potentially key to the company’s success with Apple Intelligence in MacOS 27 running on entry systems, since on-device agents and other basic AI inferencing generally relies on the integer math performed by the NE. 

And as far as I can tell from my testing, the NE’s performance increase from the M4 to the M5 was meh. I suspect the only way to improve it was by substantially increasing the cores.

Agents rely on the CPU to manage and allocate resources, so a handful of extra CPU cores matters. The M6 also updates the CPU architecture to match the M5 Pro and Max, switching to the three Super-Performance-Efficiency core types (think fast-slower-slowest) from the two Super-Efficiency types in the M4. 

Apple says the two extra GPU cores plus accelerators will deliver about a 30% compute performance improvement. In theory, that sounds about right – I’m extrapolating based on my testing, plus the typical generation-over-generation increase in memory bandwidth.

Apple/CNET

Unlike the other versions of the chips, Apple’s top-end Ultra is on an every-other-generation upgrade cycle. So the last one was based on the M3 design, which has a GPU architecture that significantly lags the M5 for both graphics (especially ray tracing) and AI. 

The Ultra chips are more or less two Max versions linked by high-speed circuitry. In this case, the M5 Ultra is based off the M5 Max with 40 GPU and 18 CPU cores for a total of 80 GPU and 36 CPU (12 super and 24 performance) cores, plus a 32-core Neural Engine. That’s the same number of NE cores as the previous Ultra, but while they’re a more recent generation, they’re not the same as the newer M6. 

Like the other M5 chips, the Ultra incorporates the on-GPU neural accelerators. It still supports a maximum of 512GB memory, though you won’t be able to get it until late October. But Apple jacked up the memory bandwidth to a whopping 1.2TB per second, up from 813GB per second for the M3 Ultra and from 614GB  per second for the M5 Max.

One of the potentially most important changes the new chip brings for pro graphics folks is support for four 5K 120Hz displays on the Ultra model, up from three.

Why now?

The timing of the announcements is atypical for Apple. Though there have obviously been exceptions, new Macs and their accompanying chips are usually announced in October and March. I can think of a host of possible reasons Apple might be changing its playbook, either temporarily or permanently. For one, an early upgrade announcement might provide a more digestible justification for the aforementioned price hike.

Shortages may have affected the timing as well. Given worsening problems obtaining components for computers in general, Apple may be extending its horizon either for reevaluating its needs in an uncertain market, or ramping up and maintaining inventory further in advance of the big shopping season. Or if the company’s already acquired the expensive new silicon, products incorporating it shouldn’t really wait around a couple months just for an event. 

While the Ultra versions of its chips have always been confined to the flagship desktops like the Mac Studio, the base versions are typically launched with entry models, not just in the Mini, but the iMac, MacBook Air and base MacBook Pro as well. Apple may be avoiding having to deal with component supplies for a lot of different products shipping simultaneously.

And upgrading the chips in a desktop is a lot simpler than in a laptop, where power consumption and heat dissipation are critical. So not tying the M6 release to potential MacBook announcements in October may have simply been a practical decision.

I’ve also been contemplating Apple’s need to compete in the AI dev machine market — the ultracompact desktop PCs used to ceaselessly run local agents like OpenClaw, for isolated coding environments, and so on. The Mini has been popular as a relatively cheap entry point, and the M6’s enhancements are likely to make it more attractive for that.

The Ultra chip in the Studio serves a similar purpose at the other end of the spectrum, and this is a case where Apple’s every-other-generation upgrades for the Ultra can’t wait for next March, when the Studio would typically get an update. The M3 Ultra was the last update, but it lacks the enhanced M5 GPU architecture with on-core neural accelerators to boost floating point performance, and my testing indicates that FP32 performance benefits from more GPU cores. The only way to get those here is with an 80-core Ultra, since the Max tops out at 40.

title: Notability can now organize meeting recordings, transcriptions, and notes around your calendar
snippet: Notability today announced a new desktop workflow that lets Mac users start recording sessions directly from their calendar events, with the resulting notes automatically organized around their schedule. Here are the details.
fullText:
Notability today announced a new desktop workflow that lets Mac users start recording sessions directly from their calendar events, with the resulting notes automatically organized around their schedule. Here are the details.

Notability now connects recordings to your schedule

Popular note-taking platform Notability today announced a feature that integrates several of its existing recording and note-taking capabilities into a workflow designed to make it easier to capture and organize meetings and lectures.

Starting today on Mac and Windows, users can record meetings and lectures directly from calendar events, then combine the recordings, transcripts, and notes taken during the session into a single document tied to the corresponding event.

Here’s Notability:

Students and professionals connect their calendar, and when they tap a meeting recording starts and the note opens, ready for input. At the end of the meeting, Notability combines the call’s transcript and any typed notes that were taken during the meeting into one comprehensive note.

So students can capture their critical lectures on anything from economics to political science without missing anything important, and professional knowledge workers can engage in essential strategy meetings and review their notes later to see what they might have missed.

Notability adds that, unlike other meeting recording solutions that require a bot to join the call, its new workflow captures system audio directly from the computer.

The company also notes that:

Every new note defaults to a recording, so capture requires no extra step.

Calendar connect turns each event into a tappable row that starts recording the accompanying meeting or lecture.

Coming soon, syllabus import will auto-structure an entire term into lectures, study sessions and exams.

A free tier that lets new users try the features before hitting a paywall.

Finally, Notability says the new feature is available to Plus ($5.99/mo or $15.99/yr) and Pro ($15.99/mo or $79.99/yr) subscribers. Pro users get unlimited live audio transcription, while Plus subscribers are subject to a usage limit that isn’t specified on the company’s pricing page.

title: CNET Finds 75% of US Adults Couldn’t Care Less About a Foldable iPhone
snippet: Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Ultra (or Fold), could cost over $2,000 according to analysts. But US adults aren’t willing to pay that much.
fullText:
Apple could release its first foldable iPhone in a few weeks at the company’s annual September event (which could be Sept. 9). The late summer showcase is usually Apple’s big reveal for new hardware. The center of attention could be the rumored iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first foldable. 

Analysts say the phone could be dubbed the iPhone Ultra (previously nicknamed the iPhone Fold and iPhone Flip). It’s expected to be a tiny iPad that folds in half, into a regular-size iPhone when closed. Rumors suggest Apple’s folding phone will feature a wide book-style fold, similar to the original Google Pixel Fold and the recently released Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a folding display with the same aspect ratio as an iPad.

The iPhone Ultra could also have two rear-facing and a single front-facing camera that works whether it’s folded or not, and come with Apple’s usual features and services. Analysts expect the phone to cost between $2,000 and $2,500, which is on par with, if not a little higher than, rival folding phones from Motorola, Google and Samsung. 

However, most US adults say they aren’t interested in buying a new foldable phone.

A CNET survey that polled 2,605 US adults found that 75% aren’t interested in buying a foldable Apple device. Even if they bought one, they wouldn’t shell out thousands of dollars for it. 

Key takeaways 

Three out of four US adults (75%) are indifferent about buying a foldable Apple device, such as the rumored Apple iPhone Ultra. 

US adults would spend an average of $781 on an Apple foldable device, which is a stark contrast to what analysts say the phone could cost (and $48 less than the base model iPhone 17). 

The RAM shortage is affecting nearly half (41%) of US adults’ plans to upgrade their phones. Some are holding onto their current devices longer than originally planned. 

Most US adults don’t want a foldable iPhone 

CNET found that most US adults, regardless of age, aren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. Older generations (Boomers and Gen X) express the least interest — 83% and 77%, respectively. Younger generations aren’t that excited either, with nearly 70% of Gen Z and millennials (69% and 68%, respectively) not interested in a foldable iPhone. And those who are excited about one aren’t willing to break the bank for it. 

Cole Kan/CNET

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, finds it surprising that only 75% weren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. “Foldable phones are niche products, and it’s impressive that 25% might be interested in an Apple folding phone,” said Holland. “That would be a killer product debut if Apple could get that many people to buy one.”

The same thing can be said for the iPhone Mini and Plus models for those who want a smaller or larger screen, but still want an iPhone. Or the E series, which is a budget-friendly model starting at $600 before discounts. 

Holland pointed out that the foldable iPhone isn’t meant to replace the baseline model; it’s about expanding the line and offering phone models at an even bigger price range. Apple could have an iPhone model at ever $100 increase between $600 and $2,000.

US adults will spend an average of $781 on a new foldable iPhone

On average, US adults are willing to spend $781 on a new foldable iPhone. That’s less than what most iPhones cost now. For context, the base model of the iPhone 17 starts at $799 (with a $30 carrier discount). 

Gen Z is willing to spend the most on a foldable iPhone — an average of $919 — whereas other generations would spend less. Millennials would spend an average of $859, Gen X would spend $690, and Boomers even less — $572. 

Cole Kan/CNET

“The fact that people want an average price that’s nearly $50 below the baseline iPhone 17 shows where we’re at financially right now,” said Holland. “A foldable iPhone is going to be expensive to make, and its retail price will likely reflect that.”

But foldable phones haven’t always been this expensive. Holland points out that the price of foldable phones has dropped for years, as with the Motorola Razr line. The first model cost $1,400, but last year you could buy a new one for half that price before discounts. Now those prices have started to rise again (because of the RAM shortage), and the rumored $2,000 price for the iPhone Ultra is proof of that. It’s a few hundred dollars more than foldable phones cost just a couple of years ago, Holland said. 

The RAM shortage is affecting iPhone upgrade plans

The evolution of AI and data centers has led to a memory chip shortage — also known as the RAM shortage or RAMageddon. Personal devices, like phones and laptops, need those chips for data storage. However, the shortage has led tech companies to raise prices on their devices. 

Apple raised prices on many of its devices in June for this very reason. The RAM shortage and price increases are making 41% US adults rethink their plans to upgrade to a new iPhone — regardless of whether it’s a foldable or another model. 

“The very companies investing in AI and building data centers to support new features and tools on phones are the ones passing the higher cost of RAM and chips on to consumers,” said Holland. “There’s a corporate Gift of the Magi happening, and it’s us who are footing the bill while companies rake in record-breaking profits.” 

Many contemplating an upgrade are weighing other options due to price increases. Some are considering older or less expensive options (5%) and switching to another brand (4%), while others are considering refurbished or used models (4%) to save money on the upgrade. Others (9%) will only upgrade if a trade-in or a mobile carrier promotion covers the price, which usually comes in the form of account credits or a multiyear commitment to stay with that carrier. 

The bigger story is that most US adults aren’t eager to upgrade due to the RAM shortage and device price hikes. Ten percent are planning to delay their upgrade and keep their phone longer, while 9% are holding onto their phone longer than originally planned.

Twenty-two percent of US adults don’t plan to upgrade anytime soon, regardless of Apple’s new devices or the impact of the RAM shortage. By generation, 19% of Gen X and 27% of Boomers don’t have plans to upgrade anytime soon, while 16% of millennials and 21% of Gen Zers share the same sentiment. Here’s a breakdown.

If you have an old phone and the battery is the only issue, replace it instead of getting a new phone, Holland said. “You’ll add another two to three years of life onto your phone and avoid paying hundreds of dollars more for an upgrade or multiyear commitment to a carrier.” 

If you’re still thinking of upgrading your phone, Holland said the best deals on phones are typically found when a new model launches or during holiday sales. And even though trading in your old phone is a good way to save money, check with third-party reseller sites, too. 

“You might be able to get more money for your old phone than from the carrier or phone-maker is offering,” said Holland. “Used and refurbished phones are definitely worth buying, as are models from a year or two ago, and often discounted by hundreds.” 

Lastly, be skeptical about that “free” $1,000-plus phone a carrier is willing to give you. These deals often come with multiyear commitments and are shown as account credit rather than cash. If you switch to a new mobile carrier before the phone is paid off, you’ll have to pay the difference.

Methodology 

All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,605 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Aug. 13 and 17, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Dashia Milden
						

						

							Editor						
					

											

				

											Dashia is the consumer insights editor for CNET. She specializes in data-driven analysis and news at the intersection of tech, personal finance and consumer sentiment. Dashia investigates economic shifts and everyday challenges to help readers make well-informed decisions, and she covers a range of topics, including technology, security, energy and money. Dashia graduated from the University of South Carolina with a bachelor's degree in journalism. She loves baking, teaching spinning and spending time with her family.

fullText:
Today, Apple updated the Mac mini and Mac Studio, bringing Wi-Fi 7 support to both product lines for the first time. Here’s the full list of Apple devices that support all Wi-Fi 7 features.

6 GHz band operation not available in all regions

Apple today published a support document detailing which of its products fully support Wi-Fi 7.

That list is different from Apple’s broader list of devices that can connect to Wi-Fi 7 networks because Wi-Fi 7 is backward-compatible.

This means that devices that only support Wi-Fi 6E can still join compatible Wi-Fi 7 networks and use the 6 GHz band where available, although they do not support the full set of Wi-Fi 7 features.

Wi-Fi 7 features include 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, and Multi-Link Operation (MLO), which can increase throughput, improve efficiency, and reduce latency, and you can read more about that here.

That said, here’s Apple’s official list of devices that support all Wi-Fi 7 features as of August 2026:

MacBook Pro with M5 Pro or M5 Max chip or later

MacBook Air with M5 chip or later

Mac mini with M5 Pro chip or later

Mac Studio with M5 Max chip or later

iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, or later (excluding iPhone 16e, iPhone 17e)

iPhone Air

iPad Pro with M5 chip or later

iPad Air with M4 chip or later

Apple notes that “Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 features that operate on the 6 GHz band are available only in regions that permit unlicensed Wi-Fi use in that spectrum,” adding that ”if regulatory approval of such operation is unavailable in your region, your device uses only the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands for Wi-Fi.”

title: Our Robot Pool Vacuum Tests Show Why Suction Power Matters Less Than You Think
snippet: Suction isn’t everything. Smart navigation and efficiency are what really define a great robotic pool cleaner.
fullText:
If you use a robotic pool cleaner every day as I do, you know what matters. Getting as much debris out of the pool as possible is the goal, but pure suction power — quantified as gallons of pool water sucked through the machine per hour — takes a back seat to efficiency. 

An efficient robot pool vacuum doesn’t just pick up debris with stronger suction; it does so strategically, so your pool is cleaned faster and you use less battery. When you’re ready to cool off in the pool — like, now — you want the fastest possible cleaning. 

This is the first year we’ve tested robots with high-functioning AI, giving them the ability to detect debris using cameras and sensors, change course and suck it up into the basket. These advanced features have upended the traditional formula for robot pool cleaner proficiency (suction power plus battery life).

Key takeaways 

Efficiency over power: Pure suction power (measured in gallons per hour) is less critical than the robot’s cleaning efficiency.

Impact of AI: Robotic pool cleaners equipped with AI debris detection (using cameras and sensors) clean more efficiently than those without such features.

Corded vs. cordless: In general, corded robotic pool cleaners are more efficient than cordless models because they have a consistent power supply and can perform back-to-back cleaning cycles. 

The corded Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus (Lab Award winner) was the most efficient of all the recommended models we tested. 

The Aiper Scuba V3 (Lab Award winner) was the most efficient cordless robotic pool cleaner tested, picking up more debris in less time than more powerful and expensive models.

CNET Lab Awards

Most Efficient (Corded): Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus (Efficiency Score: 58 items picked up per hour)

Most Efficient (Cordless): Aiper Scuba V3 (Efficiency Score: 44.64 items picked up per hour)

Pure power isn’t the end-all, be-all for pool robot cleaners

There’s more to consider in robotic pool cleaning than pure power.Aiper/CNET

When shopping for a robot pool cleaner, you might assume more suction power means better overall performance. Suction rates range anywhere from around 4,000 to 8,000 gallons per hour in robots intended for residential use.

In truth, most top pool robot cleaners have enough suction to lift the debris that’s likely to end up in your pool. Leaves, twigs and even small stones are light enough that even robot pool vacuums on the lower end of the GPH spectrum have no trouble clearing them. 

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Robot Pool Cleaners Out of More Than 20 tested					

							

		

I’ve seen plenty of robot pool cleaners with massive 8,500 GPH suction take on a pile of pebbles and leaves, with success rates similar to those of models with half that power. That got me thinking about efficiency, and so we devised a testing methodology and formula to determine the most efficient robotic pool cleaners. 

How we performed the lab tests

We ran all the cordless vacuums at once with a pool full of pebbles.

David Watsky/CNET

To measure the efficiency of each robot pool cleaner, we ran it on a full charge in a 14,000-gallon test pool with 100 pebbles and 30 leaves — more debris than you’re ever likely to have in your pool — scattered about the bottom. 

(We’d given each robot the repetitions it needed to map the pool using its cameras and ultrasonic sonar or acoustic sensors, if such a feature existed. Not all pool robot vacuums have it.)

We timed how long the robot operated for on a full charge. When it was finished cleaning, we counted how much debris was captured in the basket, aka how much it picked up from the floor and how much was left behind. We then prorated the pickup performance with the time the robot spent cleaning. This efficiency score indicates how many pieces of debris a robotic pool cleaner collects per hour. 

Cordless robot pool cleaner efficiency winners

Many of the pool vacuums performed well, but three were in a league of their own in terms of total pickup performance, leaving fewer than 5 total objects, so we separated those from the rest. After the top three, there was a notable drop-off, and the next best model left 12 pieces of debris in the pool. 

Among the three elite performers in pickup, the most efficient robot pool cleaner was the Aiper Scuba V3 with AI detection. It left just five pebbles and cleared every leaf from the pool bottom. The Scuba V3 achieved this in an astonishing 2 hours and 48 minutes – nearly 2 hours faster than the larger, more powerful robots. Its efficiency score was 44.64 items spiked up per hour.

The robot vacuum that cleared the most total debris was the Aiper Scuba X1 Pro Max. It left zero pebbles or leaves but required more than 4 hours, resulting in a lower efficiency score of 28.36 items picked up per hour. I noted that at the 3.5-hour mark of cleaning, there were still a few scattered pebbles, though it eventually picked them up.

The Beatbot Aquasense Pro, another powerful pool cleaner with a massive battery, also performed well, clearing all the leaves and leaving only three stones, but it needed 4 hours and 40 minutes to do so, giving it an efficiency score of 27.21 items picked up per hour.

The second most efficient robot pool cleaner was the Polaris Freedom. It picked up a respectable 107 items in its 2 hours and 25 minutes of cleaning, giving it a healthy efficiency score of 44.28 items picked up per hour. But because it left 23 items, including 10 leaves and 13 pebbles, it represented a noticeable dip in performance from the top of the pack. 

The Aiper Scuba S1 Pro had a similar result. High efficiency, but left more total debris than we’d like to see in a top performer. 

Suction power didn’t matter much, but AI smarts did

AI capability proved more critical to pickup efficiency than suction power.Aiper

Among the cordless test group, three robot pool cleaners stood out by picking up all 30 leaves and at least 95 pebbles. We considered this a perfect or near-perfect performance. (Remember, we littered the pool with far more debris than you’re likely to have at any given time if you use your robot cleaner somewhat regularly).

Of the top three performers in total pickup, the Aiper Scuba V3 trounced the others in its efficiency rating, despite having significantly lower GPH and battery life. It picked up 125 of the 130 pieces of debris in 2 hours and 48 minutes.

What accounted for Aiper Scuba’s dominant efficiency was its ability to detect debris with cameras, sensors, and AI for targeted cleaning. It was fascinating to watch the Scuba V3 move through the pool, stop and turn toward debris when it encountered a leaf or pebble. 

Other robots we tested roam the pool either based on their mapping or aimlessly like a screensaver, hoping to run over leaves, bugs and sticks rather than seeking them out. 

Robots with big power and battery life deliver, but there’s a price to pay

Big beasts like the Aiper Pro Max have powerful suction and battery life, but they’re more than the average pool owner needs.David Watsky/CNET

The most expensive robot pool cleaners are typically those with the largest motors and batteries. That also makes them the heaviest, with a large lithium-ion battery accounting for most of the weight. 

The two robot pool vacuums that beat the Aiper Scuba V3 in overall performance weigh 7 and 16 pounds more, respectively. When you’re pulling a cordless robot from the pool each day for charging, emptying and cleaning, that extra weight matters. 

They’re also significantly more expensive, clocking in at $1,800 and $2,199, whereas the Aiper Scuba V3 retails for around $850.

Corded models: Efficiency over convenience 

In general, corded models are more efficient than their cordless counterparts. Because they are fed consistent power through an electrical cord, suction never drops or wanes mid-cycle, ensuring heavy debris, sand and leaves are vacuumed. They also run endlessly, so you can trigger back-to-back cycles until your pool is clean. 

On the flip side, you can’t swim while a corded robot pool cleaner is working due to the risk of electrical shock. You’ll also need an outlet nearby and manage an unsightly cord running across the deck during operation.

Because of these structural differences, we put corded robot pool cleaners in their own category but used a similar equation to calculate efficiency. Corded robot cleaners often have set runtimes ranging from two to three hours. 

Of the three corded models we tested, the Dolphin Nautilus CC with Wi-Fi performed the best, clearing all leaves and all but 14 pebbles during its 2-hour run time, giving it an impressive efficiency score of 58 items picked up per hour. That’s better than the Polaris ERA could manage in its longer cycle of 2 hours and 30 minutes (45 efficiency score). The Dolphin E10 picked up only 108 of the 130 items in 2 hours of cleaning, but managed a solid 54 efficiency score. 

My expert buying advice on robotic pool cleaners 

We’ve tested nearly two dozen robotic pool cleaners. 

David Watsky/CNET

If you’re in the market for a robotic pool cleaner, prioritize efficiency and smart debris detection over raw suction power specs, especially for an average-size pool. Our lab data shows that models like the Aiper Scuba V3, which use AI-driven navigation to target debris, deliver more efficient cleaning than more powerful robots, which are often both expensive and heavy.

If you want the fastest cleanup and an easier daily lifting experience, focus on cordless models with advanced sensors. If you have the patience to manage a cord and require continuous cleaning power, a corded model remains the most reliable, high-efficiency workhorse.

The best time to buy is during seasonal shifts or major retail holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, when you can often find significant discounts on these premium units. Given the rapid advancement in AI-enhanced pool cleaning technology, check for sales or brand-specific promotions, as older models are frequently marked down to make way for new releases with improved navigation and sensor suites.
