title: Report: New Mac mini could launch before Apple’s September event
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple could release a new Mac mini “as soon as the coming days, potentially” ahead of next month’s expected iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra event. Here are the details.
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple could release a new Mac mini “as soon as the coming days, potentially” ahead of next month’s expected iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra event. Here are the details.

Likely the last product launch under Tim Cook as CEO

As reported by Mark Gurman, Apple is “gearing up to launch a new version of its Mac mini desktop computer for the first time in almost two years,” following a recent surge in demand driven in part by users looking to run AI applications and models locally.

From the report:

The Mac mini has been a particular pain point for Apple’s supply chain in recent months, with deliveries to customers taking weeks or months to be completed. Cook said the problem would take a while to resolve, and it’s unclear how the new model will affect wait times.

Gurman adds that “Apple has tested versions with both the M5 and M6 generations of its processor line,” in contrast with the upcoming iMac revamp, which will reportedly use M6 chips.

Tonight’s report comes just a few weeks after Apple reiterated that it will begin manufacturing the Mac mini at its Houston facility later this year, as Tim Cook toured the site with Trump administration officials.

The same site houses Apple’s new Advanced Manufacturing Center and is already being used to produce and ship the company’s AI servers. Apple said earlier this month that it had invested hundreds of millions of dollars into the facility in less than nine months.

It remains unclear whether the new Mac mini expected to launch in the coming days is the model Apple plans to begin producing in Houston later this year, though the odds are evidently high.

In his report, Gurman also reiterated several details about what Apple has planned for the Mac over the coming months:

Additional Macs are coming as well, though they are likely to be further out. That includes an iMac with new color options, as well as a refreshed entry-level MacBook Pro. They will use M6 chips, the upcoming generation.

The most significant Mac introduction in the pipeline will be Apple’s first touch-screen computer. The company will add that capability to new MacBook Pro models, in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, that will also include redesigned cases and OLED screens.

Looking further ahead, Gurman reiterated previous reports that Apple is expected to launch new MacBook Air and MacBook Neo models next year, as well as second-generation touchscreen MacBook Pro models powered by M7 chips.

title: OpenAI restores 5-hour Codex and Work limits for ChatGPT Plus users
snippet: Following several weeks during which ChatGPT users were subject only to a weekly usage cap, OpenAI announced today that it is restoring a five-hour limit on Codex and ChatGPT Work for Plus subscribers. Here are the details.
fullText:
Following several weeks during which ChatGPT users were subject only to a weekly usage cap, OpenAI announced today that it is restoring a five-hour limit on Codex and ChatGPT Work for Plus subscribers. Here are the details.

Five-hour cap returns to ChatGPT Plus subscribers

Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, OpenAI’s engineering lead for Codex and ChatGPT, announced tonight that a five-hour usage limit is returning to Codex and ChatGPT Work for Plus subscribers starting tomorrow (25).

After users reach either the five-hour or weekly limit, they can either wait for their usage to reset for the next cycle or purchase additional credits. OpenAI also occasionally resets users’ limits for free, while banked resets can be earned through certain promotions and referral offers.

Over the past few weeks, however, OpenAI temporarily lifted the five-hour usage limit for Codex and ChatGPT Work, leaving only the weekly cap in place.

During this period, the company also reset users’ weekly usage early on several occasions to celebrate milestones, including adding another million active users across the two (now unified) platforms.

However, as Tibo explained tonight on X:

Tomorrow we will bring back the 5h limit for Plus accounts across ChatGPT Work and Codex. I had mentioned this a while ago, but then postponed it.

This is necessary as (a) the 5h limit allows us to smoothen the load on our compute, allowing to keep the plan generous in terms of weekly usage and (b) users on the Plus plan are relatively casual and new users, but then also just accidentally eat through their whole weeks usage and then are confused, making it not a great experience.

We are for the upcoming months keeping the 5h limit not enabled for Pro $100 and Pro $200 subscriptions.

Tibo did not mention any changes for Enterprise or Edu accounts, which currently use a separate credit-based usage system.

title: Apple reverses planned Hide My Email domain change after user pushback
snippet: Apple today announced that it will no longer move iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses to a new domain, reversing course on a change announced just two months ago. Here are the details.
fullText:
Apple today announced that it will no longer move iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses to a new domain, reversing course on a change announced just two months ago. Here are the details.

Apple backtracks on controversial iCloud+ Hide My Email domain change

In mid-June, Apple announced that Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email would soon get a new shared email domain, with both services moving new addresses to private.icloud.com.

For reference, Sign in with Apple currently uses privaterelay.appleid.com, while Hide My Email addresses use the same icloud.com domain as regular iCloud email accounts.

This makes Hide My Email aliases harder for websites to identify and block, since doing so at the domain level would also risk blocking regular iCloud email addresses.

Which is why Apple’s decision to move Hide My Email to the new private.icloud.com domain sparked immediate controversy, as it would make it much easier for platforms to block the privacy feature for users who choose not to share their real email address when creating an account or filling out a form.

Today, Apple announced its decision to scrap the planned Hide My Email domain change. In a developer update, the company said that “after further consideration and reviewing community feedback, iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses will remain on icloud.com.”

Still, the company said that “new Sign in with Apple addresses, previously issued on privaterelay.appleid.com, will be issued on private.icloud.com” starting later this year, adding that “existing addresses on privaterelay.appleid.com will continue to work and forward mail to users without interruption.”

Apple recommended that developers who use Sign in with Apple ensure their account systems, email validation logic, and allowlists accept private.icloud.com alongside the existing privaterelay.appleid.com domain.

title: Apple’s Emergency SOS Live Video is now available in Brazil
snippet: Thanks to a new partnership with RapidSOS, emergency services in Brazil can now request live video from iPhone users. Here are the details.
fullText:
Thanks to a new partnership with RapidSOS, emergency services in Brazil can now request live video from iPhone users. Here are the details.

Emergency SOS Live Video expands to Brazil

Not everyone knows this, but one of the iPhone’s many emergency features is the ability to share live video with emergency services during a call.

Here is Apple on the feature:

Share live video or existing photos with emergency services (not available in all countries or regions)

If requested by emergency services you can use Emergency SOS Live Video to stream live video or upload existing photos and videos to emergency services.

Apple notes that emergency services can retain a copy of the shared video, and that users can choose whether to accept or decline a request to share video or photos. Apple also says that “Emergency SOS Live Video is available on iPhone 14 or later, is subject to device limitations, and may not be available in all situations.”

That said, public safety AI company RapidSOS announced today that Apple’s Emergency SOS Live Video is now available to emergency communications centers (ECCs) across Brazil, allowing iPhone users to “securely share live video at the request of 190 during an emergency.”

190 is Brazil’s equivalent of 911.

RapidSOS notes that this is the same technology it first enabled for emergency services in the United States with the release of iOS 18 in September 2024, and adds three key features of this integration:

Simple and Secure for Callers: During an emergency call, if the telecommunicator determines video would help, they can send a request to the caller’s device. The caller sees a prompt and can share their camera’s live video with a single tap. The feature is encrypted by default and the caller can stop sharing at any time. 

ECC-Controlled: Telecommunicators initiate every video request. ECCs decide if and when to activate the feature for their agency, and can control access by role.

Integrated into RapidSOS UNITE: The feature is accessible from within RapidSOS UNITE at no additional cost to Brazil ECCs using UNITE core modules.

Commenting on today’s announcement, RapidSOS founder and CEO Michael Martin said, “RapidSOS was proud to be the first platform to enable this capability in the United States,” adding that the company is “committed to bringing that same life-saving technology to emergency services around the world.”

title: Epic fights Apple’s bid to seal key data behind proposed fees on linked-out purchases
snippet: Epic says Apple is making overly broad requests to seal information it says is central to determining what the company can charge developers for linked-out purchases. Here are the details.
fullText:
Epic says Apple is making overly broad requests to seal information it says is central to determining what the company can charge developers for linked-out purchases. Here are the details.

Epic says Apple is trying to ‘conceal information from the public’

A few days ago, Apple submitted its proposal outlining how much it believes it should be allowed to charge as a commission on purchases completed outside the App Store through external links.

Apple’s proposal calls for:

15% for standard apps, which are subject to a 30% in-app purchase (“IAP”) commission;

10% for the Video Partner Program (“VPP”), the News Partner Program (“NPP”), the Mini Apps Partner Program (“MPP”), and subscription renewals; and

5% for Small Business Program apps.

In addition to the proposal itself, Apple submitted supporting expert reports, alongside a request to seal portions of those filings containing financial data, link-out adoption estimates, developer survey results, and other information Apple considers commercially sensitive.

Epic has now filed an opposition to Apple’s request, arguing “Apple again seeks to conceal

information from the public and unnecessarily hamper proceedings.”

According to Epic, Apple has not sufficiently justified why portions of its proffer and supporting expert reports should remain sealed or redacted.

Epic argues that there is a high bar for keeping court records out of public view, particularly when the information at issue is central to determining Apple’s proposed commission rates.

The company cites past cases in which courts rejected sealing requests for failing to demonstrate specific harm. Among them, it points to decisions finding that “broad allegations of harm, unsubstantiated by specific examples or articulated reasoning” and “tepid and general justifications” are insufficient to justify withholding information from the public.

Epic also says that some of the information Apple wants to seal is outdated, while other parts are publicly available. Epic takes particular issue with Apple’s bid to seal data showing the rate at which apps have adopted external purchase links since the court’s contempt order compelling it to allow developers to direct users to external purchasing options.

From the filing:

Apple repeatedly seeks to seal its assessment of developers’ rates of link-out adoption. For example, Apple seeks to redact the percentage of apps, based on size, that it says have adopted link-outs since the Court’s Contempt Order. (…) That information is important to these proceedings and, in any event, is not competitively sensitive, so it should not be sealed.

Epic closes out its opposition filing by asking the court to deny certain of Apple’s sealing requests, pointing to a separate 19-page exhibit in which it objects, in whole or in part, to more than 60 proposed redactions across Apple’s proffer and supporting expert reports.

Should the court side with Apple or with Epic? Let us know in the comments.

title: iOS 27 adds three new iPhone features I’ve been really loving
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features across Messages, Notes, Apple Wallet, CarPlay, and more. Here are three of my favorite new iOS 27 features so far.
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features across Messages, Notes, Apple Wallet, CarPlay, and more. Here are three of my favorite new iOS 27 features so far.

#1: Siri app

Siri is completely new in iOS 27, rebuilt from the ground up for the AI era. And one exciting upgrade is the dedicated Siri app. From Apple’s press release:

When users want to revisit a past conversation or kick off a new one, they can open the all-new dedicated Siri app. The Siri app uses iCloud to privately sync conversational history across a user’s products, so they can start chatting with Siri on Mac and continue the conversation on iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro, bringing together rich conversations in one place.

The Siri app provides a convenient, go-to home for any question you have. It’s especially great for chatbot-style conversations that go beyond a simple request.

With the popularity of apps like ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini, a dedicated Siri app makes a lot of sense. And since it’s pre-installed on the iPhone Home Screen, I suspect it could quickly become a go-to app for many users.

#2: One-tap suggestions in Messages

iOS 27 has plenty of Apple Intelligence features that don’t “feel like AI” but simply offer convenient tools. One shining example is actionable suggestions in the Messages app. Per Apple:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

Plenty of messaging apps have tried to infuse AI via an integrated chatbot in your conversation. I’ve never been a fan of that approach. 

But one-tap suggestions in Messages offer similar utility in many respects, and are quicker and easier to use than typing out an AI request. It’s the kind of AI feature I can fully get behind.

#3: ‘Smart Event Details’ in Apple Calendar

title: iPhone Ultra is coming, but it might not have these key features
snippet: Apple’s first foldable iPhone will reportedly be announced in just over two weeks. Despite potentially being branded as the “iPhone Ultra” and priced at over $2,000, it will have several big limitations.
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable iPhone will reportedly be announced in just over two weeks. Despite potentially being branded as the “iPhone Ultra” and priced at over $2,000, it will have several big limitations.

#1: Telephoto camera

The iPhone Ultra will reportedly have two cameras, including a Main camera and an Ultra Wide camera. It is not expected to have a telephoto camera. For many people, this will probably be the biggest limitation of the device’s design.

The Main and Ultra Wide cameras on the iPhone Ultra are both expected to be 48MP, similar to the current base model iPhone 17.

#2: Action button

According to various leaked iPhone Ultra dummy units, the device will not have an Action button. In fact, it appears it will be Apple’s first-ever iPhone without a mute switch of any kind.

The dummy units show that the left edge of the device is completely bare. The side button and Camera Control button will reportedly be on the right-hand edge of the iPhone Ultra. The volume buttons, meanwhile, will be located on the top edge of the device similar to the iPad mini.

#3: Face ID

The iPhone Ultra is not expected to have Face ID. Instead, it will reportedly have Touch ID in the side button. This will mark Apple’s first iPhone without Face ID since the technology first debuted in the iPhone X in 2017.

For the iPhone Ultra, Apple has likely opted for Touch ID instead of Face ID because of the device’s ultra-thin design. Additionally, Apple would also need two sets of Face ID components: one for the outer display and one for the inner display.

Apple still uses Touch ID in the power button on most iPads, including the base iPad, iPad mini, and iPad Air.

Image credit: Sonny Dickson

#4: MagSafe

While Apple may have a surprise for us, it looks like the iPhone Ultra won’t support MagSafe wireless charging. Leaked iPhone Ultra dummy units do not show the MagSafe ring on the back of the device.

The iPhone Ultra may offer standard wireless charging like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 foldable. Based on current rumors, however, MagSafe seems unlikely.

#5: Physical SIM

According to sources including Ming-Chi Kuo and Bloomberg, the iPhone Ultra will be eSIM-only worldwide.

This is likely due to the foldable iPhone’s ultra-thin design. The iPhone Air is also incredibly thin and is eSIM-only worldwide. The iPhone 17 and iPhone 17 Pro, meanwhile, are eSIM-only in the United States and select other countries. In other markets, like China, the devices retain their physical SIM card slots. 

Wrap up

It’s clear that Apple’s foldable iPhone Ultra will come with several major compromises. The question is whether the utility of the innovative folding design is enough to make up for those other limitations.

Personally, I’m looking forward to trying the iPhone Ultra. The compromise that worries me most is the lack of MagSafe. I currently use an iPhone Air, so I’m used to life without a telephoto camera. I think I could adapt to Touch ID pretty quickly. However, I have MagSafe chargers all over the place, so going back to regular wireless charging or full-time wired charging would be a big change.

title: iPhone 18 Pro’s new price might be better than expected
snippet: Apple will launch the iPhone 18 Pro soon, and a new report indicates its price might not be as high as several analysts have suggested. Here are the details.
fullText:
Apple will launch the iPhone 18 Pro soon, and a new report indicates its price might not be as high as several analysts have suggested. Here are the details.

iPhone 18 Pro could get modest $100 price increase following similar moves by Samsung, Google

Apple will unveil its flagship iPhone 18 Pro very soon, with the September event likely to be announced in the next week.

While there’s a lot we already know about iPhone 18 Pro, including rumored camera upgrades, design updates, and more—pricing remains a big question mark.

Based on rising component costs for memory, storage, and a new camera system, analysts have predicted iPhone 18 Pro pricing that starts at $1,299 or $1,399. That’s just for the base model.

But the price might not be so bad after all. Mark Gurman writes at Bloomberg:

The company has been watching how Samsung and Google respond to higher component costs. Both raised prices on their latest phones by about $100. Matching that would put the iPhone 18 Pro at $1,199, up about 9%. Given the severity of the memory crunch, that would be a fairly modest bump and suggest Apple is absorbing some of the added costs itself. The company has already warned of pressure on gross margins this quarter — a sign it’s not passing on all of its growing expenses.

Apple has reasons not to push too far. A $100 increase would keep the iPhone broadly in Samsung’s pricing territory and avoid the sticker shock of the steeper hikes imposed on some Macs and iPads. 

$100 increases would mean going from $1,099 to $1,199 for iPhone 18 Pro and $1,199 to $1,299 for iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Previous reports have indicated Apple might reserve more significant increases for its higher storage models. If the company does stick to $100 increases for entry 256GB models, we could still see $150 or $200 increases on models with 512GB, 1TB, and above.

My biggest issue when I go back and forth between a MagSafe wallet and a traditional wallet is that a lot of MagSafe wallets are really just card slots. I still carry cash and like my driver’s license to be in a clear window. The TUCCH PU Leather Mag Wallet does something different that most MagSafe wallets. MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

It actually folds like a wallet

With strong magnets, it stays closed on its own and turns into a genuinely portable, slim wallet the moment you pop it off your phone. If you’ve ever had a credit card start sliding out of an open MagSafe slot in your pocket, you’ll understand why this is nice. Again

As I mentioned in the beginning, the feature that drew me to the TUCCH wallet is the ID slot. Most MagSafe wallets have a single open pocket, so your cards just clump together. You get 6 card slots in total, including 1 clear window built specifically for your driver’s license, plus 2 quick-access cutouts for the cards you use the most. These are minor features, but they are super nice and welcome. With Walmart moving to supporting Apple Pay, I’ll need to pull out my card a lot les thankfully. 

Build quality and magnetic strength

The wallet is made of PU leather and stays flat even when all 6 slots are loaded with credit cards. TUCCH says the magnets are strong enough to stay attached even if you shake your iPhone fairly hard, and that tracks with how good MagSafe wallets in this price range have gotten over the past couple of years. 

Wrap up

At under $30, this wallet offers some nice features if traditional MagSafe-slot wallets get on your nerves. The fold-over design with the clear driver’s license window is really a nice change from what is mostly on the market. It feels like a traditional wallet with MagSafe vs. a MagSafe wallet.

fullText:
Developers can now install macOS 27 Golden Gate beta 7, just a week after the rollout of beta 6. Here are the details.

Apple rolls out macOS 27 beta 7

Last Monday, Apple ended a three-week beta hiatus with macOS 27 Golden Gate beta 6, which introduced redesigned traffic light window controls. Instead of the flat red, yellow, and green circles, macOS 27 beta 6 added Liquid Glass-like (almost Aqua-like, really) effects to the minimize, maximize, and close buttons.

Aside from that, macOS 27 Golden Gate beta 6 did not include any other user-facing new features or improvements, which suggests that Apple might be using these last few beta releases to squish bugs and work on performance and security improvements ahead of the official rollout.

macOS 27 Golden Gate introduces the new Siri app, alongside the revamped Siri AI. It also features the new AI-powered Shortcuts app, which accepts natural-language prompts to create shortcuts, as well as a prompt-based Safari extension builder.

Additionally, macOS 27 Golden Gate introduces new Golden Gate-themed wallpapers and screensavers, while reverting to fixed-radius corners for windows and apps. That reverses a change made in macOS 26, which adjusted corner radii based on the contents of each window’s or app’s menu bar.

The build version for macOS 27 Golden Gate beta 7 is 26A5421a. We are digging through the new beta and will report back with what we find.

Installing the macOS 27 Golden Gate beta

Back up your Mac

Open System Settings

Go to General ⇾ Software Update

Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates

iOS 27 is all about Siri AI

iOS 27 is one of Apple’s most AI-focused iPhone updates yet. The headline change is Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt assistant powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and new Apple Foundation Models.

Siri AI brings richer conversations, personal context, broader world knowledge, on-screen awareness, and deeper app actions across the system.

On iPhone, Siri AI also gets a new visual experience tied to the Dynamic Island, plus a dedicated Siri app for revisiting conversations across devices.

Visual Intelligence joins Siri too, including a new Siri mode in the Camera app and improvements that affect Camera Control on iPhone.

Apple Intelligence is also expanding across apps. iOS 27 adds AI-powered improvements for Photos, Safari, Passwords, Mail, Messages, Phone, Shortcuts, Home, and more. As we covered in our breakdown of Apple’s new Foundation Models, some capabilities run on-device, while others use Private Cloud Compute.

More iOS 27 features and changes

Beyond Siri and Apple Intelligence, iOS 27 includes a variety of iPhone-specific changes. Apple has refined the Liquid Glass design introduced last year, including a new Liquid Glass transparency slider for adjusting the look of system UI.

There are also performance improvements for app launches, Photos loading, Camera launch in Low Power Mode, AirDrop transfers, and Wi-Fi-to-cellular transitions.

Other iPhone changes include Photos keywords and star ratings, customizable slideshows, smoother Camera behavior, continuous sending in Messages, Dual Capture in FaceTime, custom EQ for AirPods, new recovery options, easier Apple Pay card switching, and AI-generated wallpaper creation.

title: Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Where are the upgrades? [Video]
snippet: A year in tech used to bring about big, bold changes. Today, things are iterative, merely refinements, and that has never been more apparent than going from the Pixel 10 to the Pixel 11. Here’s what you need to know.
fullText:
A year in tech used to bring about big, bold changes. Today, things are iterative, merely refinements, and that has never been more apparent than going from the Pixel 10 to the Pixel 11. Here’s what you need to know.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 10 Pro: Closer together than ever? [Video]

Protect your Pixel 11 with a dbrand case or skin sponsors of 9to5Google

Hardware

Take one look, particularly at the Obsidian Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 side-by-side, and there is basically nothing to separate the two phones. You could be forgiven for not knowing what and where the minimal changes have been made.

These phones have identical screens, almost identical dimensions, and the Obsidian model even uses the exact same shade of deep gray. Copy-paste would be a very quick and easy criticism, and it would be justified in lots of ways.

	

To push back slightly, the display is still great on both phones. 3000 nits peak brightness, but no change to the bezels, which is an annoyance. The fingerprint scanner is still fast and fluid, with no changes to how quickly you’ll get back into your phone, and the Face Unlock has not changed despite rumors ahead of launch that it might.

Yes, the Pixelsnap magnets on Pixel 11 are stronger this year

On the back of the phone, there are more alterations. The camera bar has the most changes. The metal visor edge is gone, and the camera bar takes up a tiny bit more space. It doesn’t protrude as much from the backplate, which means that when you put the phone face up, it’s flatter on a desk or surface. This feels inconsequential, but many people complain about it on other phones.

There is also a change to the camera’s LED flash. It is within the glass, so it has better diffusion. That means it should be softer when used. Whether due to these minor tweaks and less metal on the camera bar, the Pixel 11 is 6g lighter than the Pixel 10. You can notice in the hand right away. It feels inconsequential, but at 197g versus 204g, that could be important if you care about how heavy your phone is.

Software

There are so few differences in Android 17 experience on the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 that it boils down to just a few little functions that you may never even use. Gemini Intelligence was supposed to be coming to more devices per the original announcement pre-Google IO, but it looks like most of the functions will be locked to the newest devices – at least for a while. That’s a big disappointment, given that not all of the functionality is even fully here at launch.

Material 3 Expressive is maybe applied a little more liberally, and there are new Pixel-exclusive icons for the camera, calculator, and clock apps. They’ll probably get backported, but the only usability change appears to be Rambler. This is baked into Gboard and is a new, improved voice-to-text tool that can handle changes, vocal tics, and even course correction when you are dictating, a lot better than the previous voice-to-text tool.

Save that, you’ll struggle to tell the two phones running side-by-side apart. The improved storage speeds on the base Pixel 11 are something that is a good quality of life upgrade. In almost all cases, launching from cold into an application, it will be faster on the newer device. It isn’t exponentially faster, but it does make a difference. This isn’t always the case, like if something is already in RAM, but there is a speed boost.

Without trying to turn this into a benchmark competition, Tensor G5 vs. G6 isn’t much of a leap either. Most of the things we’ve tried to do are fine; games seemingly run at acceptable levels. Neither phone is anywhere near the top of the performance charts, which, to many people, is a very valid cause for concern given the retail pricing structure. Without any discounts, the Pixel 11 is one of the most expensive phones in a lot of global markets and won’t compete directly with the likes of Poco, etc.

Without giving Google a pass, you probably won’t notice unless you are trying to do lots of things at once or care about the highest benchmark scores. I feel like we’re in dire need of a big generational leap; this is not it.

Battery

The battery longevity of the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 is almost in complete lockstep. Neither device in our testing appears to have an edge over the other. The battery sizes are almost identical, the charging speeds don’t differ, save for the Extreme Charging Mode, but the reality is that the so-called “fast charging” is not exactly “fast” in the traditional sense. Y

You’ll be waiting at least an hour for the Pixel 10 or Pixel 11 to go from 0-100%. Even when using that new faster charging mode, it only works up to 50% battery level and is designed to just give you a boost of battery in a shorter period. I can’t see any major difference in charge speed when airplane mode is enabled on the Pixel 10; it feels like a nothing burger in that sense.

Neither phone has a “bad” battery, nor are these devices particularly amazing like a two-day phone. Just solid and dependable.

Camera

Google listened to some fairly harsh criticism of some of the Pixel 10 camera system downgrades and decided a new sensor was required. The 48-megapixel main sensor isn’t quite a full return to a flagship-level system like the Pro phones, but a physical sensor size increase should improve the light gathering by over 50%. 

More light will be good in all kinds of situations. Background blur is improved, giving better natural focus falloff. Every other sensor is identical. However, the zoom lens is now able to go to 30x on the Pixel 11. 

Pixel 11 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Can a re-run contend with a re-do [Video]

On the tangible changes front, color tuning is slightly improved on the Pixel 11 series using the default “Original” camera setting, but it’s the software functions that truly differentiate the camera systems on the Pixel 10 and 11.

Camera Looks are the headline addition here. This gives you the ability to set a default tonal look or add them in real-time rather than requiring tuning after the fact. There isn’t an extensive library, but you can tune all of the “Looks” to suit your own preferences.

Joining this is Magic Capture. This is a new mode that turns a short video into multiple photos of the key moments. It’s like a highlight-reel camera: you just point, record, and let Gemini pick out the best bits. It’s eerily reminiscent of the Clips camera or an upgraded Top Shot. It works, and it works really well.

There are also tons of new tools within the Creator mode section, including a built-in teleprompter, audio visualizer, new social media gridlines, and the ability to save your video files to a specific folder. All great added functions, but nothing truly groundbreaking, just “nice to have” functionality.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Is there even enough here to consider a change?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

There are no meaningful upgrades to the Pixel 11 for anyone looking with any sort of envy at it while clutching the Pixel 10. Stagnation is something the entire industry has to grapple with at the moment, and two generations of minor upgrades have left us in a no-man’s land for many people.

If you can hold on, which I think is wise when talking about any piece of technology right now, given the increased prices and lack of innovation, you will see bigger gains when you are ready to finally make the switch.

Nobody with the Pixel 10 should seriously consider the Pixel 11 unless a trade-in deal nets you the new phone for free or close to it. Camera nerds will balk at the measly upgrades, the design critics will be disappointed in seeing what is effectively the same phone again, and everyone else will scratch their heads, wondering what is actually new. Google is far from the worst offender as of late, but the company is our main focus, so criticism is due when we see little change.

To temper some of the negativity, there are good things about the Pixel 11 when compared to the Pixel 10. It does banish the slower, almost ancient UFS 3.1 storage. The new chip is another nudge in the right direction for performance. Getting back to a bigger, brighter main camera sensor that isn’t the same as the A-series is good for everyone.

We can’t tell you what to do with your money, but ask yourself, “Is there enough here for me to want to switch?” In 99.9% of cases, the answer is probably “no.”

title: The Pixel 11 Pro’s flashlight is a little bit worse because of ‘HiLight’ [Gallery]
snippet: “HiLight” on the Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t provide much utility, but making matters worse, it also worsens a common use case of every other phone’s rear LED – the ability to use it as a flashlight.
fullText:
“HiLight” on the Pixel 11 Pro doesn’t provide much utility, but making matters worse, it also worsens a common use case of every other phone’s rear LED – the ability to use it as a flashlight.

Most smartphones have a built-in rear LED that’s primarily designed as a camera flash, but doubles as a flashlight in a pinch. It’s never as good as a dedicated flashlight, but it’s good enough for navigating a dark area at night or those times when you need to shine just a bit of extra light on something. 

The Pixel 11 Pro family, though, has been noticeably worse when it comes to the flashlight.

We noticed on our review units in recent days that the flashlight simply isn’t as strong as past generations or other phones on Pixel 11 Pro / XL / Fold. Personally, I noticed this while going through my home late at night, with the flashlight simply not illuminating the room at any sort of distance. Especially after the first few feet away from the device, the lighting just became useless. Will Sattelberg calls the flashlight function “unusable,” referring to a home repair where he thought the phone had somehow set the flashlight to half-brightness. Damien Wilde further pointed out that the diffuser being used for “HiLight” is likely at least part of the cause, though that is admittedly nice for using the LED as an actual camera flash. You have to be closer to subjects, but the lighting effect does visually look better.

	

You can see the difference pretty clearly when you compare the Pixel 11 Pro to other devices, which we’ve done in the images below. Comparing Pixel 11 Pro XL to Pixel 10 Pro XL, there’s a distinct difference in the lighting intensity, though the last generation wasn’t especially bright either. Compared to even a three-year-old iPhone 15 Pro, Apple’s flash is brighter. Throwing in Galaxy Z Fold 7 for good measure, Samsung’s flash is also a tiny bit stronger than either of Google’s, but it’s abundantly clear that Pixel 11 Pro XL is the worst out of the bunch.

Pixel 11 Pro XL
Pixel 10 Pro XL
Galaxy Z Fold 7
iPhone 15 Pro

As mentioned, this gets worse at distance. We ran this test similarly to one from a Redditor, but in adding some additional subjects in the background, you can see how much quicker the Pixel 11 Pro’s lighting fades away.

Here’s another angle:

Pixel 11 Pro XL
Pixel 10 Pro XL
Galaxy Z Fold 7
iPhone 15 Pro

Meanwhile, the actual camera flash results are more or less comparable across Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 10 Pro XL, though processing differences must be taken into account. The lighting is less harsh on the newer device, and it’s also warmer in color temperature. 

Pixel 11 Pro XL
Pixel 10 Pro XL

And, to be clear, pictures can only do so much justice to this. I’d argue that the difference is bigger in real life.

	

What this whole thing brought to light for me – pun mostly not intended – is just how far behind Google is in this regard. 

The flashlight on your phone isn’t something you think about in daily use or even when comparing devices, but when it suddenly gets worse, you can’t help but notice the difference. “HiLight” has resulted in a clear, though not major difference in the Pixel 11 Pro’s flashlight this year. Google should absolutely be taking notes, because this is one of those subtle problems that rubs users the wrong way, and I’m absolutely sure someone switching from an iPhone to a Pixel 11 will notice this and take issue with it.

What do you think?

title: Gemini on Pixel 11 Pro testing ‘Device help’ tool
snippet: On the Pixel 11 Pro, we’re seeing a new “Device help” tool for the Gemini app that provides personalized and conversational assistance with your phone.
fullText:
On the Pixel 11 Pro, we’re seeing a new “Device help” tool for the Gemini app that provides personalized and conversational assistance with your phone. 

From the ‘plus’ menu inside the Gemini app or through the overlay, there’s a new “Device help” tool at the bottom of the list just above Personal Intelligence.

Badged with the “Labs” label, you can “Get help with your device.” The icon being used matches Proactive Assistance. This “Device Help Agent” can manage settings, help troubleshoot issues, and detail features:

Adjust & customize settings: Change display settings (Dark theme, brightness, screen timeout), sound and vibration modes, Do Not Disturb, and Digital Wellbeing features.

Troubleshoot issues: Diagnose and resolve problems with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data, battery drain, audio, or app performance.

Manage battery & storage: Check battery usage, set up Battery Saver, review storage breakdown, and find ways to free up space.

Review apps & permissions: Audit permissions like location, camera, and microphone access, manage app notifications, and configure app timers.

Learn device features: Provide step-by-step guidance on Pixel features, gestures, camera capabilities, and privacy controls.

That being said, it appears to just be using the existing “Device Assistance” connected app, which was previously called “Utilities.”  

	

As of this morning, we’re only seeing this on Pixel 11 Pro devices after updating to Google app beta 17.52. It’s not available on the base Pixel 11 or older phones we checked.

title: Philips Hue’s new, cheaper Sync hardware leaks with ‘Camera’ and ‘Box Lite’ [Gallery]
snippet: The Philips Hue Sync Box lets you match up your smart home lighting to what’s on your TV, but it’s not cheap. A new “Lite” version is coming, though, which cuts the price drastically by only having a single HDMI input, while a “Sync Camera” simplifies the setup for TVs without additional inputs.
fullText:
The Philips Hue Sync Box lets you match up your smart home lighting to what’s on your TV, but it’s not cheap. A new “Lite” version is coming, though, which cuts the price drastically by only having a single HDMI input, while a “Sync Camera” simplifies the setup for TVs without additional inputs.

Spotted by HueBlog on a retailer’s website – where it’s still live – the “Hue Play Sync Box Lite” promises the same core functionality as the standard Sync Box 8K that launched last year. It acts as a middleman between your device and your TV, taking signal from the HDMI input to sync your room’s lights to the content on screen.

The difference with this model is that it only supports a single device. Where the standard model supports up to four inputs, this only has a single HDMI port for input, then another for output to the TV. This model is also limited in terms of performance – 4K60 or 1080p120. 

At £109.99, it’s roughly a 60% drop in price compared to the £299.99 Sync Box 8K. In the US, it should land somewhere around $140-150, based on the 8K’s current $385 price tag. 

	

HueBlog also previously reported on another potentially more affordable Sync solution from Philips Hue, a “Sync Camera.” This TV-mounted device watches the actual TV screen to process lighting effects, doing away with HDMI altogether. While less elegant, this also comes with the benefit of being able to sync content from the TV’s own built-in apps, rather than relying on external hardware.

Pricing on the “Sync Camera” is unknown.

It’s possible both devices could arrive as soon as next month, with the IFA trade show set for early September.

title: Apple is about to launch five new products that I’m very excited for
snippet: Apple’s biggest product launches of the year are almost here, with 10+ new products coming very soon. Here are the five new Apple products I’m the most excited about.
fullText:
Apple’s biggest product launches of the year are almost here, with 10+ new products coming very soon. Here are the five new Apple products I’m the most excited about.

iPhone Ultra

The first foldable iPhone is almost here, and I’m thrilled to get what’s essentially an iPhone and iPad mini in the same device.

Even though we’ve gotten plenty of leaks about hardware, iPhone Ultra’s software is what will ultimately be a huge contributor to the overall experience. So I’m fascinated to see how Apple adapts iOS 27 to feel native and more capable on a foldable.

I haven’t tried a foldable smartphone before, but everything I’ve read makes the form factor seem like the future. Apple has clearly taken its time before entering the foldable market, and my expectations are high that it will be worth the wait.

HomePad

I’ve been wanting Apple to take the smart home seriously for many years. And when Mark Gurman first broke a detailed report on the forthcoming ‘HomePad’ in late 2024, it signaled that such a shift was coming. 

Everything about the HomePad sounds very appealing to me. I’m excited for Apple Photos slideshows, security camera functionality, Siri AI, playing Apple Music with lyrics onscreen, and more.

Siri AI delays led to a much longer wait for HomePad than expected. But all signs point to an imminent launch, and I’m ready to see how Apple casts vision for a new smart home era via the HomePad and other new Home products.

New Apple TV 4K

It’s been four years since the current Apple TV 4K launched. The product doesn’t need annual updates, but AI’s emergence has created a lot of potential for an overhauled experience.

I’m ready to see how Siri AI, a more powerful chip, and other hardware and software upgrades can combine to make for a worthwhile Apple TV upgrade.

With the new Apple TV 4K launching around the same time as the camera-equipped HomePad, I’m also curious to see if old rumors of a camera-equipped model might come true. FaceTime on the big screen without needing to use my iPhone would be really great.

MacBook Ultra

I’ve used an iPad Pro as my main computer for over a decade. And a big reason I made that switch in 2015 was that the Mac always lagged behind the iPad in getting innovative hardware and software features.

Apple silicon coming to the Mac has solved some of those problems. And macOS has increasingly been updated in-step with iOS and iPadOS too. But there are still several ways the Mac feels tied to the past rather than the future.

MacBook Ultra, I suspect, will change that. Bringing touch support to the Mac, plus OLED, a Dynamic Island, a new design, and possibly even a cellular option all sound very compelling. It’s the kind of Mac update I’ve been waiting for, so I can’t wait to see what Apple unveils.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

I’m undecided whether I’m going to choose Series 12 or Ultra 4 for my new Apple Watch this year. Either way though, I’m eager to see the new models because of one key rumored upgrade: a new S-class chip built for the AI era.

Apple Watch chips don’t change very often. Even though the company does make minor updates to its S-class chips most years, CPU performance only improves about every three years. As a result, the S9 in 2023 was the last time a new Watch chip meaningfully improved.

But rumors indicate a new, more powerful chip is coming in this year’s Watch models. It will be the first one built for the AI era, and couldn’t be timed better for Siri AI.

Which upcoming Apple products are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

title: Waze alerts are coming to navigation in Rivian’s electric vehicles
snippet: Waze’s live alerts that track police sightings, speed cameras, and more are coming to the Rivian R1 and R2.
fullText:
Waze’s live alerts that track police sightings, speed cameras, and more are coming to the Rivian R1 and R2.

The Waze app supplements driving directions with real-time alerts based on driver input from other cars on the road with you. The feature has since been picked up by other navigation apps like Google Maps. In Rivian’s vehicles, however, some of these features take time since the company chooses to use proprietary software rather than Android Auto.

According to Rivian’s Wassym Bensaid, Waze’s real-time alerts will soon be available in the R1 and R2 on its own software. The post notes the feature will roll out with support for speed cameras and police sighting reports, which likely means other alert types like crash reports might tag along at a later date.

Real-time alerts from Waze are coming to R1 and R2 in-vehicle navigation, starting with speed cameras and police reports in the 2026.31 OTA update. More data and alerts to follow! pic.twitter.com/HYUEjzuDwQ

— Wassym Bensaid (@WassymBensaid) August 21, 2026

The company says those real-time reports will be supported in the upcoming 2026.31 OTA update. Waze’s in-vehicle navigation for Rivian’s vehicles will most likely continue to expand, as mentioned, but no further details are available.

title: Affordable iPhone accessories for CarPlay worth trying
snippet: CarPlay can make any vehicle feel significantly more comfortable and family. Still, the experience is not always perfect out of the box. Some cars still require a wired connection, others lack CarPlay entirely, and what about keeping your iPhone charged and cooled on long trips? Fortunately, improving those areas doesn’t require a big investment. These affordable accessories cover everything from wireless CarPlay and MagSafe charging to cable management and complete displays for older vehicles.
fullText:
CarPlay can make any vehicle feel significantly more comfortable and family. Still, the experience is not always perfect out of the box.

Some cars still require a wired connection, others lack CarPlay entirely, and what about keeping your iPhone charged and cooled on long trips?

Fortunately, improving those areas doesn’t require a big investment. These affordable accessories cover everything from wireless CarPlay and MagSafe charging to cable management and complete displays for older vehicles.

Convert wired CarPlay to wireless

If your vehicle already supports wired CarPlay, the Carlinkit Mini Ultra 3 can eliminate the cable while retaining the car’s touchscreen, steering-wheel controls, built-in microphone, and original audio system.

The compact adapter includes USB-A and USB-C connections. After the initial pairing process, it automatically reconnects when you start the car. It also supports wireless Android Auto for Android 11 and newer, making it useful in a vehicle shared by iPhone and Android users.

One important note is that this adapter requires factory-installed wired CarPlay. It cannot add CarPlay to an unsupported vehicle.

The Carlinkit Mini Ultra 3 is available for $43.99 with Prime shipping.

Add CarPlay to almost any older vehicle

For a car without CarPlay, a portable display is often the easiest upgrade. The Krunia 9.26-inch portable CarPlay screen costs $89.99 and adds wireless CarPlay without requiring you to remove the factory radio.

The screen supports Bluetooth, AUX, and FM audio connections, along with Siri, Android Auto, and over-the-air firmware updates. It also includes a backup camera, although installing that part requires running a cable to the rear of the vehicle.

This is a compelling middle ground for someone who wants CarPlay but does not want to replace the dashboard stereo.

Install a permanent CarPlay receiver

A portable display will not suit every dashboard. For a cleaner permanent installation, the BOSS Audio BVCP9700A is a relatively affordable double-DIN receiver with a 7-inch touchscreen, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, Bluetooth, and support for a backup camera.

The receiver is available for $164.99. However, buyers should check their vehicle before ordering. A dash kit, wiring harness, steering-wheel-control adapter, or professional installation could add to the total cost.

Keep your iPhone cool while charging

Wireless charging, navigation, sunlight, and a hot dashboard can create a rough combination for an iPhone. The ESR CryoBoost MagSafe car charger addresses that with an integrated cooling fan.

It combines a magnetic vent or dashboard mount with wireless charging and active cooling. At $29.99, it is an especially good fit for drivers who use wireless CarPlay but still want to charge their iPhone during longer trips.

Skip charging with a simpler MagSafe mount

Not every route requires wireless charging. The standard ESR MagSafe car mount holds an iPhone on the dashboard or air vent without adding another charging cable.

It was available for $15.99 and includes metal rings for phones or cases without built-in magnetic support. This could also be the better option in hot climates, where charging can generate additional heat.

Replace an unreliable CarPlay cable

Many CarPlay problems come down to a worn out or poor fitting cable. The Anker Nano USB-A-to-USB-C CarPlay cable provides a braided data connection for newer USB-C iPhones and is available for $11.99.

Drivers with an iPhone 14 or older can use Anker’s PowerLine Flow USB-A-to-Lightning cable, which is available for $17.99.

Add fast charging for the best experience

The USB port that operates wired CarPlay often charges slowly. The Anker 323 car charger plugs into a 12V outlet and provides one USB-C port alongside one USB-A port.

At $14.99, it is an affordable way to charge a passenger’s phone or power another accessory without interfering with the vehicle’s CarPlay connection — or speed up your own charging with wireless CarPlay use.

Clean up the installation

A $6.99 package of adhesive cable clips can make a portable CarPlay display or wired phone mount look considerably more intentional. The clips can guide cables along the edge of the dashboard and keep them away from the shifter, pedals, and cup holders.

CarPlay doesn’t require a new vehicle or an elaborate stereo upgrade. Depending on what your car already supports, spending anywhere from $12 on a better cable to around $90 on a complete portable display can make the daily experience considerably more convenient.

Want to do more with CarPlay? See 9to5Mac’s running list of more than 120 iPhone apps that work with CarPlay.

Confirmed in a thread posted to Mastodon, GrapheneOS says that while the initial focus with its Motorola partnership is on a “regular non-folding” device, plans are in place to support future version  of the Motorola Razr Fold and Motorola Razr Ultra foldables. The latter would be the first flip form factor supported by GrapheneOS, while Pixel 11 Pro Fold will get support later too alongside the rest of Google’s latest generation.

We do plan to support Motorola’s Razr Fold and Razr Ultra (flip) devices in addition to a regular device. We already support the original Pixel Fold (Pixel 7) along with the Pixel 9 Pro Fold and Pixel 10 Pro Fold. We still plan to add support for 11th gen Pixels including the Pixel 11 Pro Fold too.

Supporting a flip device with vertical folding would be a new form factor for GrapheneOS. The main use case for those is a tiny phone to use with one hand in the folded form factor. The tablet-style folding devices we already support are extremely useful for web browsing, reading, maps, etc.

As it stands today, the 2026 versions of Razr Fold and Razr Ultra are “close” to meeting requirements for GrapheneOS, just missing a few features including memory tagging (MTE) and secure element integration, both supported on Pixel devices. Motorola is apparently integrating these into its 2027 releases, with the next generation of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips having better support for MTE.

The thread also brings out that Motorola devices with GrapheneOS will get 7 years of OS updates, with Motorola directly doing a “large portion” of the work in bringing the privacy-focused experience to its devices.

title: Google Clock and Pixel Magnifier roll out icon redesigns
snippet: While available on all Android devices, Google Clock received an icon redesign alongside the Pixel 11 launch. An update to Pixel Magnifier also brings a new icon.
fullText:
While available on all Android devices, Google Clock received an icon redesign alongside the Pixel 11 launch. An update to Pixel Magnifier also brings a new icon. 

The new Google Clock icon takes after Pixel Watch faces with thick pills used for the hour and minute hands. The blue face features a gradient effect, but no longer goes edge-to-edge. Rather, like all first-party Google apps these days, it is placed on a white background.

(This leaves Chrome as the lone major exception. Compared to Clock and YouTube Music, it is a much bigger app and does have its own identity. That said, the circular browser icon is already placed in a rounded square on macOS.)

Old vs. new

	

The non-live icon places the hands at 9:10 with a dot at the 30-minute mark. Meanwhile, the app shortcuts see some minor icon tweaks, while it’s now “Create alarm/timer” instead of “New alarm/timer.” We haven’t noticed any changes inside the app.

Version 9.1 of Google Clock is now widely available via the Play Store.

On Monday, Google also rolled out version 2.0.0.965719431 of Pixel Magnifier with a new icon. Like Thermometer, the background is no longer blue, while the magnifying glass is thicker with a gradient as the square gets filled in. The Quick Settings Tile icon has also been updated to match. There are no changes to the design of the app.

title: Google Maps bug won’t show traffic data on Android Auto and more
snippet: When it’s working fully, Google Maps is a powerful navigation app, but bugs are a bit more common than anyone wants. Over the past month, issues with traffic data have been popping up, more recently affecting users on Android Auto specifically.
fullText:
When it’s working fully, Google Maps is a powerful navigation app, but bugs are a bit more common than anyone wants. Over the past month, issues with traffic data have been popping up, more recently affecting users on Android Auto specifically.

Google Maps typically shows green, yellow, and red lines to indicate the speed of traffic. Green (or blue) means that traffic is flowing normally, yellow indicates a slowdown, and red indicates heavy and slow-moving or stopped traffic. It’s very useful in figuring out the most efficient way to get around.

Right now, though, it’s broken for many.

In July, there were quite a lot of reports around traffic data in Google Maps being broken, with Google fixing the issue late in the month. Now, it seems to be back, especially for Android Auto users.

	

Reports as far back as two weeks ago, but especially in the past several days, show that traffic data in Google Maps remains at least partially broken on Android Auto. Some map settings seem to still show traffic data, but general navigation in its default view seems to be broken. The issue is also still happening on the phone directly for some users.

Google hasn’t publicly acknowledged this latest wave as far as we can tell, but it’s obviously frustrating for those affected. Some claim that uninstalling Google Maps updates seems to at least temporarily fix the problem.

fullText:

The prompts include suggestions like:

Latest Apple products

Find my trade-in value

Explain carrier offers

Help me choose a Watch

iPhone monthly payments

Compare iPad lineup

Apple’s fine print explains:

Access to the shopping assistant in the Apple Store app isn’t available to everyone. Apple says it’s available in an “Early Preview” to select users. There’s no word on when it will expand widely.

title: iOS 27 fixes three of the most annoying Messages bugs
snippet: iOS 27 focuses heavily on bug fixes and performance improvements across apps like Safari, Mail, Calendar, and more. In the Messages app, iOS 27 fixes what I think are three of the most frustrating bugs … and the update will be released to everyone in just a few weeks.
fullText:
iOS 27 focuses heavily on bug fixes and performance improvements across apps like Safari, Mail, Calendar, and more.

In the Messages app, iOS 27 fixes what I think are three of the most frustrating bugs … and the update will be released to everyone in just a few weeks. 

iOS 27: Three key bug fixes in Messages

First, Apple says that failed messages will automatically retry sending in iOS 27. There have been countless times when I hit send on a message, immediately swipe up and go back to my iPhone’s Home Screen, then realize later that the message I thought I sent actually failed.

In iOS 26 and earlier, this required going back to the Messages app and manually tapping the “retry” button next to the message in question. In iOS 27, however, that will now happen automatically in the background. 

Second, Apple says iOS 27 enables continuous sending of photos, videos, and texts in Messages. This fixes a frustration that’s likely familiar to most iPhone users: you send a photo, it gets stuck, and a blue progress bar lingers at the top of the conversation. Until that photo finally goes through, any additional messages you send are effectively held up as well.

In iOS 27, that bottleneck is gone. Each message gets its own progress bar and is sent independently, so a stuck photo won’t prevent subsequent texts, photos, or videos from being delivered.

Finally, iOS 27 improves Messages syncing across devices. Apple says conversations will sync more reliably between your devices, making it less likely that you’ll switch from your iPhone to your Mac and find messages missing, delayed, or out of sync.

title: Pixel Watch 5 (41mm) Initial Review: New watch alert, actually
snippet: The result of two changes made by Google means I’m using the Pixel Watch 5 in an entirely different way from the previous four generations, and it feels so futuristic.
fullText:
The result of two changes made by Google means I’m using the Pixel Watch 5 in an entirely different way from the previous four generations, and it feels so futuristic.

Design

The external design is exactly the same, and I’m perfectly happy to spend another year, if not longer, with Actua 3D. I am amused by its domed nature every time I open Quick Settings, notifications, or widgets. There’s no practical benefit — beyond accelerating swipes — but it sure does complement the watch’s round nature. 

This design trait, which already feels like a hallmark of Google’s wearable aesthetic, adds a little bit of three-dimensionality to what appears on the screen. A prime example is the curved Material 3 Expressive button that appears at the bottom of widgets. This tactility is probably Google’s best melding of hardware and software.

A year later, I have no complaints about the contacts that protrude from the left edge of the Watch or the Quick Charge Dock they connect to, which I continue to applaud for its heft. The Watch batteries are only a few mAh larger, and Google did not make any changes to its 30-hour (41mm) or 40-hour (45mm) estimates. My year-old 41mm PW4 ends the day with battery life in the 50% to 55% range, while the PW5 is firmly left with about 60% over the past week.

	

Meanwhile, battery life on the 45mm size of Pixel Watch has never been a particular problem. Last year’s charging speed boost was far more impactful. My colleague Ben found a noticeable bump to battery life on his 45mm Watch 5. A single day uses as little as 40% of the battery even with AOD turned on, meaning you can almost certainly get through two days on a charge. With charging being just as fast, the 45mm model just provokes zero battery anxiety, as you’ll almost certainly never use more power in a day than a quick 15-minute top-off can refill.

The 2nd-generation Active Band, which switches to a new material that has fewer “forever chemicals,” might feel flimsier when it’s off your wrist. But the change is otherwise not noticeable in day-to-day wear.

If I have one note on the hardware, it’s the band-swapping mechanism. I’ve been ruined by how much easier it is to change bands on the Fitbit Air. The physical form factor is not one-to-one, but I change bands on the new tracker so much more often than on the Pixel Watch.

The Pixel Watch 5 gets a new chip with the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated. The 12% boost in CPU processing power and extra gigabyte of RAM aren’t things I have noticed in day-to-day usage. Some animations are slightly snappier, but the changes are subtle. I don’t really have any performance complaints.

Software

The software experience on the Pixel Watch 5 is the most refined it has been in years. It starts with expanded watch face complications that show more information. The sunset/sunrise time is now accompanied by a countdown, which led me to remove the dedicated widget that I was using for that sole purpose. Meanwhile, heart rate includes your recent range and temperature adds the high/low. These updates greatly increase the likelihood that you can simply stay on the watch face.

Old vs. new

The other big addition is color, like the red heart rate complication, that makes it much easier to distinguish information on information-dense faces. Given the small screen, it is much better than everything being themed the same.

The refinements continue with updates to Auto Bedtime Mode, with Google letting you set auto-pause for audio, while a new night vision-friendly watch face in red just shows the time and your next alarm. It’s another example of Google optimizing the UX of workflows you encounter daily.

I also want to mention Express Pay (introduced March 2026), where you can just tap your watch to an NFC reader instead of opening the Google Wallet app, as another example of reducing friction. With the Pixel Watch 5, Google updated the motion model to improve accuracy with more payment terminals. 

There are two new faces this year. Chronograph functions like its namesake, while Weave incorporates the Neural Expressive design language, which is also now live in the Gemini app, and responds to wrist motion.

My absolute favorite software addition is At a Glance. It’s a space at the bottom of watch faces for Live Updates and other real-time information. This includes media controls, timers, ongoing navigation, flight boarding passes, and workouts. Previously, you just got a small icon to resume an activity, but At a Glance shows information directly in a nice arc that curves to the display.

As part of this, Wear OS has made some tweaks like replacing the new notification dot with a line, while the Airplane Mode and microphone indicators have been moved to the top of the screen.

When combined with one-handed gestures for scrolling and tapping, I’m touching the wearable much less while getting the same utility. Google first introduced them last December on the PW4 before bringing it to the PW3 this March. With the Pixel Watch 5, gestures are supported in many more apps, while you can now customize actions in Settings:

Media controls: Play/pause or Skip

Alarm: Snooze or Dismiss

Watch face: Open ongoing notification or Always scroll notification tray

My go-to move is double-pinching to launch media controls from At a Glance on the watch face, while pinching a second time pauses the audio. I then turn or flick my wrist away for the universal back gesture. Tip: By default, Media Controls just shows a dot in At a Glance, but you can long-press to also see the track name at the bottom of your watch face.

I find this combo of At a Glance and gestures so powerful that I’ve enabled Tilt-to-Wake, which I’ve turned off on every Wear OS watch dating back to the Moto 360. It lets me perform gestures immediately instead of having to first tap and wake the screen for truly touch-free interactions.

I’m not sure that Google set out to offer a comprehensive new way to use the Pixel Watch 5, but being able to use it one-handed feels very futuristic.

Gemini Intelligence

Gemini now supports offline voice commands like controlling music (skip and volume), setting timers and alarms, turning on/off settings like Wi-Fi, controlling Do Not Disturb, Water Lock, and other modes, opening apps, and starting workouts.

They are nice if you have the non-LTE model and exercise without your phone. The use case I’ve found very convenient is around bedtime. I somewhat curiously enable Airplane Mode (and Battery Saver) on my Pixel Watch before falling asleep. When I wake up in the morning, I can now issue voice commands to disable both.

Meanwhile, Raise to Talk makes use of an updated motion model to reduce the number of false positives. I’ve come around to this being how I launch Gemini, with the Pixel Watch 5 finally convincing me to disable hotword detection.

Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions — yes, that’s the full name — just feel natural on this form factor. One-tap suggestions for addresses and phone numbers unlock actions that you’d previously have waited to do on a phone. These Suggestions only appear in notifications, starting with Google Messages. At the very least, they should also be available in the app.

Task Automation cannot be initiated from the watch. Rather, this integration just lets you see progress in At a Glance after the action is started from a phone. Google might as well let you trigger tasks from your wrist to reduce any friction.

Health 

We’re still testing the health features for the Pixel Watch 5, with more than a few features not yet live on day one. This includes the on-wrist Strength Training interface, while Blood Pressure and Insulin Resistance Trends aren’t coming until September 2026 after a month of data. Additionally, Breathing Emergency Detection is only available in Europe at launch.

What is available out of the box is the improved GPS performance, though it takes up to 10 minutes for the data to appear in the Google Health app after a workout because of the processing required. Until then, you’ll see what Google calls the “non-optimized” map. Google has also updated the workout views with a larger font, updated typography, and refreshed color palette. 

Google says the Pixel Watch 5’s latest machine learning models mean sleep stage tracking is 15% more accurate, while Smart Wake Alarms are the other notable addition. Alarms go off within a 30-minute range to wake you up during a lighter state of sleep, with more testing needed here.

One feature I want is for the Google Health app on Wear OS to add water and food logging. The latter is probably best served by Health Coach integration with Gemini voice commands. 

Conclusion 

It’s not often that a familiar product you use every day changes so drastically. The Pixel Watch 5 demonstrates that the UX of wearables can still drastically improve after all these years. 

In addition to primarily interacting with the Pixel Watch 5 touch-free, the introduction of At a Glance and more info-dense complications means I haven’t really left the watch face this past week. In making information immediately accessible (with Gemini Intelligence also playing a role to a lesser degree), I’m relying on the watch for more phone-level actions.

In many ways, Google’s narrative of being able to use your phone less is actually coming to fruition on the Pixel Watch 5.

PW4 owners have absolutely no reason to upgrade and it’s not a slam dunk either for the PW3, especially when many of these updates are software changes. Owners of the first two generations should absolutely do so for a very complete and thorough package of improvements.

title: Pixel 11 Initial Review: This probably could have been a software update [Video]
snippet: You can understand a lot about a product from its first couple of hours, and if that is anything to go by, the Pixel 11 feels like an adequate but modest update that is likely only of interest to people wanting a “new” phone.
fullText:
You can understand a lot about a product from its first couple of hours, and if that is anything to go by, the Pixel 11 feels like an adequate but modest update that is likely only of interest to people wanting a “new” phone.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube

The less it changes, the more it stays the same…obviously

It’s really tough to talk about the Pixel 11’s design when it’s practically identical as last year. I’m exaggerating a little bit, but the outright biggest change is the full glass camera bar section, which I didn’t even notice during my initial hands-on. However, it’s a great change. It looks very consistent and makes it stand out for the better.

Not many people will make the switch over from the Pixel 10, but the weight reduction of around 7g is genuinely noticeable. I figured I wouldn’t care, but I like it. Maybe the lack of metal around the camera bar helped shave some mass and depth; the phone now sits a little flatter when upright on a desk.

	

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 feel almost identical. Chunky, stable, very comfortable to hold. I paired it with the brand new Pixel Clear Case. I dislike the exposed lip on the bottom edge; it’s not worth $50, but otherwise, this is an acceptable starter case.

There are some tangible gains that you can’t see right away. Last year, I was critical of the weakness of the Pixelsnap magnets. The good news is that Google listened, and the magnets are marginally stronger this year versus last year. When you attach a kickstand or similar, the “snap” is stronger, the connection feels more stable, and it’s harder to wobble things off with a vigorous shake. I would like it to be a little stronger still, but it’s a nice year-over-year improvement.

How fast do you want your phone?

The performance at least feels better than the previous generation. I don’t doubt that Google has tailored the experience to make it feel fast and smooth out of the box. If you have come from a phone with the slower UFS 3.1 storage, then I hope you can feel it too.

Apps do load marginally faster from a cold start, but we’re talking milliseconds. There’s an smoothness that is hard to quantify on a Pixel; you know it when you see it or feel it.

I don’t know why the display stays tuned to 60Hz out of the box or by default. It should be set at the full flow 120Hz, because there’s only one chance to make a first impression.

Coming over from the Pixel 10 Pro XL, I switched without a hitch, and Android 17 just feels like a warm pair of slippers at this point. There isn’t much here that feels particularly standout from a core OS experience, and that is both a positive and a negative.

Even the new Tensor G6 chip feels identical to the G5 day-to-day. Maybe there are some minor upgrades that I haven’t noticed, but for all the kinds of things I’ve been doing, I couldn’t tell you how things have improved. I’m just glad that this is the only device in the lineup to keep RAM parity at 12GB.

Of the new software features, there really isn’t much to write home about, or at least nothing that will change how you use your phone day-to-day. I have used Rambler a little bit, and it works really well, but it doesn’t fill text in real-time like Google’s previous (and still very good) voice dictation. You talk, then hit the microphone icon, and all the text appears at once. I’ll be honest: that isn’t ideal, but it handles stutters, changes, and course corrections perfectly. I’d hesitate to call it a killer addition, though.

One minor point of contention that I have to note, but I’m not sure if it’s merely a blip with the new modem, is that my phone had some severe connection problems while connected to a VPN and a 5G network on the Three carrier here in the UK. I had to flip in and out of Airplane Mode to get pages to load and apps to refresh while connected to Proton VPN or Google Pixel VPN. However, this was only in a couple of locations in my town/city.

The connection has otherwise been really solid, but this blip has concerned me somewhat. I haven’t had that problem with any recent Pixel device in the same places. I’ll be sure to test this the longer I use the phone and work out if it was just a temporary or unique issue. For what it’s worth, nobody else on the team has had modem or connection issues at any stage thus far. I’m keeping an eye on this and hoping it was user error or a VPN issue. It could have been the two fighting while on a weaker network signal.

Camera quality and improvements

The only major hardware changes that you’ll find on the Pixel 11 this year relate to the camera. A return to a better main sensor means marginally better photos. I haven’t yet come to a definitive conclusion, but the camera is improved over the previous generation.

I find that the camera functions make bigger leaps this time around, though, rather than the hardware stack.

Take, for example, Camera Looks. They’re an overdue but important step forward for customization. I like playing around with Camera Looks, but I’ve found the controls a little finicky. As part of the Quick Access Controls options within the viewfinder, you can double-tap to bring up four tools.

Then you can scroll to access or on-device Looks. I personally would like an adjustment to how this activates, maybe a quicker way to access the function. To get deeper into the controls and adjustments, you have to tap the Settings icon, then “Looks,” and then choose the settings. Maybe something a little less cumbersome would be my preferred option, just a drop-down above the shutter or a slider carousel just below the zoom controls. Right there at your fingertips.

I can already see that Magic Capture is going to be amazing for families and, in particular, when handing your phone over to someone you might not be confident will get the photo you want of an important moment. 

Gemini Camera is capable of picking out great shots.

Camera Looks can make a big difference.

Just point the camera at the subject and let the phone do the rest feels counterintuitive to anyone who takes their photography seriously, but for the less confident, this Top Shot upgrade does a fantastic job. I liken it to when I’m shooting high-frame-rate videos and just pull stills as photos; this is just letting AI make the selection. It works well in my limited testing.

How long is long enough for a battery?

I’ve been impressed in recent years with how the base Pixel has handled even my busiest of days. The Pixel 11 is the same once again. In my week using it as my main device, I’m getting impressive longevity despite not being a quantum leap.

While screen on time is never a really solid metric, expect six hours as a minimum if you have mixed use. Think Android Auto with some GPS, texting, maybe a brief call, lots of browsing, light gaming, it’s all pretty rudimentary today. I feel like background processes aren’t sapping at this phone like maybe the older versions suffered.

With charging, I have tried Extreme Charging Mode, but it still feels so slow and outdated compared to the competition. I hoped we might get 25W charging with Pixelsnap this year, but alas, no changes to the 15W speed introduced last year.

Clarification: The Pixel 11 is are all capable of 25W wireless charging with Pixelsnap or any other 25W MPP Qi certified chargers. This will mean that your phone will charge at just 5W slower than when wired with a supported stand or wireless charging system.

Initial thoughts

I don’t quite think a week is enough to give a substantial verdict on the Pixel 11. There’s much more to test, but I already think it’s really tough to recommend to anyone without a working phone made in the last 2-3 years – especially if you’re content.

There is a growing overreliance on the AI functionality, functionality that isn’t moving the needle unless you want something specific. Google has always been a software company, and after nailing the fundamentals with the Pixel 9, it leaned more heavily into software tuning rather than attempting to make major hardware gains.

The Pixel 11 is a good phone but an expensive phone. One that is tough to evaluate without all the other market factors that make it such. In a few months, it’ll become a much better buy by virtue of discounts and sales, as it has always been with Google hardware for better or worse.

We’ll revisit the Pixel 11 a few weeks from now once we have a better opportunity to test drive every component and then again in a few months to see how updates have altered any aspects of the device.

If you are still interested in picking up the Pixel 11, you can get extensive trade-in deals that’ll knock the $899 start price down at the Google Store, Amazon, and Best Buy below:

Pixel 11: Google Store | Amazon | Best Buy

Follow Damien: Threads, Bluesky, Instagram
