title: Pixel 11 Pro Initial Review: Gemini Intelligence is the highlight, not HiLight
snippet: Historically, Google has set out to make helpful devices. The Pixel 11 Pro continues that with Gemini Intelligence, while introducing a new narrative about how you can use your phone less with HiLight.
fullText:
Historically, Google has set out to make helpful devices. The Pixel 11 Pro continues that with Gemini Intelligence, while introducing a new narrative about how you can use your phone less with HiLight.

HiLight

Narratives matter, and the one around HiLight is frankly more interesting than the hardware feature as it exists today.

I don’t think “use your phone less” is spin. Google is responding to the very real sentiment that people love their phones but are increasingly overwhelmed by them. The opposite of genuinely trying to build hardware that meets the moment is what I consider paint-by-numbers design. The only priority there is to hit a spec or brief without real vision or regard for how it comes together.

At launch, HiLight just doesn’t accomplish what it set out to do. People do put their phones face down when they need to concentrate. Knowing when an important call comes in is not a bad idea, but having that serve as the first of only two functions is not enough.

	

The Gemini status lights for listening, thinking, and responding mimic a smart speaker. I don’t really need them for voice command confirmation since hotword detection is pretty reliable these days. That said, I do use it every night when my Pixel 11 Pro is (wired) charging face down on my nightstand and I ask Google to turn off the lights. There’s a non-zero amount of whimsy that I can appreciate. Another way you can use (demo) it is when your phone is face down and the power button is set to invoke Gemini.

Unlike software (more on the Magic Cue to Proactive Assistance upgrade below), a hardware feature that doesn’t do enough feels like wasted space. I’d go as far as saying that sticking with the temperature sensor for another year to allow the software for HiLight to mature might have been the better move.

HiLight will be appreciated by some users, but it’s not there yet for me or most people until it supports messaging. It kills me that “Who will you HiLight?” is actually a good line that could have gone viral, especially if Google connects it to Pixel VIPs, which I still think is their best software feature in ages.

Hopefully, Google will enable messaging support as soon as possible — actual weeks, not the “in the coming weeks” that always means months — but so far HiLight has not made a good first impression.

Gemini Intelligence

Gemini Intelligence is just a brand that I’m not sure will gain meaningful recognition, but it does provide a more cohesive branding umbrella compared to the past two generations.

The first of two tentpole features is Proactive Assistance. Before we dive into the functionality, what’s reassuring to me is Google’s year-over-year iteration on Magic Cue. Last year’s premise of delivering contextual information and actions based on what’s happening in a conversation was correct. However, my reaction to seeing them was “not quite.”

This year, the genuine advancement is giving Proactive Assistance a user interface. In most cases, tapping slides up a bottom sheet with more context, like seeing your calendar for a specific period. That provides enough reassurance that the AI is correct in determining your schedule is actually empty before adding a new event. Seeing inline place listings instead of opening the entire Google Maps app keeps you in the conversation and feels less distracting. Showing your flight details without opening Google Search is similarly quick and helpful. At the bottom of this sheet, you can select what gets shared, and I appreciate that there are now options.

There’s an adjustment period to Gboard Rambler that’s not immediately obvious. The transcription does not appear in real time as you speak. Instead, you tap the corner microphone button, talk, and hit the checkmark once done. The transcription appears after a moment without any pauses or filler words thanks to the processing that occurs. Rambler then lets you edit and transform the output. It’s more like prompting in that regard.

In the span of a week, I’ve not adjusted to this. More than once, I’ve forgotten to tap the checkmark and ended up waiting for a transcript that will never come. Being able to immediately see what I’ve said allows me to check and make keyboard edits, which helps prolong the voice session.

Google lets you return to the previous “Standard” experience, but I haven’t taken that option yet to give it more time. Rambler is inherently a more voice-first, if not voice-only, experience that doesn’t let you mix and match input methods. There should be more of a middle ground, maybe just a preview for Rambler’s results when you pause long enough, but before you actually end the session. Until then, a good idea might be letting you quickly change modes depending on the situation right from the suggestions strip without having to go to Gboard settings.

Another Gemini Intelligence addition I quite like is checking a Google Maps listing and opening a ride-sharing app to find that place offered as a one-tap suggestion without having to manually copy the address.

Using task automation is still not second nature to me. Ride hailing is my primary use case, but I find that when I call a car, I’m usually in a rush. My default behavior in those moments is to madly type and tap, as Gemini’s phone control is just not fast enough yet.

At a Glance can now show membership cards when you visit a store. This is Google finally taking full advantage of the dedicated space it has reserved at the top of your lock and homescreen since the start. The feature is still in “preview,” but it’s already promising.

Hardware

In the past year, my daily drivers have been the Pixel 10 Pro from August to March, followed by the Pixel 10a until early July. I came back to the 10 Pro ahead of this review and my main takeaway is that I miss the platonic ideal of a phone that is the flat and light Pixel 10a. As seen with the base Pixel 11 shrinking how far its Camera Bar protrudes and the plateau disappearing with a case, I believe Google has its eyes on that design goal. No bar means no collection of dust and small fibers on the Bar from your pocket or bag, an occurrence I noticed immediately after switching to the flagship.

I like how clean this edge-to-edge Camera Bar is. There is some personality in the old approach that melds metal and glass, but I prefer the more minimalist aesthetic.

I’ve used the Fog Pixel 11 Pro for the past week with its shiny rails and continue to believe that the polish does not actually achieve the intended premium look. As evidenced by the matte Obsidian, Google is beginning to get the message.

The phone is three grams lighter and that’s obviously not appreciable to a normal human being. Similarly, being 0.2 mm thinner doesn’t do anything for me. Having used the iPhone Air as my iOS device this past year, I am firm in my belief that thin phones feel like the future, but I’m in the minority in being willing to accept the inherent trade-offs that currently come with that.

The Pixel 11 Pro I’m reviewing has 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. I would have been happy to review the 12 GB model, having been perfectly fine with the 8 GB on the Pixel 10a for six months.

The Tensor G6’s CPU improvements of 15% quicker app launches and 25% faster browsing are not noticeable in day-to-day usage. What’s worth mentioning is how the upgraded Image Signal Processor (ISP) and 50% more powerful Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) make computational photography faster, with Instant Night Sight being the marquee example.

The new NFC chip placement doesn’t make a difference for tap-to-pay, but I do like Tap to Share for sharing one-off images.

To test HiLight, I had to put my phone face down. That’s a problem if you don’t use a case like yours truly. I tried using this phone with Google’s Pixelsnap Clear Case and made it less than 24 hours. Putting your phone face down on a couch or bed is perfectly fine, but I have a glass work desk.

For science, I did that. It was excruciating fine after three days, but my colleague Will managed to scuff up the “2x Scratch Resistant Display Coating” already with a metal keychain in his pocket with the phone.

Early battery life testing on the Pixel 11 Pro has not differentiated greatly from last year. Officially, Google switched to a “30+ hour battery life estimate” from “24+,” with the typical capacity dropping 20 mAh.

Finally, at the risk of sounding like a broken record, the Quick Tap gesture that lets you hit the back of the phone twice to play/pause music or launch apps isn’t more accurate than before. Maybe next year.

Camera

My colleagues will have more to say about the camera in our Pixel 11 Pro XL review, but I’d add that Camera Looks are just fun. There are a ton of apps that offer similar functionality, including the wonderful and shockingly free Snapseed from Google. However, making it a built-in feature greatly increases the likelihood you’ll use it. When I want to capture a sudden moment, I double-click the power button on instinct.

Joining the Original Pixel HDR look are Natural (for relaxed details), Shadows (deeper contrast), and Vanilla (warm, golden glow). These four options can be set as your default look that will persist when you close and reopen Pixel Camera. A week in, I still haven’t determined whether I’ll switch from Original.

Then you have Stylistic Looks that reset after every session: Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal. The latter is of note for embracing the less-processed look also led by third-party apps.

My favored way of switching between Stylistic Looks is using the updated Quick access controls that let you pick which sliders (up to four) appear to the left and right of the viewfinder. Your options are White Balance, Shadows, Exposure, Looks, Focus, Shutter Speed, or ISO. In general, this is a much better approach for surfacing Pro Controls than opening the bottom-right corner menu with its carousel and horizontal sliders.

Instant Night Sight is noticeable every time you use it and a literal time saver that means you’re more likely to get an in-motion shot. Google touts up to 4.5x speed improvements compared to the Pixel 8-10, with the improved sensors, redesigned camera software, and additional TPU compute credited for making this possible.

Google is so confident in Magic Capture that you can set Pixel Camera to launch that mode when pressing the app icon or double-clicking the power button. (Video can also be set instead of Photo.) Additionally, the mode switcher in the Camera app is now Magic Capture, Photo, and Video.

Despite their confidence, I’m glad they introduced a manual shutter button while the feature is active, with Magic Capture offering an elegant user interface overall. You can also grab images from the video after the fact, with Google clearly caring about not being responsible for a missed moment.

The only proper occasion I had to try it out was during Made by Google 2026 to record the musical performance from very far away. I can’t wait to actually use this during concerts, with the phone placed against my chest as I actually watch what I came for, while the Pixel team tells me they’ve found great value using Magic Capture at parties.

Stay tuned this week for more on Magic Capture.

Conclusion

At this stage of the game, a smartphone looking mostly the same for a few years should not incur a penalty.

Adding AI to products these days invites cynicism. It’s especially problematic for Google as it builds more assistive features powered by AI and commits physical hardware to that aim. Google selling phones on this premise requires buyers to believe the company is earnest. That it is worth learning to use a feature and trusting it to actually work. HiLight could be a good idea and it should have launched with more features to give it the best possible shot, but is ultimately ignorable.

Ultimately, the Pixel 11 Pro is a fine phone waylaid by narrative and circumstance (RAMageddon) more so than any specific faults. The hardware, software, and AI – they’re all quite good.

Where to buy

Google Store

Amazon

Best Buy

title: Google’s inevitable ‘Pixel Watch Ultra’ should copy the Fitbit Air
snippet: It feels rather inevitable that Google will give in to the whole “Ultra” smartwatch fad, and when something along the lines of a “Pixel Watch Ultra” does arrive, I really hope it pulls influence from Fitbit Air. This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!
fullText:
It feels rather inevitable that Google will give in to the whole “Ultra” smartwatch fad, and when something along the lines of a “Pixel Watch Ultra” does arrive, I really hope it pulls influence from Fitbit Air.

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

If it weren’t clear, I don’t get the whole obsession with “Ultra” smartwatches. I’m glad something as advanced as the Apple Watch Ultra or the Galaxy Watch Ultra exists, but let’s be honest: 80% of the customer base buying these don’t need everything these products have to offer, and they know it. In that sense, I’m glad Google hasn’t jumped into this market yet. But with Pixel Watch 5 starting to feel like it’s at a wall of either needing to change or at least expand, it’s all the more likely Google might move into this market – it’s certainly popular. 

The Pixel Watch sits in a weird spot as it stands today. Google has been continually pushing this as a fitness-focused wearable, but its premium design almost feels out of place in sporty or demanding environments. The domed glass isn’t as scratch-resistant as sapphire, and it’s fully exposed. Back before Google got around to making this design repairable, I was actually wary of wearing my Pixel Watch in those kinds of settings. It’s a gorgeous smartwatch, don’t get me wrong, but it’s certainly more stylish than it is sporty.

	

Compared to Samsung and Apple, the Pixel Watch doesn’t look like it’s even in the same product category.

So, “Pixel Watch Ultra.” How does that differ?

I think a sports-focused version of a Pixel Watch is a radically different product, ditching the domed display and pebble-looking nature of Google’s existing timepiece completely for something a bit more rugged. That could mean leaning into the metal chonkers that Apple and Samsung have been putting out, but there’s a different direction I’d personally prefer.

Google has a smash hit on its hands with the Fitbit Air – I want a Pixel Watch that follows that lead. 

One of the key things I’d love to see copied is the band mechanism. Fitbit Air’s core pebble pops out of the band, and that feels doable with a sporty smartwatch too. A case, as long as it’s sturdy, could surround the watch and leave the display exposed, with a little lip to help protect a display that, hopefully, would be made from sapphire or maybe that new ceramic Pixel 11 Pro Fold display covering. 

Will it happen? We’ll see. I think it’s almost inevitable that we get a more sports-focused Pixel Watch down the road; this is just my idea for what it should be. Just as likely is we keep getting more fitness trackers instead, maybe one with a screen.

title: Report: Apple launching updated iMac with M6 chip and new colors later this year
snippet: After a two year hiatus, Apple is working on a new iMac with the M6 chipset and updated color options, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. It should release “before the end of the year.”
fullText:
After a two year hiatus, Apple is working on a new iMac with the M6 chipset and updated color options, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. It should release “before the end of the year.”

The iMac isn’t frequently refreshed. It skipped the M2 and M5 families of chips, and it’s still yet to receive a larger display option – with Apple instead directing high-end users to use a Mac Studio or Mac mini alongside a Studio Display. Nonetheless, Apple is preparing a new version with the M6 chip.

Gurman outlines that there’ll be “some new color options” with this refresh, but didn’t mention what would change. Apple slightly adjusted the color palette with the M4 refresh in 2024, though the actual 7 color options remained the same – just with different shades. The iMac should also be out by the end of the year:

Nevertheless, if you’ve been holding out for a new iMac, your wait shouldn’t be much longer. All signs point to the M6 models being close to launch, and you should be able to buy one before the end of the year.

This means that this fall could be a pretty major one for the Mac. Overhauled MacBook Pro models with touchscreens and Tandem OLED, a new base model 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, new M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios (dependent on supply availability), and the new iMac with M6. Another possibility is a refreshed Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro, though that’ll likely come later.

Apple’s M6 chip will be the first Mac chip based on the new 2nm process, though there reportedly won’t be an M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra chip – with the company instead accelerating the launch of the M7 family.

title: Here’s what people who have used the iPhone Ultra like most
snippet: We’re just a few weeks away from the rumored launch of the foldable iPhone Ultra. As we’ve written before, excitement for the device is mounting. A new report from Bloomberg today outlines what people inside Apple who have used the iPhone Ultra love about it.
fullText:
We’re just a few weeks away from the rumored launch of the foldable iPhone Ultra. As we’ve written before, excitement for the device is mounting.

A new report from Bloomberg today outlines what people inside Apple who have used the iPhone Ultra love about it.

iPhone Ultra is coming: Real-world impressions

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman offers a detailed recap of the foldable iPhone. In particular, he says he has “spoken to several people” who have used the device. Those people say they like these things in particular:

How well it fits in a pocket. Rumors say it has a 5.5-inch outer display.

The durability of the hinge.

The new “iPad-like app layouts” that take full advantage of the inner display, which reports suggest measures around 7.8 inches and is wider than it is tall. 

How well it serves as a “camera viewfinder.”

Multiple reports suggest the iPhone Ultra will cost upwards of $2,000. It’s expected to have a main camera and an ultra-wide camera, but not a telephoto camera. It will reportedly use Touch ID instead of Face ID for biometric authentication.

9to5Mac’s Take

I’m incredibly excited for iPhone Ultra, and these tidbits from Gurman only make me even more optimistic it’s the device for me.

I was originally skeptical of the foldable iPhone’s form factor. However, as we’ve learned more about the specific size and its benefits, I’ve come around to it.

The positive reviews of Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 have also offered great real-world insight into a very similar form factor to the iPhone Ultra.

There will, of course, be limitations compared to the iPhone 18 Pro. I use an iPhone Air right now, so I’m used to life without a telephoto camera, and a return to Touch ID doesn’t seem like much of an adjustment.

title: Apple Stores preparing ‘significant’ changes for new Home product launches: report
snippet: According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing significant changes at its retail stores in preparation for upcoming Home product launches. At the very least, Apple should debut a refreshed HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K this fall, though the changes would suggest a third, more significant product is also on its way.
fullText:
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing significant changes at its retail stores in preparation for upcoming Home product launches. At the very least, Apple should debut a refreshed HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K this fall, though the changes would suggest a third, more significant product is also on its way.

Apple’s had a long backlog of Home products pending release, largely because of all of the delays involving the company’s Siri revamp. Now that Siri has come together, we should see some of these products finally hit the market after years without a refresh.

That said, reports indicated that Apple would release a refreshed HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K first, and that the companies first smart home hub (otherwise known as HomePod with Display or HomePad) might debut a little bit later.

However, it’s now sounding like the smart home hub might release alongside the updated Apple Tv and HomePod mini, at least based on what retail stores are planning. From the Power On newsletter:

Apple is preparing significant changes to those sections this fall, including rearranging parts of the Avenues and adding accessory bays to showcase new products. The company is already planning an upgraded Apple TV set-top box and a new HomePod mini for this time frame. But the scale of the retail changes suggests something else is coming: the long-anticipated home hub with a display. The planned modifications appear too extensive to be solely about routine updates to existing products.

Of course, we’ll never know for certain until Apple holds its September keynote. Based on today’s reporting though, it sounds like we might get our first glimpse at Apple’s all-new smart home hub quite soon, alongside refreshed Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini models that should support Siri AI.

Wrap up

As a refresher, Apple’s smart home hub is rumored to sport a 7-inch square display and come in two versions: one with a built in speaker, and another with magnets on the rear that’ll support wall mounting. The product will run a new OS that’ll offer widgets on the home screen, be useful for FaceTime calls, and of course serve as the hub for all of your smart home accessories and Siri. It’ll include an A18 chip as well.

Another new rumor for Apple’s Home lineup is that the new Apple TV 4K might offer a refreshed Siri Remote, though it isn’t clear what changes will arise.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

On the Apple TV, gaming is a little bit of an afterthought for developers. Compared to iPhone, iPad, and even Mac – there aren’t a ton of options. Luckily, CloudGear exists as an all-in-one solution for bringing every major cloud gaming platform into one interface. It’s also available for iPhone and iPad.

Highlights

CloudGear supports every major cloud gaming platform: GeForce Now, Xbox Cloud Streaming, Amazon Luna, and Boosteroid. It streams in up to 5K resolution at up to 120FPS, and also supports HDR, 10-bit color, and Dolby 7.1 Surround Sound.

Beyond those details, CloudGear also offers a few nice-to-have features. It supports controller vibration – and if your controller doesn’t have vibration, it’ll use your iPhone’s Taptic Engine. There’s also a feature to hand games off to your Apple TV from the iPhone or iPad app, in case you don’t want to do all the searching on your TV.

On iPhone and iPad, CloudGear offers home screen widgets – allowing you to bookmark games and quickly launch into them without interacting with anything else.

Lastly, CloudGear supports AR glasses plugged into your iPhone – like the XREAL glasses, allowing you to play games on a massive display right in front of your face.

Download the app

CloudGear is available for free on the App Store for iPhone and iPad running iOS 17.6 and later, as well as Apple TV models running tvOS 18.6 and later. For the full feature set, you can subscribe for $1.99/month, $14.99/year, or $39.99 for a lifetime purchase. A 7-day free trial is available for subscriptions, and you can learn more about the app on the website.

title: We’re just two months away from the first touchscreen MacBook: Here’s what to expect
snippet: After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be rolling out its first touchscreen MacBook as soon as October. This’ll come alongside the next MacBook Pro redesign, potentially dubbed MacBook Ultra.
fullText:
After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be rolling out its first touchscreen MacBook as soon as October. This’ll come alongside the next MacBook Pro redesign, potentially dubbed MacBook Ultra.

Of course, rumors are rumors – though essentially every reputable source has aligned on the idea of the MacBook Pro gaining support for touch later this year. Apple even left a few hints in macOS 27: Touch Support in Sidecar, pull to refresh support, and slightly bigger menu bar items.

As a 13-inch MacBook Air user, the last one was particularly annoying because things that used to fit on the left side of the notch were now spilling over.

One could call all of this a mere coincidence, but it’s probably exactly what it looks like. Regardless, here’s what the first touchscreen MacBook will have to offer.

OLED, Dynamic Island

On the display panel side of things, the redesigned MacBook Pro will come with a Tandem OLED display. This will be similar to the iPad Pro, which is often touted as one of the best mobile displays on the market. Tandem OLED comprises of stacked OLED panels, which allows for incredible colors, strong contrast, and increased brightness.

Reports also suggest it’ll come with a Dynamic Island, and it’ll be a bit smaller than the one on the iPhone. It won’t, however, come with support for Face ID.

Software optimizations

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple will have some special optimizations for the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, beyond what’s already visible in the betas of macOS 27:

“For instance, if users touch a button or control, the interface will bring up a new type of menu surrounding their finger that provides more relevant options for touch commands.

The software will also display the most appropriate set of controls based on users’ prior interaction. And if a person taps an item in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the set of controls will enlarge to be more easily selectable with a finger.”

M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Despite initial reporting suggesting that we’ll be seeing the debut of the M6 Pro and Max in the redesigned MacBook Pro, Apple is now skipping the release of those chips to accelerate the M7. This means that the first iteration of 2nm chips won’t be making their way to the redesigned MacBook Pros, and they’ll instead offer the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

There won’t be a base model version of this computer quite yet, though rumors suggest that Apple will be launching a base version of the redesigned MacBook Pro with an M7 chip as early as next spring.

Slightly thinner chassis

One design rumor for the new MacBook Pro is the fact that it’ll be slightly slimmer and lighter – though it’s unclear how meaningful this will be. The last MacBook Pro iteration made the computers look and feel quite chunky, so a bit of progress here would likely be welcome – so long as it doesn’t come at the compromise of thermals.

Wrap up

	

All in all, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro is shaping up to be an exciting upgrade. It will come in at steeper price points due to Apple’s June price hikes from the memory crisis – so I’d expect at least $2499 for the 14-inch and $2999 for the 16-inch.

title: iPhone 18 Pro event date: When Apple announced its event over the last six years
snippet: When should we expect the iPhone 18 Pro event, and when will Apple officially announce the date? Apple hasn’t sent invitations yet, but its announcement history gives us a remarkably consistent window.
fullText:
When should we expect the iPhone 18 Pro event, and when will Apple officially announce the date? Apple hasn’t sent invitations yet, but its announcement history gives us a remarkably consistent window.

Apple’s iPhone event announcement dates: 2020–2025

Apple has announced its annual iPhone event two weeks in advance for four consecutive years. Here’s when Apple announced each of its last six iPhone events, plus what those dates suggest for September 2026.

The pandemic disrupted Apple’s regular iPhone event schedule in 2020 and 2021. The iPhone 12 event moved to October, and Apple provided only seven days’ notice for both the iPhone 12 and iPhone 13 events.

Since 2022, however, Apple has been remarkably consistent. Every iPhone event has been announced exactly 14 days before the presentation.

When is the iPhone 18 Pro / iPhone Ultra event?

Apple hasn’t officially announced the next iPhone event date, but Wednesday, September 9, is currently the leading possibility.

Apple offered its first official clue this week when it opened applications for US retail employees to work its Event Support Experience Program in California. The company told employees that the event will occur during the first half of September.

Bloomberg suggests that Wednesday appears slightly more likely because Labor Day falls on Monday, September 7. A Wednesday event would preserve the workday travel window Apple has historically provided attendees.

When will Apple announce the new iPhone event?

If Apple holds its event on September 9 and maintains its four-year pattern, it would announce the date exactly two weeks earlier on Wednesday, August 26.

That makes August 26 the strongest prediction for Apple’s iPhone 18 event invitation. Tuesday, August 25, remains another possibility, but it would create a 15-day gap rather than continuing Apple’s recent 14-day pattern.

What to expect at Apple’s September 2026 event

This year’s product lineup should make the event unusually significant. Apple is expected to unveil three new flagship iPhones: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable iPhone, possibly called iPhone Ultra.

Noticeably absent will be the standard iPhone 18. Apple is expected to split its release schedule beginning this cycle, saving iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2 for spring 2027.

September is also when Apple traditionally unveils new Apple Watch hardware. AirPods sometimes join the presentation as well, although they aren’t guaranteed to receive annual updates.

The event will mark another first for Apple. John Ternus becomes CEO on September 1, while Tim Cook moves to executive chairman of the board. That will make this the first iPhone event of the Ternus era.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Shadow AI is happening whether IT is ready or not

According to the survey results, 46.5% of IT leaders said AI-driven automation as their top investment priority for the future. That’s the highest-ranked category in the entire survey, coming out ahead of vulnerability remediation (42.5%) and device visibility (42.1%).

One of the more shocking (and not great) results: 78% of employees are already using personal AI tools at work. Fleet shows separate data showing that the average enterprise runs 14 AI tools internally, while IT is only aware of 4 of them.

That gap for IT managers and teams is a visibility problem, while also a cost and security issue. The survey says that one company that burned through its entire 2026 token budget in 4 months after rolling out an AI coding tool to 5,000 of its engineers. IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that breaches caused by shadow AI cost an extra $670K on average compared to a typical breach.

The IT teams responsible for securing all of the AI tools still don’t have equivalent tooling for their own work. I’ve argued privately with folks about how big a challenge AI is for IT teams right now. It’s a huge industry, and IT was just expected to “handle it”. IT teams are expected to handle security, cost management, vulnerability management, and training as well. This is on top of their existing jobs and roles. Nothing is getting taken away. This reminds of me of when IT had to learn enterprise Wi-Fi- during the mobility era and manage it on top of existing roles and responsibilities.

Wrap up

The entire survey is a good read and points out some issues I’ve believed for a few years now. IT has been given the mission to drive AI usage in a healthy, secure, and cost-effective way, but really lacks the tools to do it across their fleets. There’s a lot of work to be done here in terms of device management, network filtering, education, and telemetry. For me, one of the troubling aspects of this era is that it’s yet another thing IT has to absorb and figure out without additional headcount.

title: Please don’t buy Google’s wildly overpriced Pixel 11 Clear Case
snippet: Buying a new smartphone usually means buying a new case alongside it, unless you’re one of those risk-fueled daredevils who opt to go caseless. And while there’s no shortage of third-party case options piling up at your local Best Buy or in Amazon warehouses, sometimes, going the first-party route just makes sense — especially if you’re able to pick one up with store credit. If you’re salivating over the new Pixel 11 series, I beg of you: please don’t choose Google’s wildly overpriced Pixelsnap Clear Case. It’s simply not worth the cost.
fullText:
Buying a new smartphone usually means buying a new case alongside it, unless you’re one of those risk-fueled daredevils who opt to go caseless. And while there’s no shortage of third-party case options piling up at your local Best Buy or in Amazon warehouses, sometimes, going the first-party route just makes sense — especially if you’re able to pick one up with store credit. If you’re salivating over the new Pixel 11 series, I beg of you: please don’t choose Google’s wildly overpriced Pixelsnap Clear Case. It’s simply not worth the cost.

I’m a little picky (okay, very picky) when it comes to phone cases, which I know puts me in the minority among general smartphone shoppers. But even if you’re the kind of person who opts for a clear shell rather than something with a little more character, Google’s Pixel 11 Clear Case just isn’t it. I have actual critiques about the case itself, but I think I can convince most shoppers to stay away with a single number: $50. That’s the same price as the colorful (and still not very good) Pixel cases Google’s been selling for a few years now, and only $25 less than Bellroy’s leather wallet case for the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which, if you didn’t know, uses genuine leather.

If you’re still looking for reasons not to pick this up, don’t worry — I have more ammo than just the price tag. Google’s offering doesn’t elevate the experience above any other generic TPU-based shell. If I’m being generous, you could argue that official Pixelsnap support could elevate its magnetic grip over third-party rivals, but I can’t say I’ve noticed a difference. Save for the circular support magnet, this feels virtually identical to this Spigen offering that is currently up on Amazon for $15 (or $17 for Pro XL users).

Actually, that’s not entirely true — Spigen’s is probably better. While the left and right sides of Spigen’s case do have a little more flex than Google’s (something that won’t matter once it’s on the phone), Google’s case leaves the entire bottom gap effectively unprotected. I’m not saying it’s guaranteed, but I wouldn’t be surprised if a drop at an unlucky angle could leave your Pixel 11’s display shattered or the surrounding frame nicked. Google’s case is also noticeably yellower than Spigen’s, even right out of the box, and considering that all clear TPU cases eventually oxidize, you’re probably better off starting with one that’s at least making an effort.

	
This is an accident waiting to happen, Google.

This isn’t an appeal to specifically buy Spigen’s clear case; it’s simply the go-to third party default for most phones these days. Rather, this is simultaneously a PSA to Pixel shoppers not to go with first-party case offerings, and a plea to Google to step up its absolutely lackluster case designs. Despite growing success, Pixel users still lack the breadth and depth of options that the iPhone and Samsung’s flagship devices see with every generation. It’s getting better, but in the meantime, it would be great to have a solid option from Google to point at during a hardware launch. Ah well — maybe the Pixel 12 will fare better.

title: Which do you plan to buy: iPhone 18 Pro or foldable iPhone Ultra? [Poll]

Rather than unveiling four closely related models, rumors point to a flagship-only September lineup consisting of three premium models: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple’s first foldable, widely expected to be called iPhone Ultra.
fullText:
Apple’s fall iPhone event is expected to look different this year. Rather than unveiling four closely related models, rumors point to a flagship-only September lineup consisting of three premium models: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple’s first foldable, widely expected to be called iPhone Ultra.

With three premium iPhone options, which will you choose?

For the familiar option, iPhone 18 Pro rumors include a smaller Dynamic Island, a 2nm A20 Pro chip, Apple’s C2 modem, longer battery life, and major camera upgrades. The larger display Pro Max could stand apart with a significantly larger battery, while retaining the traditional iPhone design and three-camera system.

The rumored iPhone Ultra is this year’s most radical choice: a book-style foldable with a roughly 5.5-inch outer display and 7.8-inch inner screen, a thin titanium body, Touch ID instead of Face ID, and just two rear cameras. Reports suggest a crease-free display and A20 Pro performance, but also a starting price around $2,000 or higher.

Assuming the rumors hold, which new iPhone are you planning to buy? Let us know in our poll, and share your thoughts on why in the comments!

fullText:
Users who rely on ChatGPT for quick visual searches can now add photos to a conversation more quickly with a new gesture. Here’s how.

ChatGPT makes it easier to attach recent photos to a conversation

While iOS has had Visual Intelligence for nearly two years, the feature is still limited to relatively recent iPhones and isn’t available in every region.

For users who rely on ChatGPT to perform similar visual searches, attaching a photo meant tapping the + button, then tapping “Photos,” and then selecting an image from their photo library.

While this process wasn’t exactly cumbersome, OpenAI made it a bit faster this week to add recent photos to a conversation with a handy new gesture.

As noted by OpenAI’s Adam Fry on X, users can now long-press the + button on the left-hand side of the prompt box to bring up their four most recent photos.

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold still doesn’t survive bend test, but at least it didn’t ‘explode’ this time [Video]
snippet: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has gone through the typical torture test of JerryRigEverything and, while it faired better than last year, Google still has work to do.
fullText:
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has gone through the typical torture test of JerryRigEverything and, while it faired better than last year, Google still has work to do.

Google has yet to make a foldable that didn’t break when it was bent in half, but last year’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold literally finished off its test with a bang. While the word “explode” has felt a bit strong, the battery ruptured, which is exceptionally rare in these tests.

The good news? Pixel 11 Pro Fold didn’t break to quite that degree, but it still didn’t fair very well.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold still broke, right at the antenna line just like in every other model. The same mistake just keeps repeating itself, despite Google boosting the overall durability this year. That can be seen in the ceramic outer display covering, which essentially did not scratch at Level 6 on the Moh’s hardness scale, where every other phone tends to scratch. There were still pretty deep grooves at Level 7, though. The back “glass compositive fiber” is, as suspected, basically just sturdy plastic, scratching with a knife.

	

The bend test itself goes on to see the phone ripped apart with bare hands. No tools, just a front panel that literally pops off and a back panel that’s remarkably easy to rip off. Oof. 

With Google having teased new redesigns for Pixel every “2-3 years,” we’re certainly due for a revamp at this point, and there are some very obvious places that need to be fixed up.

title: Epic accuses Apple of sidestepping App Store antitrust deal in Brazil
snippet: Apple has until Monday to respond to a complaint Epic Games filed with Brazil’s antitrust watchdog, where it accuses the company of adopting restrictive interpretations of its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust deal in the country. Here are the details.
fullText:
Apple has until Monday to respond to a complaint Epic Games filed with Brazil’s antitrust watchdog, where it accuses the company of adopting restrictive interpretations of its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust deal in the country. Here are the details.

A bit of background

Two months ago, Apple announced that developers were now allowed to distribute apps through alternative app marketplaces in Brazil.

The change came as part of a settlement resolving a years-long antitrust investigation that began after Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre filed a complaint over Apple’s App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces, and offer payment methods outside Apple’s IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% Core Technology Commission on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. You can learn more about that structure here.

Epic challenges Apple’s implementation

As reported today by O Globo (via MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with CADE, Brazil’s antitrust watchdog, accusing Apple of creating “structural, technical, and access barriers” that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic says that while Brazil’s new terms apply only to iOS apps, Apple’s deal with CADE “clearly covers iPadOS.”

The company is also reportedly pushing back against so-called “scare sheets” that discourage users from installing apps outside the App Store, as well as the current installation process, which it says requires nine steps, compared with six steps under Apple’s current implementation in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic adds that Apple’s original installation process in Europe required 15 steps, but after the company was compelled to reduce it to six, “download abandonment rates fell from 65% to 25%.”

Finally, Epic tells CADE that Apple’s reporting requirements “go far beyond what is necessary to calculate fees,” and that this allows the company “to monitor competitors’ business models.”

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to file its response. Apple has not commented publicly on the matter.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 to get one big upgrade at perfect time
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are launching next month, and rumors indicate they’ll pack a big upgrade—a new, more powerful chip—that will arrive at just the right time.
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are launching next month, and rumors indicate they’ll pack a big upgrade—a new, more powerful chip—that will arrive at just the right time.

New Apple Watch models to have more powerful S-class chip just in time for Siri AI

Most Apple products get more powerful chips all the time—but Apple Watch is the exception.

New Apple Watch models debut annually, but more often than not, ‘new’ S-class chips don’t actually pack an improved CPU. True performance upgrades only happen every few years.

Last year was even worse: Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Series 11 had the exact same S10 chip as their predecessors.

But rumors indicate we’re getting a truly meaningful chip upgrade this year.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will debut a brand new chip, probably named S11 or S12.

Mark Gurman recently wrote that this year’s new models will get a “long-awaited bump in chips and speed.” The last time an Apple Watch chip brought performance gains was the S9 in 2023. 

But watchOS 27 launches next month, and its tentpole addition is Siri AI—a feature that could truly benefit from a more powerful chip.

Siri AI on Apple Watch isn’t a lesser version of the assistant. It’s the same new and improved Siri found on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more. That’s a big part of why watchOS 27 cuts off support for many older Watch models.

	

Throughout the watchOS 27 beta, Siri has been a bit less responsive than I’d hope. And I suspect that’s in part due to the older chip, which far predates any AI version of Siri.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will have the first Watch chip built for the AI era. And it couldn’t come at a better time.

How is Siri AI running for you in the watchOS 27 beta? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple paid Ireland $17 billion last year as EU back-tax case came due
snippet: The Financial Times reports that new tax disclosures showed Apple paid Ireland $17 billion in corporate income taxes in 2025, accounting for 40% of its worldwide total. Here are the details.
fullText:
The Financial Times reports that new tax disclosures showed Apple paid Ireland $17 billion in corporate income taxes in 2025, accounting for 40% of its worldwide total. Here are the details.

Apple says figures don’t tell the full story

According to The Financial Times, Apple’s tax payments to Ireland reached $17 billion last year, as disclosed in reports required under new EU rules for large companies.

The $17 billion total includes back taxes from a long-running EU dispute that ended in 2024, when the bloc’s top court ruled that Ireland had granted Apple unlawful state aid, and upheld an order requiring the country to recover up to €13 billion in unpaid taxes.

The FT added that according to the new filings, “a quarter of Apple’s global pre-tax profits in the year to September 2025 were booked through its Ireland entities, where it employs about 3 per cent of its workforce.”

From the FT:

Apple booked pre-tax profits of $6mn per employee in Ireland, compared with just $51,000 per employee in Germany, where it paid $153mn in cash taxes, or 0.3 per cent of its total. Apple employs 5,575 people in Ireland, which is home to its European headquarters, and 4,089 in Germany.

Throughout Apple’s dispute with the EU, the company denied receiving unlawful state aid and argued that it had complied with Irish tax law. Apple said the profits at issue were attributable to intellectual property developed in the US and should therefore be taxed there.

However, the EU’s top court sided with the European Commission, which argued that two Irish tax rulings allowed Apple to allocate most of the profits recorded by Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe to “head offices” that had no employees or physical premises.

Back to today’s report, Apple told the FT that it is “consistently one of the world’s largest taxpayers,” and argued that the new disclosures don’t capture the full scope of what it pays across different countries.

Apple said that the figures focus on corporate income taxes tied to where assets are held, rather than other taxes (such as VAT), which are collected based on where customers are located.

title: Pixel Watch 5 lets you customize double pinch to dismiss alarms, skip music, & more
snippet: Besides expanded availability across apps, the double pinch gesture on the Pixel Watch 5 benefits from being able to “Customize actions” across music and alarms.
fullText:
Besides expanded availability across apps, the double pinch gesture on the Pixel Watch 5 benefits from being able to “Customize actions” across music and alarms.

On the Pixel Watch 4, you can only snooze an alarm with the double pinch gesture. The new model lets you change the behavior and set it to dismiss. 

Go to Settings > Gestures > Hand gestures and scroll down for Customize actions.

Media controls: Play/pause or Skip

Alarm: Snooze or Dismiss

Watch face: Open ongoing notification or Always scroll notification tray

Skipping music is also convenient, while scrolling the notification tray ensures you haven’t missed anything important.

	

The settings description suggests that the Pixel Watch 5 might offer wrist turn customizations, but there are only settings for double pinch today.

Another setting Pixel Watch 5 owners should know is how they can long-press media controls in At a Glance to set whether they just see an icon or both “Icon and text.” The latter shows the song name, though the large font size might cover too much of the watch face. It’s a nice look with a minimalist face.

title: Apple lays off 200+ people across Vision Pro and Siri teams
snippet: Apple is cutting jobs across multiple teams, according to a new Bloomberg report. All told, the company has cut more than 200 jobs across teams working on Vision Pro, Siri, and software engineering.
fullText:
Apple is cutting jobs across multiple teams, according to a new Bloomberg report. All told, the company has cut more than 200 jobs across teams working on Vision Pro, Siri, and software engineering.

In a statement, an Apple spokesperson said the changes were made “to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users.”

“While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles. We are grateful to these team members for their contributions, and we are committed to supporting them throughout their transition, including opportunities to apply for other roles at Apple.”

The report says around 100 of the job cuts come from the Vision Pro group. As part of this, Apple is “largely shutting down a Vision Pro team focused on gaming.” The company is also scaling back the team working on producing Immersive Video for Vision Pro.

Going forward, Apple still plans to produce “a smaller number of videos in-house” and will also encourage third parties to create immersive content.

The report continues:

The company has told employees that the Vision Pro and its visionOS operating system aren’t going away. In the near term, however, Apple is focused on launching smart glasses that wouldn’t support immersive video or advanced gaming titles. The company is still considering a new Vision Pro model for release as early as the end of 2028, Bloomberg News has reported.

Meanwhile, Apple has also cut around 100 positions from its Siri and software teams.

The Siri reorganization is related to the launch of Siri AI, the report says. Apple’s new Siri AI platform is built on a revamped technical architecture, which changes “the necessary expertise” required for the Siri team. Apple therefore decided to “eliminate a small number of existing roles, reallocate resources and create new positions supporting the updated Siri.”

Apple’s “Intelligent Systems Experience team” is also impacted by these cuts.

The changes to the Intelligent Systems Experience team reflect an effort to reorganize work on AI-powered capabilities. As more groups bring AI functions to apps, features and services, Apple is realigning teams to match priorities and accelerate development. The restructuring will eliminate some existing positions while creating new roles.

Today’s Bloomberg report builds on an earlier report that said Apple had laid off around 60 employees from the Vision Pro team.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Homey secures Matter 1.5 certification to expand bridging and energy support
snippet: Athom has announced that it has officially achieved Homey Pro mini, and the Homey Self Hosted Server. This update brings important upgrades for both native device integration and cross-platform device bridging.
fullText:
Athom has announced that it has officially achieved Matter 1.5 certification for its Homey software component, covering the Homey Pro (2023 — 2026), Homey Pro mini, and the Homey Self Hosted Server. This update brings important upgrades for both native device integration and cross-platform device bridging.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

“Most people already own devices that will never speak Matter natively, and those should stay just as usable as anything they buy tomorrow,” said Stefan Witkamp, CEO of Athom.

What is New in Matter 1.5 for Homey

The update adds native support for energy-focused hardware categories, including EV chargers, heat pumps, solar panels, and major appliances.

Matter 1.5 is rolling out via firmware version 13.3.0 for supported Homey Pro and server installations.

Homey Pro and Homey Pro mini feature built-in Thread Border Routers, while self-hosted instances can integrate Matter over Thread accessories utilizing an available local Thread Border Router network

Bridging legacy protocols to Matter

One of Homey’s standout strengths remains its multi-protocol architecture, which supports Zigbee, Z-Wave, infrared, Bluetooth, 433 MHz, WiFi, and proprietary APIs. Through the Matter Bridge app, Homey allows users to expose non-Matter devices to Apple Home/HomeKit, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant.

Homey maintains direct control over the native device locally, while sharing standard accessory representations, including lights, sockets, thermostats, locks, window coverings, and sensors, downstream to receiving platforms via Matter.

9to5Mac’s take

In an ideal world, all of your devices would support Matter out of the box, but until then, I love products like Homey that aim to bring your non-Matter devices into Apple Home. Homey is one of the few smart home products certified for Matter 1.5. Amazon Alexa is currently on Matter 1.0, Apple and Google are on Matter 1.4, while Home Assistant is on Matter 1.3.

You can pick up a Homey device from Amazon.

title: iPadOS 27 adds three features to make iPad more like the Mac
snippet: iPadOS and macOS used to be very different software platforms. But especially since iPadOS 26, the two have become a lot more alike. And that’s even more true this year, with iPadOS 27 adding three features that make the iPad more Mac-like than ever.
fullText:
iPadOS and macOS used to be very different software platforms. But especially since iPadOS 26, the two have become a lot more alike. And that’s even more true this year, with iPadOS 27 adding three features that make the iPad more Mac-like than ever.

#1: App names in status bar

I work on an M5 iPad Pro that‘s attached to a Magic Keyboard all the time. And one issue the iPad has long had for keyboard users is the lack of a clear ‘active app’ indicator.

If you only have one app on-screen, this isn’t a problem. But if you have several apps visible at once, keyboard shortcuts become tricky. I can’t count the number of times I’ve tried a keyboard shortcut thinking it would trigger in one app, only to be surprised that a different app was targeted instead.

The Mac solved this problem long ago by putting the active app’s name in the top-left corner of the screen. And now, iPadOS 27 does this too.

iPadOS 27 users will find the active app’s name right next to other status bar elements like the time and date. It’s a small, but welcome change that makes using an iPad with a keyboard a far more pleasant experience.

Another welcome iPadOS 27 change is the option for an always-on menu bar.

Last year Apple brought the menu bar to iPad for the first time. But unlike the Mac, iPadOS 26’s menu bar would only appear onscreen when explicitly summoned.

In iPadOS 27, the Settings app has a new toggle under Multitasking & Gestures. It reads: ‘Automatically Show and Hide Menu Bar.’

With this toggle turned off, the menu bar will stay visible all the time. I’ve been using my iPad this way during the iPadOS beta and it’s one of my favorite changes this year.

#3: Mac-like speed for everyday tasks

As much as I love my iPad, and appreciate its new powers in iPadOS 26 and 27, I also get frustrated at times by how slow some basic tasks can be. For example, earlier this year I wrote: “Right-clicking in iPadOS often feels slow and laggy, while on a Mac it’s just instant.”

Thanks to Apple’s focus on bug fixes this year, I’m happy to report that iPadOS 27 offers speed improvements for everyday tasks like this.

Apple says context menus now open faster when using a cursor, and I’ve definitely noticed. Browsing files and transferring them to an external drive is now “up to 5x faster,” which Apple says makes it just as fast as Finder on the Mac. Apps now launch more responsively, and window management gets faster too when closing, switching, or dragging windows.

There are still areas where the Mac is quicker and the iPad can feel sluggish. But overall, iPadOS 27’s speed upgrades are a great step in the right direction.

title: iPhone 18 Pro release date: Here’s when Apple’s new flagship is coming
snippet: Apple’s new flagship iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra will be unveiled soon, following the same release pattern the company has kept for years. Here’s when to expect the iPhone 18 Pro announcement and release date, plus details on the lineup.
fullText:
Apple’s new flagship iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra will be unveiled soon, following the same release pattern the company has kept for years. Here’s when to expect the iPhone 18 Pro announcement and release date, plus details on the lineup.

iPhone 18 Pro launch event coming in September, but with a catch

The iPhone is Apple’s most important product. It makes up the vast majority of the company’s earnings. And one way Apple keeps the iPhone business healthy is by launching new flagship models every year.

For many years now, those new iPhone models have launched in September—and all signs point to that happening again this year.

Here are the last three iPhone unveiling dates:

2025: Tuesday, September 9

2024: Monday, September 9

2023: Tuesday, September 12

As you can see, Apple’s schedule with iPhone announcements is very predictable. The company unveils its major new flagships around the second week of September.

One wrinkle this year is that Labor Day is unusually late, set for September 7. Apple probably won’t ask press to travel on a US holiday, which rules out a September 8 date.

That means the event could happen as early as Wednesday, September 9. 

September 9 would be the exact same date as the last two years. It would also follow what Apple did in 2022, when the new iPhone was unveiled two days after Labor Day.

If it doesn’t happen September 9, the latest expected event date would be early the following week.

In any case, early-to-mid September is when to expect the big iPhone 18 Pro reveal.

However, one key change expected this year is that the base iPhone 18 model won’t actually release until early 2027. Instead, Apple’s flagship fall lineup is rumored to consist of just three models:

iPhone 18 Pro

iPhone 18 Pro Max

iPhone Ultra

When to expect iPhone 18 Pro’s official release date

While the exact date of Apple’s iPhone event always varies slightly based on Labor Day, once the unveiling happens, Apple tends to ship its new models on a very consistent day: the Friday of the week following the event.

So if the iPhone 18 Pro is unveiled on Wednesday, September 9, we can expect pre-orders to open on September 11 (or Saturday the 12th, to avoid 9/11). New models would then ship to users on Friday, September 18.

Looking at Apple’s history with recent iPhone launches confirms this pattern.

2025: iPhone 17

Announced: Tuesday, September 9

Pre-orders: Friday, September 12

Release date: Friday, September 19

2024: iPhone 16

Announced: Monday, September 9

Pre-orders: Friday, September 13

Release date: Friday, September 20

2023: iPhone 15

Announced: Tuesday, September 12

Pre-orders: Friday, September 15

Release date: Friday, September 22

Unless Apple goes against its normal patterns this year, September 18 is when users can expect to get their hands on an iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro release date: wrap-up

In summary, here’s what we’re expecting from the iPhone 18 line unveiling and release date, based on Apple’s previous patterns.

2026: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Ultra

Announced: Wednesday, September 9

Pre-orders: Friday, September 11 or Saturday, September 12

Release date: Friday, September 18

iPhone Ultra might ship later than iPhone 18 Pro, but there’s still no consensus on that front.

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold is changing how I multitask on a foldable with ‘App Handles’ [Gallery]
snippet: Previewed in a recent Canary build, Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold ships with the “App Handles” multitasking feature that’s a welcome addition to the experience.
fullText:
Previewed in a recent Canary build, Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold ships with the “App Handles” multitasking feature that’s a welcome addition to the experience.

Built on top of “Bubbles,” this new “App Handles” feature is essentially a dock for floating windows. You can pick any app and drag it off to the far bottom-right corner of the display, and it will launch into a floating window that’s locked into that spot rather than loosely floating around the UI. But it still pops up over whatever else you’re doing.

The biggest benefit is a swipe-up gesture from that bottom corner that activates the app, hence the name “App Handles.” 

You can store multiple apps in this location, switching back and forth as needed. It’s almost like adding a whole second layer of multitasking. You can still put two apps side-by-side on the inner display, with a little pop-up phone that can be running its own apps in a window on that larger canvas.

	

Over my first week with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, this has been my favorite feature. Despite having used a Galaxy Z Fold series device for years with floating windows, I’ve never really used them as they can be a bit finicky. But Google’s implementation of “App Handles,” especially the quick access gesture, has me immediately finding value in it. It’s also nice that when you close the display, whatever apps were set up as a “Handle” just turn into a “Bubble” on the cover display.

Unlike full split screen, it’s a way to multitask without getting in the way. As useful as a foldable’s inner display is for side-by-side multitasking, that’s not always what I want to do, whether that be for formatting errors in the app, wanting the full canvas for one app, or any other number of factors.

Some quick examples of how I’ve been using this:

Having Google Keep at the ready for taking notes

Keeping a messaging app readily available without fully leaving your current app(s)

Quick access to Chrome for additional research when reading in another app

There are a ton of use cases for this, and you’ll probably find at least one that’s unlike how anyone else will use it. 

This is probably my favorite new foldable feature since “Open Canvas” on 2023’s OnePlus Open, and this one might even have more utility in real life. 

I really hope other Android brands, Samsung in particular, jump on adopting this one.

title: Another disguised Russian banking app has topped the US iPhone App Store
snippet: Back in June, we flagged three instances of U.S.-sanctioned Russian banks sneaking client apps onto the App Store. Two months later, another example has climbed to the top of the iPhone App Store.
fullText:

title: Pixel Camera adds ‘Launch control’ and new ‘Quick access’ slider controls on Pixel 11 [Gallery]
snippet: The Google Pixel camera app is adding new “Quick access” controls on the Pixel 11 series, but it’s a little annoying that not only are they disabled by default, but the way you use them isn’t the most intuitive thing either.
fullText:
The Google Pixel camera app is adding new “Quick access” controls on the Pixel 11 series, but it’s a little annoying that not only are they disabled by default, but the way you use them isn’t the most intuitive thing either.

“Quick access” already existed in the Pixel camera app before, arriving back in 2024. But, with the Pixel 11, Google has redesigned the feature. Instead of large slider bars, they appear as slider dials, showing two on each side of the display. These are customizable in layout through the camera settings (found on the overflow button on the setting on the left side of the UI – yes, it’s a bit convoluted) and can include “Looks” on Pixel 11.

Notably, the feature was disabled out of the box on our Pixel 11 devices, but your results may vary.

Also new on the Pixel 11 is a “Launch mode” setting, which lets you open the camera app straight to video mode or to Magic Capture. The default is still photo, and this setting appears right next to the slider settings.

	

Going back to “Quick access,” the sliders themselves aren’t always visible. Instead, you need to tap the screen to get them to show up. A little annoying if you ask me, but also a little unintuitive as there’s no indication these sliders exist until you tap. It’s hard to think of another way this could be implemented, but perhaps a simple toggle to have the sliders show all of the time, maybe even in a condensed state.

Either way, the functionality is simple. Slide up or down to adjust the setting you’ve picked, with an undo button appearing at the bottom once any changes are made. There are no text labels here, but values are shown when changes are made. 

This is yet another UI update debuting on Pixel 11 – ironically in Pixel Camera v11.0 – that we’d expect to show up later on other Pixel devices in one form or another. Existing Pixels are on v10.4.

title: Pixel 11 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Can a re-run contend with a re-do [Video]
snippet: How close does the Pixel 11 Pro get to the iPhone 17 Pro? Does Google’s best of 2026 contend with Apple’s best of 2025? Find out here.
fullText:
How close does the Pixel 11 Pro get to the iPhone 17 Pro? Does Google’s best of 2026 contend with Apple’s best of 2025? Find out here.

Pixel 10 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max: What can Google learn from Apple? [Video]

The iPhone 18 series is on the horizon, but with Google opting to go out in front of Apple and as the market leader in the “premium” segment, it’s always good to use it as a yardstick for where the Pixel should be for the upcoming year. Whether Android or iOS, a few things that are easy to distinguish, so let’s get into the details.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Hardware and design

In any other year, it would be someone pointing out that the iPhone hasn’t changed, but it’s the inverse or has been for a couple of years on the Pixel side of the fence. I like that Google has refined the design again.

	

If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, and yes, that applies to the Pixel this year. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL take a well-received, standout design and make admittedly tiny changes. Nobody would have expected this just a few years ago. We had Pixels evolving on a yearly basis, while Apple is the company shaking up its key phone design.

Metal and glass versus glass and metal is the best way to describe the two designs. You’ve seen one before, and the other is genuinely a great take on what a modern iPhone should be. I do hate how much better the iPhone’s magnets are at the back of the phone. Pixelsnap is not quite as grippy; it’s better than last year, but could be a little stronger. With a violent shake, you might be able to dislodge your phone from a mount, but it would have to be very violent, put that that way.

The displays are where things deviate a little bit as the Pixel 11 Pro gets another panel bump, which elevates the maximum brightness up to 3,600 nits peak. The iPhone 17 Pro Max is still solid at 3,000 nits, but the display tuning is quite different. Apple’s display tuning favors muted, natural colors out of the box, while Google leans into rich colors and contrast. You can change this at almost any time, which is great.

On the iPhone, the hardware gimmicks are the Action button and Camera control buttons. I’d hasten to add that they are not “gimmicks” in the same way that HiLight is on the Pixel. Sure, the LED has some utility, but bringing back notification LEDs that only work in certain circumstances feels a little like a lack of new ideas.

Apple has a history in hardware, almost always at the top of its game. Google has closed the quality gap in the last few years. There’s not as much separating this duo as in years gone by.

Again with the AI

I was worried last year that Google might try to do the stupid thing of trying to replicate Liquid Glass. Instead, we’ve seen something weird happen. Gaussian blur and somewhat frosted glass are being put into more places with Android 17 and the upcoming Android 17 QPR1 – which will release in a few weeks.

With iOS 27, Apple is playing catch-up in a few more AI areas. There’s an attempt at something akin to Gemini Intelligence, which includes a new Siri overhaul. It’s worth noting that Apple enlisted the help of Google to bolster Siri by using Gemini models as the foundational layer. This helps drastically, but the “Agentic AI” is somewhat like certain Pixel features in that it doesn’t always work as intended.

Gemini Intelligence is coming first to Pixel 11 phones, and this is the first proper step in a realized experience that Apple is similarly trying to chase. Getting information at the point of contact with a friend or relative, surfacing that key information when it would help the most. It’s an ongoing process, and it improves drastically over Magic Cue, which is effectively rebranded here.

What is interesting is that Apple offers more controls for Siri than you’re given with Gemini. Pause controls, speaking rate, the ability to disable spoken responses entirely, credit where it’s due, this is a glaring omission on Pixel phones. This goes beyond the basic, as you have true accessibility options for the voice assistant, something which should definitely come to Gemini at some stage.

Siri is allowing continued conversations, which works similarly to Gemini Live, but I can’t deny that the ability to customize the voice is something that Android fans will definitely be jealous of. On iOS 27, Siri stops listening too early, so you have to keep jumping in or chatting to have any real flow. Gemini still handles this better and with more frequent model updates, plus the deep integration with Personal Intelligence has the edge for anyone using a Google account.

Camera

Fundamentally, the camera experience on the Pixel 11 Pro and the iPhone 17 Pro is quite similar. With the introduction of Camera Looks, we have a replica of the Photographic Styles, which was always a great functionality to try to copy or at least mimic to a lesser degree.

Google is much more willing to put AI directly into the camera experience. Pro Res Zoom, Magic Camera, Video Boost, the tools are right there, and AI is a key component. On the iPhone, AI is kept at arm’s length, which many photographers and videographers will arguably prefer.

Camera tuning also still feels markedly different. The skin tone reproduction on Pixel 11 Pro is among the best out there. Real Tone has done wonders, while Apple’s warmer color palette is an acquired taste that many people swear by. 

Google needs to walk a fine line, as hardware is still important in a camera system despite some sensor changes. It’s getting annoying to rely heavily on AI, as at that point, we’re getting further and further into the realms of image creation rather than photography. Sure, add neat AI-enhanced functions that help you take better photos, but don’t over-rely on those. Again, credit where it is due, like any Apple smartphone, the iPhone 17 Pro Max just does more with its camera hardware than the Pixel 11 Pro.

Is the Pixel 11 Pro a worthy opponent to the iPhone 17 Pro Max?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

Google is once again getting ahead of Apple in the release cycle, with the Pixel 11 Pro having precious time on store shelves before the iPhone 18 launches. It’ll be around a month before the next iPhone is available, but there isn’t much to write home about with the Pixel 11 series as a whole.

Apple isn’t moving the needle on software right now. While the Pixel 11 Pro isn’t enough of a visual change for people to instantly know that this is a newer device when compared to last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. You could ask people to spot the differences between the previous generation, and the visual changes to the iPhone might be enough for someone to understand that it’s a newer phone.

That might hurt the Pixel this year, and that is before we get into some of the internal changes and downgrades. A base model Pixel 11 Pro, when pitted against the base model iPhone 17 Pro, feels like a bad value product – and that is before we talk about the good components such as the software, AI functionality, and solid camera tricks.

title: Android brands struggle in Europe amidst RAMageddon, with Apple catching up
snippet: While Apple absolutely dominates the US market, Europe is much more diverse in terms of smartphone market share. According to a new report, Android brands are struggling in Europe amid the RAM pricing crisis, and Apple isn’t missing the opportunity.
fullText:
While Apple absolutely dominates the US market, Europe is much more diverse in terms of smartphone market share. According to a new report, Android brands are struggling in Europe amid the RAM pricing crisis, and Apple isn’t missing the opportunity.

In Q2 of last year, Apple held 25% of the European smartphone market (based on new device shipments), sitting in second place behind Samsung’s 31%. Fast forward a year and the entire market has dropped 10% year-over-year, and Apple has closed that gap.

Counterpoint Research reports that Apple has jumped up to 34% in Q2 2026, matching Samsung’s 34%. Meanwhile, brands such as Xiaomi, Oppo, and Honor have all dropped in share. The report attributes this to “a challenging macro climate, exacerbated by the Iran War, which resulted in spiralling inflation, meant consumer demand was weak compared to the same period last year” while “budget segments were squeezed and most Chinese OEMs struggled.” In other words – RAMageddon continues, and the financial impact of the Iran War didn’t help anything.

It’s been a busy week for rumors surrounding Apple’s upcoming AirPods with cameras. Here’s a roundup of everything we’ve learned about camera-equipped AirPods Pro this week.

The latest on AirPods Pro with cameras

The fun started on Monday, when a video in a macOS 26.7 beta showing off AirPods with cameras was discovered. In the video, a person wearing AirPods Pro holds up a book and asks Siri to remember that book using Visual Intelligence.

In the video, the AirPods Pro with cameras look nearly identical to the existing AirPods Pro 3.

Beyond the video, macOS 26.7 includes plenty of code references to AirPods with cameras, with more details on how they will work.

According to code viewed by 9to5Mac, Apple will use a new AccessorySensorMgrd framework to control image capture and other aspects of AirPods with cameras. In the code, Apple refers to the camera sensor as the “Kino Sensor.”

Each AirPods Pro bud has its own camera, and they are meant to act as a pair and take pictures simultaneously. AccessorySensorMgrd will pair the images together. However, if only one image is captured, the framework generates an empty counterpart.

There are two “capture modes” referenced in macOS 26.7: active and passive. Active mode appears to capture an image from each AirPod bud, or provide a “capture rate” to continuously send images at a specified rate.

The framework monitors factors including image width and height, pixel binning, left/right X/Y offsets, and more.

The framework includes references to AirPods Pro having a privacy indicator light that turns on when images are being captured.

Meanwhile, a MacRumors forums user also found some details on the resolution of the AirPods Pro cameras:

The active capture mode starts with a 640×640 capture and returns a processed 1024×1024 image. That’s about 0.4 megapixels of sampled image data, and a little over 1 megapixel for the output frame.

There is also a lower-resolution passive capture mode with a 320×320 capture that can return 320×320 or 512×512 output, depending on the capture mode.

These are capture-specific resolutions, and the physical sensor’s native resolution may be larger.

The forum member also has more details on “passive mode,” which is described as “lower-resolution and supports environmental awareness.” macOS 26 outlines five possible conditions for a passive capture:

Ambient speech

Audio scene change

Posture change

Head rotation

“Circular region, where the user has moved out of a defined spatial radius.”

AirPods with cameras release date

Naturally, the inclusion of the video and references in a macOS 26.7 beta quickly led to speculation that the product was imminent and could launch as soon as next month’s Apple event alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra.

According to Bloomberg, however, that’s not the case. In a report on Wednesday, Mark Gurman said AirPods with cameras remain on track for a 2027 launch.

Gurman explained that there are two versions of this product in development inside Apple:

B790: The version shown in the video. Essentially a modified version of AirPods Pro 3, but with cameras.

B798: A new generation of AirPods (like AirPods Pro 4), also with cameras added.

It remains unclear which version Apple ultimately plans to ship, but whatever it is, it won’t arrive until next year at the earliest.

Bloomberg’s report also once again reiterated that the AirPods Pro cameras won’t be able to take photos and videos. Instead, they are designed to “scan the surrounding environment and provide context to the Siri digital assistant and other AI tools.”

Wrap up

Ultimately, this week has offered a ton of new information on AirPods with cameras, including features and details on how they will work.

What do you think of Apple adding cameras to AirPods Pro? Do you think it’s a good idea? Let us know down in the comments.
