title: Apple TV has three big new releases coming very soon
snippet: Apple TV has the long-awaited Ted Lasso season 4 airing now and it’s proven a huge hit, but there are three more big new releases coming very soon.
fullText:
Apple TV has the long-awaited Ted Lasso season 4 airing now and it’s proven a huge hit, but there are three more big new releases coming very soon.

#1: Dark Matter

Sci-fi fans have plenty of excellent shows to enjoy on Apple TV. And while Severance and Pluribus are common household titles, one fan-favorite series you may have missed is Dark Matter.

The show is based on Blake Crouch’s bestselling novel and stars Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly.

Dark Matter season 2 premieres Friday, August 28 with its first episode, followed by weekly releases through October 30.

Watch Dark Matter on Apple TV

Here’s Apple’s series summary:

Hailed as one of the best sci-fi novels and celebrating the 10th anniversary of its release this year, “Dark Matter” is a story about the road not taken. In season one, the series followed Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton), a physicist, professor and family man who — one night while walking home on the streets of Chicago — is abducted into an alternate version of his life. Wonder quickly turns to nightmare when he tries to return to his reality amid the mind-bending landscape of lives he could have lived.

#2: Mayday

Apple TV has a packed lineup of new movies coming this fall, most of which will debut first on streaming with no theatrical run.

The first film coming is Mayday, an action-buddy comedy starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh in a twist on the classic spy thriller.

Mayday premieres Friday, September 4 exclusively on Apple TV.

Add Mayday to Apple TV Watchlist

Here’s Apple’s plot summary and the trailer:

Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh team up in “Mayday,” a genre-bending, action-packed buddy comedy that flips the spy thriller on its head. When hotshot U.S. Navy pilot Lieutenant Troy “Assassin” Kelly (Reynolds) is sent on a top-secret mission into Russian territory at the height of the Cold War, the operation implodes, leaving him stranded behind enemy lines. Discovered by Nikolai Ustinov (Branagh), a gruff ex-KGB agent with a penchant for American culture, Troy thinks he’s toast — but could an unlikely alliance between the two lead to Troy’s rescue and a bond neither saw coming?

#3: Slow Horses

One of Apple’s most acclaimed series, Slow Horses, is back soon.

In the streaming era, viewers often have to wait several years for new seasons of a favorite show. But Slow Horses has consistently returned every year, offering highly entertaining espionage exploits with Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb and crew.

Slow Horses season 6 premieres Wednesday, September 16 with its first episode, followed by weekly releases through October 21.

Watch Slow Horses on Apple TV

Here’s Apple’s series summary:

This darkly funny espionage drama follows a team of British intelligence agents who serve in a dumping ground department of MI5 due to their career-ending mistakes. Led by their brilliant but irascible leader, the notorious Jackson Lamb (Academy Award winner Sir Gary Oldman), they navigate the espionage world’s smoke and mirrors to defend England from sinister forces.

title: These cheap Fitbit Air bands are better and cheaper than the official options
snippet: After a few months of daily wear with my Fog colored Fitbit Air, I hit a stage where I wanted some alternate accessories and, so, I took a punt on some cheap bands from Amazon, only to be blown away with how good they actually were.
fullText:
After a few months of daily wear with my Fog colored Fitbit Air, I hit a stage where I wanted some alternate accessories and, so, I took a punt on some cheap bands from Amazon, only to be blown away with how good they actually were.

My first bit of advice for anyone with the Fitbit Air is to go for a darker color than you usually would choose. The default fabric band on the Fog color is especially bad for staining and picking up dirt, not to mention that, because it’s an off-white-blue color, it almost looks like faded denim, and if you’ve ever owned a light pair of jeans, you’ll know how quickly they can look dirty. As much as I loved it when I picked one up, I regret choosing this option for that reason.

Wearing in the gym, in bed, going for a run, just general day-to-day tasks like cooking and whatnot have already taken a toll on the fabric band. I managed to stain the band just washing my hands while at a gig a few weeks ago, as the liquid soap was such a deep green color that I now have a patchwork of discolored sections that, I’ll be honest, looks gross.

At launch, there were not many alternative options to the vastly overpriced official Fitbit Air bands, at well over $30. We’ve seen some really cool mods and attachments to integrate the tracker into classic watch bands and more. The reality is that most of us just want a nice, cheap band that’ll do the job.

	

So after staining my band and being patient, Amazon is now littered with cheap alternatives to throw the Fitbit Air “pebble” in and then adorn your wrist with. I took a punt on a few, and I’m actually blown away by how high-quality they are. I don’t think I’ll bother picking up an official option again now.

In the UK, we don’t have access to the official Stephen Curry strap. So this has been a way to get a solid replica that is like 95% of the way there. Not quite 100% as the metal clasp isn’t quite the same color, but that isn’t too big of a deal anyway.

I picked up a double pack of bands from a brand called “iBesky,” but I feel like an idiot because it looks like the company does a triple pack in the US. I paid around $23 for two with exchange rates, which I thought was excellent value for money. After a few weeks of wear, I doubt I’ll go back to the official bands that came with my Fitbit Air, and if, like me, you regret the color you chose, then try these out for size. I highly, highly recommend them, and I’ll be trying some more in the coming weeks.

title: YouTube Premium is getting another price hike for some users all around the world

fullText:

Google is now bringing price hikes to other international regions. These vary by region, but seem to be around 10-15%, mirroring the US price hike.

Here are a few YouTube Premium price hikes we’ve seen pop up online from various regions:

	

Parts of Europe: €13.99 > €15.99

Finland: €14.99 > €16.99

Romania: RON 29.00 > RON 32.00

Singapore: $13.98 > $15.98 (Family $27.98 > $31.98)

Those affected will see the higher price kick in with their next billing date on or after September 23, 2026.

fullText:
August 21, 2026: Apple Watch Series 12 is rumored to include a ceramic option for the first time since the Series 5 was discontinued. With that in mind, I’m resharing my hands-on post of my favorite Apple Watch from September 2019. Seven years later, it’s still the best version I’ve ever owned. I hope you enjoy!

Apple Watch Series 5 introduces the return of the ceramic Edition after being notably absent from the Series 4 lineup. That means this is the first time ceramic has been an option with the redesign that debuted last year, and the new look is stunning. Check out our initial hands-on with the Apple Watch Edition before our full Series 5 review later next week.

Unboxing ceramic Apple Watch Edition

Starting with Apple Watch Series 5, Apple is adding titanium and bringing back ceramic as case material options. These are in addition to aluminum and stainless steel. Titanium comes in two brushed metal finishes, one silver and the other space black. Ceramic returns in the same white finish we saw with Apple Watch Series 2 and Series 3. There’s no gray ceramic finish like we saw with Apple Watch Series 3.

Both ceramic and titanium models are in the Apple Watch Edition collection. There are fewer packaging perks with Series 5 than we saw with Series 2 and Series 3. Both Apple Watch Edition case finishes include a Sport band in the box. This is in addition to whichever band you choose at purchase (just like the Hermès collection). However, two things are missing this year.

Apple Watch Edition models used to include Apple’s Magnetic Charging Dock and a special book on how the material was created. Both are absent with Series 5, possibly to accommodate a standard box for all watches. The $79 Magnetic Charging Dock can be purchased separately.

Here’s a look at the Series 5 packaging for Apple Watch Edition. It carries over the same experience as Series 4:

Apple Watch Edition tucks the bundled Sport band in the main box and includes both small/medium and medium/large straps.

Underneath the main box is the band chosen at purchase. Apple Watch Edition can be bought with Sport Loop, Leather Loop, Milanese Loop, Link Bracelet, or Sport bands. This is configurable through the new Apple Watch Studio experience.

The paper sleeve wraps the main box and band packaging together. It’s similar to what we saw with Series 4, minus some color and band designs.

A front-to-back makeover

This is the first time the redesigned Apple Watch has been offered in ceramic. That means the Apple Watch Edition has a different look than Series 3 versions of ceramic.

The back cover shifted from aluminum and steel to all ceramic starting with Apple Watch Series 4. That continues with Apple Watch Series 5. The back cover blends with the dark-colored optical heart rate sensor on all Series 4 and Series 5 watches. This creates a strong contrast with the white ceramic finish.

The Digital Crown also has a new look with the ceramic Apple Watch Series 5. The original ceramic model had a black cap inside the white crown. The second ceramic version shifted to a red cap like other cellular watches. The new version — which includes an electrical heart sensor for the ECG app — has a more subtle black cap with a red accent ring.

A new line of Sport Loop band colors debuted with Apple Watch Series 5 this month, including two-tone options like the new Anchor Gray option seen here.

The ceramic Apple Watch Edition still includes a special Sport band with a ceramic pin that isn’t sold separately. Originally paired with an off-white color called Cloud, Apple added the Soft White version seen below with Series 3.

More ceramic Apple Watch Edition views

Apple Watch Edition in ceramic comes in two case sizes: 40mm and 44mm. It’s priced from $1299 to $1749 depending on band selection. Apple Watch Series 5 in other case materials starts at $399. Larger displays and cellular models are priced higher, but different case materials include the same features.

title: Here’s how iPhone 18 Pro will differentiate itself from prior models
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next month, and many iPhone users might be asking: what’s going to be truly different this year? Here are some key ways Apple plans to differentiate iPhone 18 Pro from prior models, per the latest rumors.
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next month, and many iPhone users might be asking: what’s going to be truly different this year? Here are some key ways Apple plans to differentiate iPhone 18 Pro from prior models, per the latest rumors.

Big changes for Main camera

Every year, Apple upgrades the iPhone’s camera system in various ways. But it’s rare for big changes to impact the Main camera.

iPhone 17 Pro brought an overhauled front camera and improved Telephoto. With iPhone 18 Pro, Apple is rumored to have even more Telephoto upgrades, but also big changes for the Main camera. Leaker Fixed Focus Digital recently hinted as much.

He says the iPhone 18 Pro line’s Main camera upgrade is “confirmed” and results in a more than 2mm increase in the “aluminum alloy back panel.” In other words, the camera plateau may be getting even thicker this year than what had previously been rumored.

Why such a significant increase? In a follow-up post, the leaker says it’s due to an “Enlarged main camera module.”

Mark Gurman has said on multiple occasions that iPhone 18 Pro will have “some of the biggest camera hardware upgrades in the lineup’s history.” We’re expecting a variable aperture feature, but it sounds like there’s a lot more to the story with this year’s camera changes.

Apple-designed C2 modem

Apple started transitioning away from Qualcomm 5G modems last year when iPhone 16e launched with a C1 modem designed in-house. iPhone Air continued the trend by using a C1X modem. But Apple’s most popular models—iPhone 17 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone 17—all stuck with Qualcomm.

Rumors indicate iPhone 18 Pro will make the transition to an Apple-designed C2 modem. This should bring advantages like:

improved battery efficiency

new privacy feature: ‘Limit Precise Location’ 

better reliability in tough data spots

Best-ever battery life, especially in iPhone 18 Pro Max

Partly because of C2, and the new A20 Pro chip, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to offer the best iPhone battery life ever.

But iPhone 18 Pro Max should be especially impressive. That’s because regulatory filings point to a roughly 10% larger physical battery.

Last year’s Pro Max model offered very generous battery life. But iPhone 18 Pro Max could take things to a whole new level.

Design firsts: Dark Cherry color and new Dynamic Island

Source: Sonny Dickson

Apple historically has avoided bold, bright colors on its Pro models. But that changed last year when Cosmic Orange became a huge hit among iPhone 17 Pro buyers.

For iPhone 18 Pro, the new flagship color will be a Dark Cherry/Burgundy shade that could prove similarly popular. This will be the first time Apple launches a color quite like this. And it’s the first red shade ever on a Pro model iPhone.

Additionally, a new Dynamic Island design will debut on iPhone 18 Pro. It’s expected to be 35% smaller than the current Dynamic Island.

snippet: Google announced today that tap to pay with Google Pay is coming to Walmart stores in the US.
fullText:
Google announced today that tap to pay with Google Pay is coming to Walmart stores in the US.

The retailer has historically been one of the lone holdouts against supporting NFC payments. Instead, it wanted customers to use the QR code-based Walmart Pay inside the Walmart app.

That’s now changing, with Google Pay support starting to roll out to select Walmart stores and Sam’s Club locations in the US beginning August 24.

The plan is to add support at all US stores and clubs by the end of 2026, with fuel stations coming online in mid-2027.

	

Walmart says “Tap to Pay gives customers and members another familiar and convenient way to pay at checkout using contactless payment methods.” Stores will continue to support cash, credit cards, and Walmart Pay.

title: GrapheneOS phone from Motorola arrives next year, ‘higher end’ compared to Pixel with a price to match
snippet: The privacy-focused GrapheneOS is making its way to dedicated hardware soon, with a device in the works from Motorola. According to a quick update on that device, it’ll be “higher end” than a Pixel with a price to match, and it’ll be coming sometime next year.
fullText:
The privacy-focused GrapheneOS is making its way to dedicated hardware soon, with a device in the works from Motorola. According to a quick update on that device, it’ll be “higher end” than a Pixel with a price to match, and it’ll be coming sometime next year.

Motorola first confirmed that it was working with GrapheneOS early this year, but without much to share about what that device would bring to the table. It was always going to be a flagship-tier device given the requirements of GrapheneOS, though.

In a post on Mastodon, GrapheneOS shares that the “initial devices” – note, plural – “should be available in 2027.” They’ll apparently offer “higher end hardware” compared to Google Pixel devices that currently run Graphene, “at a higher price” too. Qualcomm’s flagship chips are specifically mentioned here, with “lower end” devices not meeting requirements around updates and security features.

The initial devices with GrapheneOS support should be available in 2027. The initial devices will be flagships so they’ll be higher end hardware than Pixels at a higher price. Lower end devices will take more time to meet our requirements since the updates and security features aren’t as good. It’s mostly due to how Qualcomm handles it. The latest Snapdragon flagships have the best security features. We’ll also need Motorola to start paying them for longer updates below flagships.

As it stands, only Google Pixel phones can run GrapheneOS, with every Tensor-powered Pixel having builds available. The expansion to Motorola is a big deal, but we’ll have to wait and see when these arrive to know if they’ll stick the landing amidst privacy-conscious buyers.

title: Pixel Watch 5’s AI watch face generator keeps the same form factor feeling fresh [Gallery]
snippet: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 isn’t some radical new redesign, but it does bring about some welcome enhancements. And while I’m still wrestling with mixed feelings around the use of generative AI nowadays, the Pixel Watch 5’s AI watch face generator has been a surprising delight.
fullText:
Google’s Pixel Watch 5 isn’t some radical new redesign, but it does bring about some welcome enhancements. And while I’m still wrestling with mixed feelings around the use of generative AI nowadays, the Pixel Watch 5’s AI watch face generator has been a surprising delight.

I’m a smartwatch wearer for a number of reasons, from notifications to health tracking, but a pretty big part of it is customization. If I was a traditional watch guy, I’d probably have dozens of watches to swap out depending on the day. But, with Pixel Watch, I’ve really just settled into swapping watch faces and bands to suit whatever I’m feeling on that particular day.

So when Google first showed me this new feature that lets me create a new watch face from just a voice command, I was immediately intrigued to try it in person. 

This is an extension of Gemini Intelligence on the Pixel Watch 5 and, unlike the rest of the catalog, it’s a point that Google isn’t really talking about all that much. It’s not mentioned anywhere on the Google Store listing, for example. It works more or less how you’d expect. Go to switch your watch face, tap the big ol’ “Create” button, and Google will either let you describe your desired face or pick from a variety of guided categories. In that sense, it’s not all that different from AI-generated wallpapers on Pixel phones.

	

But “Create your own” is where this really shines. Using voice commands, you can just describe what it is you want and Google will give you the result within about 10-20 seconds. While the core styles are always either a vertical digital face, a vertical digital face with complication arcs, or a horizontal face with a single complication, the actual digits and theme are up to your imagination. You can get surprisingly specific with the design. If you don’t like the results, a “Try again” button will retry your existing prompt and spit out a new result.

I’ve had a lot of fun with this, matching my watch face to my band or to some vibrant-colored shirts. Here are a couple of the creations I’ve been using this week. The blue face was generated using the prompt “make a watch face using blue and white colors in a marbled pattern” while the yellow and purple one was “make a watch face with yellow and purple colors with a dotted pattern kind of like lava.”

The biggest problem is really just that this is locked into a specific layouts. Even if you specifically ask, there’s no way to get an analog watch face. I’m sure this can be added later, but it seems like a pretty big oversight on Google’s part.

Still, this has been a nice refresh to the experience. Outside of the updated gestures that really change the way you use the Pixel Watch 5 – more on that in Abner’s review – I think it’s my favorite update this year.

Technically speaking, I’m sure Google could implement a version of this feature on existing hardware. The extra horsepower and memory on Pixel Watch 5 surely plays a role in making this feature usable on the actual smartwatch, but there’s nothing saying you can’t just offload this to the phone, creating the face over on the Pixel Watch app and then sending it over. If Google ever expands this to prior generations, that’s the only way I can see it happening. 

Pixel Watch 5 is available now starting at $399.

title: John Ternus as CEO could bring ‘bigger acquisitions,’ new product categories: analyst
snippet: Tim Cook is in his final weeks as Apple CEO, with John Ternus set to take over the top job on September 1. And per Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan, Ternus could usher in a bolder, riskier era at Apple.
fullText:
Tim Cook is in his final weeks as Apple CEO, with John Ternus set to take over the top job on September 1. And per Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan, Ternus could usher in a bolder, riskier era at Apple.

John Ternus expected to take more risks as CEO with new products, acquisitions, R&D

Apple’s CEO transition is almost complete. So far, the company has worked very hard to emphasize the continuity Ternus will bring to the role.

But not everyone at Wall Street seems to believe Ternus will follow Cook’s example as closely. 

In a research note seen by The Street, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan reiterates a strong ‘Buy’ rating for Apple. And a key part of that endorsement relates to expectations that Ternus will maintain Cook’s legacy while also having a bigger “risk appetite.” Moz Farooque writes:

The bank underscored Apple’s move away from its net-cash-neutral objective as an early signal that its management might be more willing to deploy capital. That would translate into heavier R&D spending, more CapEx, and potentially bigger acquisitions, areas that weren’t major features of Cook’s strategy.

Under Ternus, BofA sees the possibility of Apple moving much more quickly into new categories, including AI glasses, camera-equipped AirPods, smart rings, home automation, personal assistants, and robotics.

Essentially, BofA believes Ternus will maintain Cook’s legacy of turning Apple into a highly profitable global machine. But he’s also expected to leverage the company’s position of strength to make riskier moves in the future.

We likely won’t see any major changes right when Ternus takes over as CEO. But perhaps in the months to come, any potential differing priorities will start to become clear.

title: Walmart finally launching Apple Pay support next week
snippet: Walmart has announced that it will finally begin rolling out Apple Pay support next week. The retailer has resisted offering Apple Pay support for more than a decade, despite pressure from shoppers.
fullText:
Walmart has announced that it will finally begin rolling out Apple Pay support next week. The retailer has resisted offering Apple Pay support for more than a decade, despite pressure from shoppers. 

Apple Pay is finally coming to Walmart

Walmart announced the news in a press release today. The company will roll out contactless support, including Apple Pay, to select Walmart and Sam’s Club locations starting on August 24. The feature will come to all stores in the United States by the end of this year, as well as fuel stations by mid-2027.

Walmart is adding broad contactless payment support, so that includes Apple Pay on iPhone and Apple Watch, Google Pay, contactless cards, and other payment platforms. Shoppers will also be able to add their Walmart and Sam’s Club cards to Apple Wallet and other platforms. Contactless support will exist alongside existing payment methods, including Walmart Pay. 

The company says: 

Tap to Pay gives customers and members another familiar and convenient way to pay at checkout using contactless payment methods. Whether picking up groceries, gifts or everyday essentials, they can check out using eligible contactless card, phone, or smartwatch. Customers and members can also add their eligible Walmart, Sam’s Club and OnePay cards to their digital wallets, giving them another convenient way to use their cards.

Walmart is one of the final major Apple Pay holdouts, so this is big news for consumers. For years, the retailer refused to offer contactless support in favor of Walmart Pay, its QR code-based payment system. 

As recently as last year, Walmart doubled down on its belief that Walmart Pay was a more convenient solution for shoppers than Apple Pay. To use Walmart Pay, however, you have to add a debit or credit card to the Walmart app on your iPhone, then scan a QR code at checkout to pay with your iPhone.

A quick search on social media shows just how frustrated users had become by Walmart’s refusal to support Apple Pay.

After all, there is a reason that most other longtime Apple Pay holdouts caved years ago, including Kroger, Home Depot, and H-E-B.

Did Walmart’s lack of Apple Pay support impact your shopping habits? Will you be more inclined to shop at Walmart and Sam’s Club once they roll out Apple Pay? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Narwal Freo 20 robot vacuum has a flagship-tier mop for hundreds of dollars less
snippet: The robot vacuum scene has heavily focused on improving mopping tech in recent years and, right now, the flagship models are better than they’ve ever been. For those of us without bottomless pockets, though, the Narwal Freo 20 offers a flagship-tier mop and overall cleaning experience for a much lower price tag.
fullText:
The robot vacuum scene has heavily focused on improving mopping tech in recent years and, right now, the flagship models are better than they’ve ever been. For those of us without bottomless pockets, though, the Narwal Freo 20 offers a flagship-tier mop and overall cleaning experience for a much lower price tag.

Available starting this week, the Narwal Freo 20 is the most advanced release in the history of Narwal’s Freo lineup. Freo has always focused on delivering high-end features at a more affordable price tag.

This year’s Narwal Freo 20 is the most advanced yet, and it’s not close.

It all starts with Freo 20’s key feature: support for Narwal’s FlowWash mopping system. This delivers a wider track mop that is constantly cleaned and refreshed with hot water as the robot cleans your floors, while also applying pressure to ensure the best possible clean. It covers roughly 7x more surface area with each pass through your home.

	

This not only removes dirt more effectively, but also helps avoid an issue that plagues many other robot mops where dirty water and debris can get pushed off to the side, requiring additional runs to actually clean up the floor. 9to5Google has reviewed this system on Narwal’s flagship model.

It’s not just the mop that is powerful on Narwal Freo 20. The robot packs 31,000 Pa of suction power, rivaling some of the best options on the market, while using Narwal’s DualFlow Tangle-Free system, reducing hair tangles and, ultimately, maintenance. It also has Narwal’s typical inclusions with extendable mop and brush mounts to help clean corners more fully, while the 3.74-inch (95mm) build can fit easily under most tables for a thorough clean. 

Beyond that, Narwal Freo 20 has TwinAI Obstacle Avoidance that utilizes built-in RGB cameras and AI processing to not only go around obstacles but also determine what the robot is seeing to help avoid issues with getting stuck in household items such as cables. 

The on-board AI processing also helps support Narwal’s Pet Care Mode – which can increase suction or go and find your pet in the home – as well as a Baby Care mode, with the latter decreasing suction to avoid waking a sleeping child. 

Finally, there’s the dock.

Where many older robot vacuums made you choose between automatic dustbin emptying or mop cleaning, the Narwal Freo 20 supports both. The dock can automatically empty the dustbin for up to 120 days of running the robot, while the mop is cleaned using on-board clean and dirty water tanks. The mops are washed in hot water and then dried with heated air. Plus, the whole dock has an updated look that’s clean and refined.

Narwal Freo 20 generally sells for $1,099, which is already a bargain compared to the flagship-tier systems that it battles. At launch, though, you can get it for just $899 – an absolute steal! That price runs from today, August 20, through September 3. For an even better deal, use the exclusive code 925GGF20 to take an additional $50 off your purchase through August 26.

title: Apple reportedly lays off 60 Vision employees amid shifting priorities
snippet: AppleInsider reports that Apple “has just laid off an entire team dedicated to VR development,” with at least 60 employees reportedly affected. Here are the details.
fullText:
AppleInsider reports that Apple “has just laid off an entire team dedicated to VR development,” with at least 60 employees reportedly affected. Here are the details.

Apple reportedly scales back Vision team

According to the report, which cites reliable sources, “Apple has laid off at least 60 employees tied to Apple’s VR team, the Apple Vision Group, and similar positions.” Apple has not confirmed nor commented on the report.

More than a year ago, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple had broken up the Vision Products Group, while Mike Rockwell, who used to oversee the group, was put in charge of the Siri revamp. Last May, Gurman recapped his report as follows:

I reported over a year ago that Apple had broken up the Vision Products Group, or VPG. That means the staff went from a single entity that combined Vision hardware and software and were split up and moved to Apple’s larger hardware and software engineering organizations.

Gurman would go on to say that Apple remained committed to visionOS and its broader spatial-computing ambitions, even as it deprioritized major new enclosed headsets in favor of other AI wearables.

Today’s news also comes just two months after Spatial Insider’s Justin Ryan asked Apple Senior Director Steve Sinclair, who leads product marketing for visionOS, about reports that Apple had put Vision Pro “on ice” and broken up the team behind it.

Sinclair replied:

It’s still early innings for spatial computing. And so, there’s a lot of things that we’re doing, we’re learning, and continue to improve on and continue to invest in. And so I would hope that updates like visionOS 27 and all the things that we’re adding, and all the capabilities that we’re unlocking, whether it’s for consumer use or it’s for business use, serves as evidence that we are invested in this platform and we’re invested in this idea of spatial computing and building these capabilities that just can’t be done on any other device.

Sinclair’s response also echoed comments made by incoming CEO John Ternus in April, when he said Apple was still in the “early innings” of spatial computing and described Vision Pro as an “extraordinary product,” pointing to growing use cases in enterprise and medicine.

	

Last October, Apple Vision Pro got a hardware upgrade with the M5 chip, which enabled 10% more rendered pixels and refresh rates of up to 120Hz, while keeping the price at $3,499. Then, last June, Apple raised it to $3,699 amid the ongoing memory crunch, which also led to price hikes for other products, including Apple TV, iPad, Mac, and HomePod.

AppleInsider’s report also comes against the backdrop of Apple’s reported shift in priorities, with resources increasingly moving toward AI-powered smart glasses.

The first model, expected to be unveiled at WWDC 2027 and launch later that year, is said to rely on cameras, Siri, and Visual Intelligence rather than an AR display. Apple had reportedly hoped to unveil the glasses this year and launch them in early 2027, but pushed the timeline back as it rethinks privacy-related aspects of the product amid growing backlash against Meta’s AI glasses.

title: Google Home update lets you set light color temperature to your favorite kelvin using voice commands
snippet: Google Home is rolling out an update that addresses some of the most overlooked pain points for the voice assistant, like refined broadcast commands, better Spotify request recognition, and granular smart light color temperature control down to the kelvin. Don’t be shy; we all have a favorite kelvin rating.
fullText:
Google Home is rolling out an update that addresses some of the most overlooked pain points for the voice assistant, like refined broadcast commands, better Spotify request recognition, and granular smart light color temperature control down to the kelvin. Don’t be shy; we all have a favorite kelvin rating.

Google has been rolling out quality Home updates in a steady stream recently. Most of the updates focus on improvements to Gemini for Home and the polish that’s needed since it’s still stuck in early access. Today’s update, though, is bringing some solid changes to issues that have plagued even the lightest Google Home users.

The August 20 update includes three changes to the Google Home voice assistant – Gemini. First, Spotify command recognition has reportedly been cleaned up. Google says it’s “improved how [it] recognize[s] the songs, artists, and playlists you request on Spotify.” For the seasoned Google Home users, requests for certain songs have always been a little hit or miss. Further, general voice commands often get mistaken for music requests, and random tunes begin to play at an uncomfortable volume. Hopefully, this update lessens that occurrence.

Changes to how broadcasts are handled is packed into the changelog, too. Google notes that broadcasts will now be a two-step process. You ask for Gemini to broadcast a message, wait, then let it know what the message is. Much better than the one-line request prone to miscommunication.

	

The last voice assistant change will make the color temperature nerds happy. Google Home will now recognize voice commands with specific color temperature requests. You can say “Hey Google, set the living room lights to 2700 kelvins,” and you’ll get an accurate color shift. This has always been an option in the app, but not something easily done with voice controls. You may need to learn color temperature ratings by heart.

The changelog adds that several adjustments are taking place in the app, like consistent temperature unit of measurements across all devices. European-style door locks are gaining support, as well.

Google says there should be fewer app crashes on iOS devices and better offline camera controls that remain consistent during connection issues. This comes after Google recently added support for more third-party cameras.

On Android, the update fixes an issue where camera streams could get stuck at 360p. If the connection allows, affected cameras should stream at full resolution.

Lastly, failed payments for Google Home Premium will result in a clear alert, so there isn’t a lapse in features or camera storage.

Google’s August 20 update for Google Home should be rolling out to users starting today.

title: Apple bucks downward trend as reports show global smartphone shipment and sales declines
snippet: Four Counterpoint Research reports published this week reveal drops in smartphone sales and shipments in India, Latin America, Europe, and China. Here are the reports.
fullText:
Four Counterpoint Research reports published this week reveal drops in smartphone sales and shipments in India, Latin America, Europe, and China. Here are the reports.

Apple sees growth as smartphone market keeps sliding

While the slowdown in smartphone sales and shipments is not a recent phenomenon, four reports published by Counterpoint Research this week help show just how much memory shortages and rising prices are affecting demand across the globe.

According to a report published yesterday, smartphone shipments in Europe dropped 10% year-over-year in the second quarter, reaching a three-year low.

Even so, Apple gained nine percentage points, matching Samsung at 34% of the shipments share each. Chinese brands Xiaomi, Oppo, and Honor all lost share, ending the quarter at 15%, 4%, and 3%, respectively.

Moving on to a report on smartphone sales in China during the first 30 weeks of 2026, Counterpoint said the market contracted 8.6% year over year, “with the decline returning to double digits after the 618 shopping festival amid seasonal weakness and continued memory cost inflation.”

The firm added that Apple entered its “seasonal slowdown” in July ahead of the launch of its new iPhone lineup, expected next month, while “a meaningful portion of demand” had already been pulled forward around the 618 shopping festival.

Another market that saw a steep decline in sales was India, where Counterpoint recorded three consecutive weeks of year-over-year declines following July’s major online sales events. Across weeks 14 through 31, sales grew year over year in just two weeks, both of which occurred around major promotional events.

Counterpoint says sales were down 14% during weeks 14 through 31, with Apple once again countering the trend with a 15% year-over-year increase, “the strongest sales growth during the period, (…) driven by sustained demand for the iPhone 17 series and continued affordability offers.”

Finally, in a report released today on smartphone shipments in Latin America during Q2 2026, Counterpoint said the market declined 10% year over year, with Apple and Samsung the only major brands to post growth, up 5% and 6%, respectively.

From the report:

Apple shipments increased 5% YoY. This performance was driven by the brand’s decision to absorb the price hike, alongside consistent demand for the iPhone 17 Pro Max. The iPhone 17e continued to build momentum during Q2 following its launch in late March, while legacy models sustained steady demand.

Counterpoint also noted that “Apple leads LATAM’s high‑end and premium price segments (>$600) with around a 51% share, while Samsung stands as the only significant competitor, reaching about 40% of the segment.”

title: Pixel 11 Gboard Writing tools offer ‘Personalized suggestions’ with Gemini Intelligence
snippet: On the Pixel 11 series, Google has updated Gboard’s Writing tools with Gemini Intelligence to offer “Personalized suggestions.”
fullText:
On the Pixel 11 series, Google has updated Gboard’s Writing tools with Gemini Intelligence to offer “Personalized suggestions.”

The big upgrade is how Gboard now “provides draft suggestions tailored to your personal style” as part of a new “Suggested” tab. It is “based on analysis of your current conversation, text input, and typing patterns.”

If you type “7 PM Spanish restaurant?” in a messaging app text field, the “Suggested” tab may rewrite it to “That sounds like a great plan! How about dinner on Thursday at 7 PM at the Spanish restaurant?”

Specifically, Gboard will use your “typing history, as well as screen context taken at the time of use from supported first and third-party messaging apps.” The latter is “obtained by taking a snapshot of your screen only at the time of use.” Like other features, Private AI Compute cloud processing is leveraged:

With Google’s Private AI Compute, your data is encrypted and processed in a private, dedicated space on your device and in the cloud. No one can see your data, not even Google.

There’s a new menu in the top-right corner that lets you enable/disable these “Personalized suggestions.” Google notes if they are “unavailable for this app” or “at this time,” in which case the tab does not appear.

	

Pixel 10 vs. 11

Additionally, a new smart reply feature “provides quick response options based on your screen context” and writing style. 

The “Predefined rewriting styles” are unchanged, but will use screen text if Personalized suggestions are enabled: 

Proofread: Check and correct your texts for grammatical or spelling mistakes.

Rephrase: Offers alternative phrasing for clearer or more appropriate communication.

Professional: Adjusts tone for formal communication.

Friendly: Changes tone to be more casual and approachable.

Emojify: Adds emojis to messages for expressiveness.

Elaborate: Expands text with more details.

Shorten: Condenses text for conciseness.

The carousel that lets you access them has shrunk a bit to fit the “Describe your edit” button. This lets you manually enter a prompt (“How should this text change?”).

This Pixel 11 feature is supported in Google Messages, Google Chat, Line, and “other chat apps” with the following languages:

English (Australia, Canada, India, UK, and US)

Chinese (Simplified and Traditional)

French (France and Canada)

German (Germany)

Italian (Italy)

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese (Portugal and Brazil)

Spanish (US, Mexico, and Spain)

Available in all supported countries or regions, excluding the European Economic Area (EEA).

title: Google Messages RCS breaks with ‘3100’ error for some, especially Galaxy switchers
snippet: An issue with Google Messages appears to be breaking RCS for some users, with much of the problem tracing back to Samsung Galaxy devices.
fullText:
An issue with Google Messages appears to be breaking RCS for some users, with much of the problem tracing back to Samsung Galaxy devices.

Update 8/20: Google, confirming this is a carrier issue, says that it is working with partners to fix this problem, providing the following statement to 9to5Google.

We’re aware of this issue and are working with our carrier partners to get it fixed as soon as possible.

Over the past few days, a number of Reddit threads have popped up from Google Messages users who are unable to use RCS to send or receive messages. But this doesn’t appear to be any kind of widespread outage, but rather something to do with those on Galaxy phones, especially when switching to a new device or network.

Affected users are seeing error code “3100” in the Google Messages app, which a Google account says is “Trouble connecting. Awaiting retry.” In other words, the device isn’t properly connecting to RCS servers. Those affected appear to either be upgrading to a new device – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in two posts – or moving to a new carrier. The same account brings out the potential that this could be an error between porting numbers for one user, or Samsung’s Smart Switch having “transferred corrupted cache files” in the other.

	

So, there’s no clear cause for this just yet.

The problem has only shown up for Galaxy users thus far, implying that could be part of the problem.

Google’s troubleshooting steps include turning RCS off, clearing data for “Carrier Services,” rebooting the device, and then turning RCS back on, but success seems hit or miss. Android Authority notes that one user details a six-step process that includes temporarily turning off 2-step verification and clearing Play Services data. While it apparently works, you should probably try Google’s steps before doing anything with 2FA – and you should turn that back on immediately if you do turn it off.

We’ll update this article if Google provides any further details about what might be wrong. Let us know if you’re running into this problem, and what device you’re using.

title: Google Pixel screen savers add new styles and iPhone-like switching [Gallery]
snippet: Google Pixel 11 phones ship with an update to screen savers, with support for a new style and the ability to select more than one option and switch through them – much like iPhones do.
fullText:
Google Pixel 11 phones ship with an update to screen savers, with support for a new style and the ability to select more than one option and switch through them – much like iPhones do.

Screen savers aren’t enabled by default on Pixel phones, but they are getting quite a bit more useful on the Pixel 11 series. 

That starts with a new piece of functionality – you can now set more than one screen saver and switch between them. That’s something that Apple’s “StandBy” feature on iPhone also supports, though it works a bit differently on Pixel. Where it’s just a simple swipe on iPhone, Pixel’s version is tied to the back gesture. You need to swipe in from the edge of the display to move between screen savers – which is a little tricky on the Fold given the side-mounted fingerprint sensor.

And you might have noticed something new in those screenshots, a new screen saver style. Google has added “Charge” to the lineup, a dedicated screen saver theme that shows the time at the bottom with your battery percentage taking up most of the display. The minimalist design also has a bar that includes stops at 80% and 100%, the former as that’s generally when fast charging tends to slow down. There are time estimates for both.

	

Google has also introduced updates to the “Clock” screen saver, with the digital and analog styles merging into one and now being much more customizable. You can pick from styles inspired by the lockscreen clocks introduced back in Android 14.

This is all available out of the box on Pixel 11 devices – which is why our screenshots are unwatermarked – and presumably will arrive on older Pixel models later on.

title: Pixel 11’s Magic Capture perfectly solves a very modern parenting dilemma
snippet: Over the past week, I’ve probably shot more video of my kids than in the previous year combined. I’m a photographer, so I take photos — thousands of them — but rarely swipe over to that tempting toggle that displaces the moment for momentum. The dichotomy between photo and video has existed as long as there have been cameras capable of doing both. Many attempts have been made to bridge the gap, from HTC Zoe in 2013 to Apple’s Live Photos and Google’s subsequent Motion Photos years later, but most technical limitations have largely kept the two functions separate.
fullText:
Over the past week, I’ve probably shot more video of my kids than in the previous year combined. I’m a photographer, so I take photos — thousands of them — but rarely swipe over to that tempting toggle that displaces the moment for momentum.

The dichotomy between photo and video has existed as long as there have been cameras capable of doing both. Many attempts have been made to bridge the gap, from HTC Zoe in 2013 to Apple’s Live Photos and Google’s subsequent Motion Photos years later, but most technical limitations have largely kept the two functions separate.

Magic Capture doesn’t eliminate that friction entirely, but like so many notable technological improvements, it pares it back just enough to make it feel invisible. Debuting on the Pixel 11, it’s an entirely new mode that ostensibly captures video for up to two minutes, but adds a pipeline that prepares the video for photo processing, editing, and AI-powered extraction.

If that sounds complicated, let me get specific: I was at the park the other day and my daughter, who is seven and loves to pretend she’s singing to an arena of 80,000 people, serenaded me with one of her many takes on Taylor Swift’s oeuvre. Normally I would shoot a regular video and then, a few seconds later, take some stills for posterity. With Magic Capture, I shot two minutes of video and got five perfectly framed photos free of charge, at the camera’s full 12 megapixel resolution.

	

Magic Capture’s success rests on its simplicity; because you don’t have to distinguish between framing a photo and shooting a video, you can attempt to do both. You have two minutes to move around, bring the camera to different heights and distances from the subject, and know that your effort will be paid off handsomely. I’ve shot a dozen or so videos using this method and the tool has pulled out at least one good photo every time.

It’s important to make that distinction, though: you’re shooting the video and leaving Google’s AI to decide, based on factors that aren’t quite clear, what constitutes a good photo. In its defense, though, Google has been doing this same thing consistently well since Top Shot debuted in 2018. The company says that it analyzes up to 400 frames per capture to determine which ones win the prize, but thankfully it’s simple to pluck additional stills from the video itself if you want more.

Magic Capture has a few understandable limitations: video output is 4:3 at 1080p, and I’ve noticed that while the metadata shows an output of 24fps, the actual number is considerably lower, leading to skipped frames and judder, particularly when the camera is moving.

Thankfully, the video can go through the same Video Boost pipeline as regular content, but upscaling and sharpening won’t fix mediocre video, and that’s what you’re getting with Magic Capture.

It’s for these reasons that Google likely made Magic Capture a separate third mode next to Video and Photo in the camera app. As a toggle inside the video mode, it would be less useful and more confusing, introducing compromises that users may be unhappy with. At the same time, that it’s a separate mode entirely will require some retraining on the user’s part.

The good news is that it’s worth dealing with the cognitive overhead of remembering to slide over to Magic Capture instead of Video whenever you want the best of both worlds. I’ve even set my camera app to default to it so it’s ready to go when I first open the app. I’d rather have a few seconds of mediocre video and AI-selected photos than miss a photo or video entirely because I couldn’t make up my mind.

title: Samsung’s custom widget creator appears in early One UI 9.5 build
snippet: Samsung is readying a custom widget tool in an early version of One UI 9.5, similar to what Google announced earlier this year.
fullText:
Samsung is readying a custom widget tool in an early version of One UI 9.5, similar to what Google announced earlier this year.

One UI 9.5 and Android 17 are developed in lock-step – that’s hardly a secret. Naturally, Samsung’s One UI features are derived and developed, in part, with Google as it pushes Android further. Android 17 just launched in full on the Pixel 11 series, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra were the first devices to run Samsung’s One UI 9.5.

The latest build in testing was obtained by a leaker online, and some of its features dug into. Courtesy of @fahadaljivad on Twitter/X, we now know what Samsung’s custom widget tool could look like.

Another neat find in the One UI 9.5 build 👀

​Samsung is testing a native "Make your own Widget" / "My Custom Widget" modular split layout right out of the box. Interactive action deep-links directly in the card.

​#OneUI95 #SamsungLeaks pic.twitter.com/Tx6ixSgojF

— Fahad Ali Javed (@fahadalijaved) August 20, 2026

The post notes that the widget shown is laid out in a modular split structure, with two widgets coexisting in the same tile. Both are custom and have no app anchor. It’s not shown, but Samsung’s creation process will likely be similar to Google’s, in which users can describe what they want in a widget, and the apps needed will be directly used to provide data and shortcuts.

	

In this example, Samsung surfaces in the widget picker; it looks like both calendar integration and messages can be linked to one widget. 

Google announced the feature in May 2026, adding that it would launch on both Pixel and Samsung Galaxy devices this summer. Google says it will be able to cobble together custom widgets to give you any information you want, based on your needs. It lists anything from topic surfacing, weather alerts, and countdowns to important dates. The limitations will be clear when it actually rolls out.

title: Someone already figured out how to fully control Pixel 11 Pro’s ‘HiLight’ and make it useful [Gallery]
snippet: “HiLight” is one of the biggest hardware features on Google’s Pixel 11 Pro devices, but it’s also one that the company hindered by heavily limited what you can do with it. Android being Android, someone already figured out how to hijack “HiLight” and make the Pixel 11 Pro’s RGB light a lot more useful.
fullText:
“HiLight” is one of the biggest hardware features on Google’s Pixel 11 Pro devices, but it’s also one that the company hindered by heavily limited what you can do with it. Android being Android, someone already figured out how to hijack “HiLight” and make the Pixel 11 Pro’s RGB light a lot more useful.

Highlighted by David Imel (currently working with The Verge), @Dhananjay_Tech already figured out how to control the Pixel 11 Pro’s “HiLight” LED, even though Google explicitly said it wouldn’t open the feature to third-party developers. 

“HiLight Studio” is the result, an app that gives users full control of the Pixel 11 Pro’s light to do basically anything. Where Google solely supports call notifications and a status light for Gemini, this app lets you use it as a notification LED with patterns, custom color choices, and more. It’s customizable on a per-app basis with granular settings beyond that. You can also build and export presets to share with other users. You can also just have “HiLight” active all of the time if you want.

It’s almost exactly what we wanted from this feature.

	

Pixel 11 Pro’s ‘HiLight’ missed its opportunity to be the perfect notification LED

	

The downside? Setup is very complex. 

You’ll need to sideload the app from Github, then use Shizuku and ADB sideloading from a computer to finalize the install. Even once installed and active, you’ll need to reactivate the app every time the phone is rebooted. Google didn’t exactly make “HiLight” easy to control – shocker.

It’s still wild to see that someone figured out how to do this on day one, and it just opens up hope that Google might make this all possible directly through the software someday. But, seeing as this is sideloaded and using advanced permissions, install at your own risk.

title: Google now lets you chat to customize Discover, tune News audio briefings
snippet: Google is rolling out updates that let you customize Discover and the Google News audio briefing.
fullText:
Google is rolling out updates that let you customize Discover and the Google News audio briefing.

You can now customize the Google Discover feed via a prompt-based interface. This lets you “tell Google the exact topics or links you want to see more (or less) of, in your words.” Google can ask follow-up questions to further tune what is surfaced.

Your feed will adjust on the fly, and remember your requests. By letting you refine your tastes in real time, Discover can connect you with content that genuinely matches what you care about right now.

Once available, tap the three-dot overflow button or the dedicated card to enter a prompt. Testing started last year, and this is now rolling out in the coming days.

Meanwhile, Google News will let you customize its daily audio briefing. This lets you select specific topics across Headlines, Business, Entertainment & lifestyle, Sports, Science & technology, and more. 

	

Underneath each category, you can get more granular. For example, the Entertainment category lets you choose from Arts & Design, Movies, Music, Theater, and TV.

The final announcement today is for publishers. Google now offers an interactive “Preferred Sources” button that can be embedded into websites. Clicking the button adds the publication as a Preferred Source “and immediately directs [readers] back to where they left off on the publisher’s page.” This applies to the Top Stories carousel in Search, AI Overviews, and AI Mode.

title: Google Pixel 11 flaunts its haptics with vibrations that match your ringtone
snippet: Google’s Pixel phones have had killer haptic motors for several generations now, with the Pixel 11 further emphasizing these with a new ability to match the vibration patterns to your ringtone.
fullText:
Google’s Pixel phones have had killer haptic motors for several generations now, with the Pixel 11 further emphasizing these with a new ability to match the vibration patterns to your ringtone.

A new feature in the Pixel Sounds app that has debuted with Pixel 11, added quietly, pairs your ringtone with a specific vibration pattern. So instead of the default pulsing you can now feel the tone resonating through the device. 

Each ringtone’s vibration pattern is different, with some also being subtler than others. It’s also not universal, only being supported on select ringtones. As far as we can tell, this includes only a handful of options from the “Pixel Sounds” collection including “The Next Adventure,” “Your New Adventure,” “The Big Adventure,” “Copycat,” “Crackle,” “Flutterby,” “Hotline,” “Leaps & Bounds,” “Lollipop,” “Lost & Found,” “Mash-up,” “Monkey Around,” “School’s Out,” and “Zen Too.”

Any other ringtone can have a custom vibration pattern attached to it, also new on Pixel 11.

	

It’s a fun way for the Pixel to flaunt its excellent haptic motors, something Google has snuck into bits and pieces of the software over the years. 

All of this first surfaced way back in early 2025, but is only live now for the first time.

Notably, these new vibration patterns are also customizable on a per-contact level, as Android Authority notes. Through the Google Contacts app, you can assign both a custom ringtone and a custom vibration pattern to individual contacts.

title: Book-style foldables are taking over, with Samsung fighting for second place
snippet: A new forecast shows that the foldable market is poised to continue growing, with book-style foldables taking over the popularity of clamshell devices – but Samsung is no longer the king, instead fighting for second place.
fullText:
A new forecast shows that the foldable market is poised to continue growing, with book-style foldables taking over the popularity of clamshell devices – but Samsung is no longer the king, instead fighting for second place. 

Omdia reports that the global foldable smartphone market is set to grow by “more than 20% annually through 2028,” totalling around 36 million units by then. In the first half of 2026 alone, shipments reached 5.1 million units. That was down over 20% year-over-year, in part because flip phone (clamshell) foldable shipments are down 47% year-over-year. 

Book-style devices are taking over. In the first half of the year, 69% of foldable shipments were book-style devices, and the report brings out that wide devices like Samsung’s hit Galaxy Z Fold 8 are set to build future growth.

Yet, Samsung is not the leader in this space anymore.

	

Instead, it’s Huawei with the top spot. The Chinese manufacturer currently accounts for 57% of global foldable shipments, while Samsung made up just 18%. That’s when zoomed in to look at just the first half of 2026, though, so it’s not accounting for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 launch. Still, it’s a staggering difference given that Samsung founded the category, and that Huawei is largely limited to sales in China alone. 

Honor, Oppo, Vivo, and other assorted brands make up the rest of the foldable market globally, in that order.

The report closes out on the reminder that, while becoming ever-more popular, foldables are expected to remain a very small part of the market, accounting for “less than 3% of total global smartphone shipments” at around 45 million by the year 2030.

title: Pixel Journal update brings Auto format, Sleep data, and more [U]
snippet: With the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is rolling out a handful of updates to the Journal app that are already appearing on older devices.
fullText:
With the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is rolling out a handful of updates to the Journal app that are already appearing on older devices.

Update 8/20: Version 2026.07.27.x has widely rolled out, with Google sharing a changelog for the “Journal August 2026 Updates”:

Auto format to organize text

Sleep data from Health Connect

Daily custom routine reminders

Interactive live map search

To enable Sleep data, you have to go to Pixel Journal’s App info page > Permissions > Health, fitness and wellness and turn on the “Sleep” toggle.

Original 8/14: On the compose screen, the Inspiration bottom sheet, which has a new icon up top, adds a “Refresh” capability and explicit “Close” button.

	

There’s also now a new Customization tab to control Media layout. Your options are Compact or Full for an entry. 

The big update here is the ability to “Auto format an entry in simple mode” or “expressive mode.” Accessed from a new icon at the top, this feature leverages Private AI Compute in the cloud instead of being exclusively on-device. Other Pixel apps have been moving in this direction.

More power, same protection

Pixel Journal is now powered by Google’s Private AI Compute, allowing you to enjoy AI experiences with industry-leading privacy safeguards. To ensure your data stays private to you, Pixel Journal works in a secure, isolated environment on your device and in the cloud. You can turn off AI features in Journal settings.

The app can now send journaling reminders at set times:

Morning around 7 AM

Afternoon around 2 PM

Evening around 9 PM

Finally, Google has tweaked the dark theme for the Entries tab to improve visibility of the bookmarks icon. The Insights tab also picks up some visual tweaks to the calendar.

We’re seeing version 2026.07.27.x of the Journal app on our Pixel 10a. This update is not yet widely rolled out.

title: XREAL teases the price of its Android XR glasses as early-bird deal sells out
snippet: XREAL Aura, the company’s first pair of Android XR-based glasses, are set to officially get a price point soon as the first sales figures have come in, and it’s pretty popular so far.
fullText:
XREAL Aura, the company’s first pair of Android XR-based glasses, are set to officially get a price point soon as the first sales figures have come in, and it’s pretty popular so far.

Taking a step back, XREAL Aura are Android XR-based glasses with a display. Unlike the smaller glasses expected to start showing up next year, Aura has built-in displays and somewhat mimics the functionality of a VR headset, just in a much smaller form factor. Unlike previous XREAL glasses, Aura includes a control puck that houses the components needed to run Android XR.

And, apparently, it’s a bit of a hit. 

XREAL has confirmed today that it has surpassed 10,000 reservations for Aura since June – probably not bad given we don’t even know how much this hardware will cost outside of that it will be “under $1,500.” The company calls this an “exciting signal” of demand for Aura.

	

This also comes as the early bird reservation deal has ended. Initially, interested buyers could deposit $99 to get a $199 credit when orders actually opened. That’s now gone, the company says, but $199 deposits remain available on XREAL’s website. 

XREAL also mentions that it will “share more on pricing and availability soon,” still saying on its website that the price will be “under $1,500 before tax.” That’s slightly updated, as far as we can tell, with the page originally saying XREAL Aura’s price “will not exceed US$1,500, excluding applicable taxes.” More or less the same message, though.

title: Camera Looks on the Pixel 11 delivers what I’ve wanted from Google’s photos for years
snippet: The Pixel 11 lineup has earned its reputation as a safe upgrade — or boring, if you’re looking to be a little less generous to Google — but it’s delivering one thing I’ve been begging for literal years: Camera Looks. I’ve been experimenting with them while working towards my eventual Pixel 11 Pro XL review, and I have to say, I’m mostly satisfied. Mostly.
fullText:
The Pixel 11 lineup has earned its reputation as a safe upgrade — or boring, if you’re looking to be a little less generous to Google — but it’s delivering one thing I’ve been begging for literal years: Camera Looks. Google’s take on the iPhone’s Photographic Styles have been a long time coming, and appear to be set to play a big role in shaking up the conversation around the Pixel’s evenly-lit, HDR-heavy processing. I’ve been experimenting with them while working towards my eventual Pixel 11 Pro XL review, and I have to say, I’m mostly satisfied. Mostly.

Camera Looks is, at long last, an acknowledgement that Google’s photo “optimizations” have gone too far since Marc Levoy left Google for Adobe in 2020. While I’m not trying to make it sound as though one single person was why the Pixel’s camera system was so universally beloved in its pre-Tensor era, the philosophy around Levoy’s approach to computational photography — something he’s now experimenting on with an iOS-only app at Adobe — certainly feels from a bygone era. While photos captured on the Pixel 8, or 9, or 10 certainly look good by its textbook definition, they’re also lacking the personality and character found on devices like, for example, my beloved OnePlus 13 from a couple of years ago.

This menu is, unfortunately, the fastest way to jump through Google’s non-default processing options.

And so, with a growing chorus of voices tired of Google’s ultra-clean processing that reduces contrast, saturation, and all of the other elements that can make a photograph really stand out from the crowd, Camera Looks arrives. It’s a Pixel 11 exclusive, a decision I think is borderline insulting to the company’s fans. While these settings really do change the underlying processing applied to a final shot — rather than, say, applying a simple filter prior to tapping the shutter button — I certainly don’t see enough of a performance gap between the last few generations of Tensor that would require this tool be kept for Google’s latest, most expensive lineup yet.

But I digress. The long and winding road that brought us here might be filled with bad decisions, but now that we’ve seemingly arrived at a proper solution, how does it actually perform? That’s a surprisingly difficult question to answer, believe it or not; it all comes down to your own personal taste, your level of patience and experimentation, and whether Google can make a couple of changes to improve the overall user experience. But so far, I’m pretty happy.

	

Camera Looks are personal, extremely flexible, and a little daunting

Let’s start right away with some examples, before I explain why making a final judgement call on the strength of Camera Looks is so difficult. For this review period, I’ve been capturing shots in all four “default” styles, along with one example each for the additional looks that need to be reapplied every time you open the camera app.

For every gallery in this article, I’ve kept these styles in the order as they appear below, unless otherwise labeled.

Those four styles are as follows:

Original: The typical processing you’d expect from previous generations of Pixels.

Natural: Softer and warmer than Original.

Shadows: Much more contrast-y, with an emphasis on shadows over all else.

Vanilla: The warmest of the bunch, with hazier colors.

If, like me, you end up finding that not one of these meets your Goldilocks qualifications, you can tweak them further to your heart’s content. Camera Looks is annoyingly buried — tap on the lower-right button in the viewfinder to open pro-level settings, then tap the Looks button in the lower-left corner — but once you’re in this menu, there’s plenty to do. Each of these default styles supports adjustments to their overall contrast, highlights, shadows, vibrance, tint, warmth, sharpness, and grain. They can all be reset at any time, either individually or with a single tap at the end of this list. Again, this can take some time and patience, but if you’re willing to put the work in, you can basically make the Pixel 11’s camera feel exactly how you want it to feel.

If that’s all Camera Looks was, it’d be good enough to satisfy. Even if the four base options in their default states don’t immediately win me over, there’s plenty of flexibility to be found. But Google didn’t stop at four; there are six more additional presets that might look more familiar to Snapseed users. Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal all add additional looks, ranging from a contrast-friendly black-and-white mode to digital camera-inspired styles to a minimally-processed look. Black Tie even lets you adjust how color is filtered for more granular style options when shooting.

Honestly, my biggest takeaway here is how disappointing that you can’t set these filters as your default shooting mode; they must be selected every time, either from the Looks menu itself or by enabling Quick Access controls in settings and making sure Looks is enabled. I get Google doesn’t want to cede total control here, nor do they want users feeling overwhelmed by the options available. But, come on. Hide it beneath 20 menus if you want, Google, but allow those of us who might prefer Digi or Editorial or Minimal to use it as our default. There’s room for nuance here.

Limitations aside, Camera Looks feels like what I’ve wanted from Pixel for years

As for how these modes actually perform, well, it’s tricky for me to judge. If this hasn’t already become clear, Camera Looks is definitely designed with personalization in mind, and so what I like (or dislike) in a photo, you might dislike (or like). I also captured all of these photos on the Pixel 11 Pro XL with every customization left untouched, which is definitely not how I would prefer to capture shots outside of a review period. In experimenting with these settings over the weekend, I think Shadows with increased warmth might become my go-to default style, but it’s early days, and difficult for me to really cement where I might end up.

Not every image I captured has a clear-cut winner, even in my own eyes. Sometimes the deeper contrast delivered with Shadows was exactly what the doctor ordered. Sometimes that warm, hazy tone delivered by Vanilla just felt right for a sunny, late-August day. Sometimes, I genuinely appreciated the added character brought by one of the non-default modes, like when I captured a section of Buffalo’s Japanese Gardens in Velvet (see the first image in the slideshow above). I wouldn’t call the shot perfectly accurate to the colors around me, but the feeling — or, dare I say, the vibe — it delivered made it easily my favorite of the five shots I took. Cooler tones, deeper shadows. It just felt like it fit. I only wish I’d cranked the grain setting up before capturing, but I suppose that would corrupt the point of this whole trial.

Camera Looks are not enough of a reason to upgrade to the Pixel 11, particularly because I’m hoping Google decides to reverse its decision to not bring these styles to older hardware. Paired with those new sensors, though, it’s undoubtedly the biggest leap forward for photography we’ve seen on the Pixel in ages. There’s some room for improvement, but of all of the new initiatives Google is pushing this year, it’s by far the most successful.

For the first time in multiple generations, I’m genuinely excited to go out and just try things. It sort of feels like the first time I had a real digital camera land in my hands as a kid. And in the era of AI and computational photography, you sort of have to hand it to Google for finally ceding some control over how its output really feels.

title: The Pixel 11 ditches the ‘Powered by Android’ boot logo for Gemini Intelligence
snippet: Yes, you read that headline correctly. The Pixel 11 no longer shows the “Powered by Android” boot logo, which has been a staple for a few years now.
fullText:
Yes, you read that headline correctly. The Pixel 11 no longer shows the “Powered by Android” boot logo, which has been a staple for a few years now.

With Gemini taking an even greater portion of Google’s development efforts as of late, in some cases, to the detriment of Android, this is arguably not that much of a surprise. Recent Pixel phones have been positioned as the “Gemini phone” in marketing and by the media as a way to help differentiate what the devices do differently from the millions of other Android phones sold each year globally.

When you boot into any of the brand new Pixel 11 lineup, the bottom portion of the screen is notably absent of the classic “Powered by Android” splash with the older Bugdroid logo that has now been superseded by “The Bot” and has lived on since the Pixel 9 added the first Gemini animated boot screen. You can see the boot logo change below on the Pixel 10 Pro XL side-by-side with the Pixel 11 Pro XL:

When you’re used to seeing the splash message, it is odd, or at least a little jarring, to see it removed with Google being the custodian of the platform. 

	

Coincidentally, boot times have improved significantly on the Pixel 11 series in our testing, and this is a really inconsequential change, given that most of the time you want your phone to power on quickly and not hang around in the boot sequence. I’m not sure anyone is rebooting their phone enough for this to be a problem, but it’s a definite branding decision that’s for sure.

That said, let’s pour one out for the bootscreen Bugdroid; he had a good run.
