title: The trials and tribulations of reviewing a Pixel
snippet: Good morning and happy Thursday. We’ve got Pixel reviews galore, a new look at Insomniac’s upcoming Wolverine game, a crazy story about prolific phone scammers, and an updated version of Qwen 3.8 that I’ll be spending the next few days tweaking to my liking. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter you should be able to read in around 95 seconds. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.
fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. We’ve got Pixel reviews galore, a new look at Insomniac’s upcoming Wolverine game, a crazy story about prolific phone scammers, and an updated version of Qwen 3.8 that I’ll be spending the next few days tweaking to my liking.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter you should be able to read in around 95 seconds. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

The big story today is, of course, Google’s new Pixel phones and smartwatches. Reviews are live, and in his famously unfiltered way, our own Damien Wilde says it best: “This probably could have been a software update.”

	

On one hand, that’s a bit disappointing: no big, flashy hardware upgrades to tempt new buyers. On the other hand, it’s reassuring: many of the major upgrades will eventually arrive on older Pixel phones once Google gets around to optimizing them. A handful of features may be gated to the faster Tensor G6 inside the phones — the excellent Magic Capture mode comes to mind — while others like Proactive Assistance (née Magic Cue) and Rambler will likely be backported within a few months.

But among the wider press circuit, there appears to be a prevailing ambivalence toward the new Pixel products, a consequence of rising prices and a hardware platform that feels a few steps behind its closest competitors.

Damien’s early Pixel 11 review:

The Pixel 11 is a good phone but an expensive phone. One that is tough to evaluate without all the other market factors that make it such. In a few months, it’ll become a much better buy by virtue of discounts and sales, as it has always been with Google hardware for better or worse.

Abner’s initial Pixel 11 Pro review: 

Ultimately, the Pixel 11 Pro is a fine phone waylaid by narrative and circumstance (RAMageddon) more so than any specific faults. The hardware, software, and AI – they’re all quite good.

Ben’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold impressions:

There are a couple of factors really holding me back here. First, there’s the hardware itself. Google is objectively two years behind the competition in regards to overall fit and finish. I could also throw in moderate complaints around the cameras and the display crease, but neither of those really bother me personally. The biggest complaint so far has been battery life, and it might be a serious problem.

While none of these pieces are final reviews — we prefer to take our time rather than meet a company’s embargo if it’s a short turnaround — they echo what many others in the industry are saying.

Paul over at Android Authority likes a lot about the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s camera, particularly the 5x zoom lens, but complains about inconsistency in video capture. GSMArena praises the Tensor G6’s real-world performance, which is a marked improvement over the G5. And The Verge’s David Imel loves many of the Pixel 11 Pro’s new features, including Rambler and Magic Capture, but finds the time-saving claims of Proactive Assistance half-baked.

More from 9to5Google’s Pixel team:

Pixel Watch 5 (41mm) Initial Review: New watch alert, actually

Yes, the Pixelsnap magnets on Pixel 11 are stronger this year

Pixel 11 introduces unified ‘Pixel search,’ hides it in the drawer

✉️ Inbox

Google Pixel strategy is now ‘attack,’ 13 million phones in 2026, ending China production. A project that’s been going on for years is nearing completion: Google is almost finished moving its Pixel production out of China and into Vietnam, which reportedly successfully built the entire Pixel 11 lineup.

Fairphone officially starts selling its new repairable Android phone in the US for $649. The Fairphone Gen 6 Plus is now available in the US, and despite its mediocre specs, may be one of the best long-term investments you can make in a piece of tech. iFixit gave it a 10/10 repairability rating, and its $649 asking price makes it even more tantalizing.

Gemini in Chrome and auto browse roll out on Android in the US. Google is pushing further into do-it-for-you browsing by more tightly integrating Gemini into Chrome for Android. Just ask for something and the built-in agent will (try to) make it happen.

Claude can now send emails in Gmail, even without your approval. Claude already works with your Google Workspace account, but now it can send emails on your behalf. Just remember that no one wants to receive AI-written emails.

Google ‘gradually’ rolling out Android’s ‘advanced’ sideloading ahead of developer verification. Google’s long-awaited app sideloading limitations are rolling out, requiring users to wait 24 hours after unlocking the ability to perform their first installs, in an attempt to limit coercive scams.

The reMarkable Paper Pro can technically run Android, but it’s a hassle. I love my reMarkable Paper Pro and have no intention of ruining the experience by installing Android, but I kind of love that it’s possible.

Pixel 11 ships with Android 17’s new 3D emoji [Gallery]. A lot of people are hating on these new emoji, but I’m not one of them. You can send me a 3D distorted face emoji any day.

GeForce Now adds Firefox support five years after Chrome, now live. I’m someone who wants to play more games, and I continue paying for GeForce Now because of it. I’m also a Firefox user. And yet I doubt I will ever play it this way.

Gemini Live adds Deep Research as Notebooks come to AI Mode. Google’s announcing a bevy of back-to-school updates to benefit students, including free AI Pro or AI Plus accounts for a year (depending on location), and Deep Research ability inside Gemini’s voice-enabled Live mode.

 🤑 Action items

Writing tablets are a dime a dozen these days, but reMarkable sits apart from the crowded market by religiously building premium hardware and spare-to-a-fault software. As I said above, I love my reMarkable tablet because of its relentless focus on writing. While it’s great you can browse and game and read on various Boox tablets, for note-taking and sketching I haven’t found anything better than reMarkable, even as competitors like Supernote and Amazon’s Kindle Scribe have sought to catch up.

What reMarkable isn’t is cheap: the devices themselves almost never go on sale, and the company keeps a strict lock on retail partner prices. Now, after launching its $399 reMarkable Paper Pure, the company is discounting its Pro devices with a stylus and matching folio cover for the price of the device alone. I wouldn’t say it’s a great deal, but it’s the best you’ll find for arguably the best writing tablets out there.

reMarkable Paper Pro Move bundle — $469 (was $569)

reMarkable Paper Pro bundle — $679 (was $779)

🙃 FWD: 

US Army soldiers are being offered a 4-day pass to escape the base and play the most anticipated game of all time. From Task & Purpose:

According to the memo signed by Lt. Col. Ryan Hodgson, the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion commander, soldiers in the unit who reenlist between Aug. 1 and Nov. 14, 2026, will get a “special 4-day pass” that is “specifically designated to coincide with the highly anticipated release of the video game Grand Theft Auto 6.”

GTA 6 is top of mind for other reasons, too: days before a massive Netflix timed-exclusive reveal, footage from the game has been released in four separate leaks (IGN). The group behind the leak calls itself CyberLeek and is advertising a memecoin alongside the footage and blames its release on Rockstar’s decision not to release a physical disc version of the game.

I’m also ridiculously excited for the upcoming stop-motion Laika Studios film, Wildwood. Beautiful hand-crafted animation, an emotional, heart-wrenching story about love and family, and talking animals fighting the forces of evil. What else could you want from a movie?

🗑️ Trash

I first learned about the theremin in a novel called Us Conductors by fellow Canadian Sean Michaels (no, not that one), who has since written a prescient book about AI’s disruptive power called Do You Remember Being Born?.

Now you, too, can mimic the famous jazz hands of theremin creator Leon Theremin by waving them in front of your webcam to approximate the pitch- and volume-controlling powers of electromagnetic fields. Have fun!

Thanks for reading, and have a great weekend.

title: Gboard starts rolling out new ‘Emoji size’ setting
snippet: As the Pixel 11 series gets Rambler and Google’s new 3D emoji, Gboard is rolling out a new “Emoji size” setting to beta users.
fullText:
As the Pixel 11 series gets Rambler and Google’s new 3D emoji, Gboard is rolling out a new “Emoji size” setting to beta users.

Going to Settings > Preferences > Appearance reveals the new slider located underneath Font size. This lets you “Set the size and number of emoji shown in a row,” with Gboard offering a preview just above the control.

The default we’re seeing is 9, with 5 at the opposite end. On a Pixel 10 Pro, the increments are 9, 8, 8+, 7, 7+, 6, and 5. The ‘plus’ options in the middle make the emoji slightly bigger while preserving the density.

Go to the Emoji page to really test out these changes, with this setting not applying to the Emoji Kitchen row at the top.

	

This change helps you appreciate the detail in Google’s updated design. 

We’re seeing Emoji size with beta version 18.0.3.x of Gboard.

title: Samsung confirms August 27 event for the ‘newest addition to the Galaxy S26 family’
snippet: Samsung is teasing a new entrant to the Galaxy S26 series coming at an event on August 27, but it’s probably not going to be that exciting.
fullText:
Samsung is teasing a new entrant to the Galaxy S26 series coming at an event on August 27, but it’s probably not going to be that exciting.

In a brief announcement, Samsung confirms an event scheduled for August 27, roughly a week from now. The virtual-only event takes place at 8am ET / 5am PT and will be livestreamed on YouTube. 

Samsung says:

On August 27th, Samsung Electronics will hold ‘Galaxy Event August 2026’ to introduce the newest addition to the Galaxy S26 family — purposefully designed to bring many Galaxy S26 experiences from camera to AI, along with the latest One UI, to those who look for what truly matters most to them.

It sounds intriguing, but we know exactly what to expect.

	

The Galaxy S26 FE.

The budget-oriented device is expected to adopt an updated design to match the rest of the series, but leaked specs suggest it will be virtually unchanged from last year’s Galaxy S25 FE, which itself was barely changed from the prior generation. A promo image (that Samsung says was at least partially AI-generated) hints at the updated camera module design as well as the light-green color we’ve seen in leaks.

It’s very possible this event could also bring the debut of Galaxy Tab S12 and perhaps some of Samsung’s elusive upcoming Galaxy Buds.

title: Pixel 11 introduces unified ‘Pixel search,’ hides it in the drawer
snippet: With the new phones this year, Google is introducing “Pixel search” as a “dedicated search companion designed to help you find personal information faster than ever.”
fullText:
With the new phones this year, Google is introducing “Pixel search” as a “dedicated search companion designed to help you find personal information faster than ever.”

Whether you need to locate an app, find a file in Google Drive, or pull up a photo, your core device data is now accessible from a single search bar.

However, the “single search bar” mentioned by Google is not the one at the bottom of your homescreen. It’s the field available after opening the Pixel Launcher app grid.

Previously, Pixel Launcher search integrated with Clock, Contacts, Pixel Tips, Play Store, Settings, and Wallet.

Pixel 10 vs. 11

	

On the Pixel 11, this list has expanded to include Calendar, Drive, Files by Google, Gmail, Messages, Photos, and Pixel Screenshots. Those with multiple accounts can set a specific address for Google Drive and Gmail.

When you search for a term, you’ll see Calendar events, documents in Drive, emails, a row of photos, and chats from Google Messages. It takes just a second for all the results to populate.

Like before, you can quickly open applications, as well as access app shortcuts, though they now appear more prominently. There’s also support for your work profile.

This is a good unified search experience, but not being the one-tap default hurts it a great deal. AI Mode (the Google app) taking over the homescreen search bar continues to be quite inelegant, following the rollout of that change last December.

Google presumably wants consistency when you tap the search bar on any Android device, but this mandate just degrades the utility of device search. It greatly reduced my usage of Pixel search this past week.

The best workaround is setting Pixel Launcher search to automatically open the keyboard when you swipe up on your homescreen.

title: Gemini Live adds Deep Research as Notebooks come to AI Mode
snippet: With the back-to-school season underway, Google is introducing new study tools across the Gemini app and Search.
fullText:
With the back-to-school season underway, Google is introducing new study tools across the Gemini app and Search.

Gemini Live is rolling out Deep Research integration. This lets you ask for research reports by voice and then discuss what’s generated.

College students in the US can get one free year of Google AI Pro ($19.99 per month), while there’s a bundle with YouTube Premium that offers up to 70% off. Internationally, the offer is a year of AI Plus ($4.99 per month). 

A new “Student” hub (gemini.google.com/students) in the Gemini side panel surfaces offers and tools, like flashcards and practice quizzes.

	

Meanwhile, the study notebooks introduced in June are getting new features. At the moment, you can upload notes and other class material to get lesson plans and quizzes. Over the coming weeks, Google is adding graphs and images, as well as Google Calendar integration that can schedule due dates and exams based on your syllabus.

Meanwhile, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode are adding a host of study tools. Search can generate custom tools and simulations to explain complex topics:

“You can do a search like “ph scale” and quickly get an interactive visual in an AI Overview to help you understand the basics.” Fully available in coming weeks. 

“To go even further, you can follow up and ask to see something more specialized, like plotting citrus fruits on the pH scale, and AI Mode will create a customized experience just for your question.”

This joins custom practice quizzes for various topics and standardized tests, including the ACT, AP, ENEM, GRE, JEE, LSAT, MCAT, NEET, and SAT.

“create a quiz with the most commonly tested vocab words to help me prep for the SAT”

AI Mode is getting integration with Gemini Notebooks. Appearing in the side panel, Google recommends setting up notebooks for every class or project, and then adding slides, syllabi, and articles.

You can even add your previous AI Mode threads on related topics. Your notebook brings it all together in one place, letting you ask questions and analyze topics based on your reference materials, while you build on your ideas over time.

Another addition lets you “create ready-to-use study documents based on your uploaded files or AI Mode threads.”

For example, you can add a photo of your handwritten notes along with lecture slides and ask Search for a one-pager that outlines the key concepts.

Google Lens is getting a new interactive learning experience that can discuss “tough concepts and confirm if you’re on the right track.” Available in the coming weeks (globally in English), you just snap a photo of the problem.

title: GeForce Now adds Firefox support five years after Chrome, now live
snippet: Nvidia says it set a “high bar” for any browser integrating GeForce Now without added programs, and Firefox has seemingly met its standards as in-browser support for the game streaming service goes live.
fullText:
Nvidia says it set a “high bar” for any browser integrating GeForce Now without added programs, and Firefox has seemingly met its standards as in-browser support for the game streaming service goes live.

GeForce Now isn’t new to browsers. Chrome has supported the game streaming service since 2021, even if the GeForce Now standalone app has been made available for nearly every OS at this point. But access from a browser like Google Chrome just plays further into the idea that Nvidia’s GeForce Now works just about anywhere with good internet.

GeForce Now’s list now includes Firefox on Windows machines, as Mozilla and Nvidia announced that the browser officially supports cloud gaming. There’s little to do on the user’s end – connect to GeForce Now’s website and start playing. It’s expected to perform similarly to other avenues of play, and it should play nicely with multiple tabs open at the same time. Nvidia says Premium members can expect up to 1440p and 120 frames per second in-browser.

Mozilla does give a hint as to why the integration has taken some time beyond the simple fact that it isn’t Chromium-based. Firefox has been built to stand on privacy and granular user controls, and cloud gaming can demand a lot in terms of performance and data, as massive titles need the bandwidth for millisecond response. Nvidia also notes that it “set a high bar for browser support” in the same press release.

	

This seems to be the latest in a long string of partnerships with Nvidia. Recently, the company announced integration with Fire TV and said the GeForce Now app is available to play on more TVs with third-party streamers.

Unlike on TVs, streaming GeForce Now through Firefox doesn’t require a controller. It’s the same story as in Google Chrome and on the standalone app.

Nvidia and Mozilla say there’s more ahead for those who prefer to stream their games.

snippet: Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is going to be a tame upgrade, at least in terms of fit and finish, as a leaked image reveals that the design is almost entirely unchanged.
fullText:
Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is going to be a tame upgrade, at least in terms of fit and finish, as a leaked image reveals that the design is almost entirely unchanged.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra continues Samsung’s ongoing lineup of monstrous Android tablets, with the 14.6-inch behemoth rumored to debut in the next couple of months or so. A new chipset, Android 17 out of the box, and other tweaks can be expected, but this is a wholly unchanged piece of hardware.

At least, that’s what it looks like in a low-res image of the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra posted by Android Headlines. Like last year’s model, there are thin bezels, a metal build, a teardrop selfie camera notch, and two cameras on the back. 

Side by side with last year’s Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra, there are no clear differences at all. 

	

Just to reiterate, we lined up the leak with an official image of the Tab S11 Ultra as closely as possible, and the slider speaks for itself.

Tablets are a pretty mature form factor, but this design really hasn’t changed much at all since its inception. The Tab S11 Ultra shrunk the display notch and moved the S Pen charging station to the frame, but even Tab S10 Ultra and Tab S9 Ultra – and Tab S8 Ultra, for that matter – all looked exactly like this.

We’ll have to wait and see if there’s anything under the hood to make this one stand out.

title: The reMarkable Paper Pro can technically run Android, but it’s a hassle
snippet: A YouTuber who took their reMarkable Paper Pro and converted it into an Android device shows off the process in a recent video, even if it defeats the purpose of the e-paper tablet.
fullText:
A YouTuber who took their reMarkable Paper Pro and converted it into an Android device shows off the process in a recent video, even if it defeats the purpose of the e-paper tablet.

The e-reader corner of the tech market doesn’t have many Android options. One of the biggest names that comes to mind is Boox, which makes solid e-readers and note-taking tablets with a minimal skin over some of the more recent versions of Android. But reMarkable has built its tablets on its own proprietary OS to keep things minimal and clean.

It turns out the reMarkable Paper Pro can run Android 13 if you put in a little effort. Chalid Raqami uploaded a video on YouTube of the process and how it works on a tablet that wasn’t designed to handle it.

The main constraint is hardware. E-paper tablets aren’t stacked with RAM and heavyweight GPUs because it isn’t necessary to produce a monochromatic image at moderate refresh rates. To offer a pleasant experience, the main focus seems to be on display and stylus input quality. Those don’t require a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. The reMarkable Paper Pro simply needs the NXP iMX8 Mini that comes with it and 2GB of RAM to power its own OS and color display.

	

To run Android 13, that seems to work just fine. Chalid says most of the device’s functions work just fine. Front light control, Wi-Fi, and even Bluetooth accessories are operational. The home screen is filled with apps like any Android device, and navigation controls show up in the bottom corner. They even mention that the reMarkable Paper Pro’s pen can be used with latency “near-stock” using a dedicated pen mode.

They also added the option to switch back to reMarkable OS in a matter of seconds – a necessary safety switch if Android doesn’t perform properly on a tablet that wasn’t designed to handle it.

As expected, the refresh rate is a hard thing to look past. But Boox has this issue too, and it comes down to the e-paper display’s capability. The video details how Android would get bogged down in the beginning on the reMarkable Paper Pro, and the port was more of a proof-of-concept. But following optimization, Chalid says memory tuning and GPU acceleration did a lot to improve usability.

The entire project seems to make the tablet more usable. With Android 13, apps otherwise blocked can be installed. That includes e-book libraries like Kindle, which isn’t something supported on reMarkable’s tablets. That becomes a turn-off if your library is hard-locked to one service.

This isn’t going to work for everyone, though. The process is somewhat complicated, and the results, for now, seem to leave it up in the air whether the effort is worth the trade-off. That question carries even more weight when you consider the reMarkable Paper Pro is designed for minimal distraction, which Android doesn’t take too seriously.

For those looking to try the same process, it doesn’t look like a port is available for the time being. That may change if reMarkable OS treats the switch any differently and doesn’t undo everything with each update. But for now, it’s a nice proof of concept for a dual-wielding reMarkable Paper Pro on Android.

title: I really want to love the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, but it’s not off to the best start
snippet: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is debuting into an increasingly tough market because, really, everything is good now. My first week with Google’s latest foldable has been one that started off hopeful, but is slowly turning a bit sour.
fullText:
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is debuting into an increasingly tough market because, really, everything is good now. My first week with Google’s latest foldable has been one that started off hopeful, but is slowly turning a bit sour.

As mentioned in another piece, I feel that the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the fourth-best foldable you can buy today, with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and the Motorola Razr Fold taking the upper three spots, at least in a conversation mainly about the US market. Google was always going to face an uphill battle here, but a week of use has not improved its position.

So far, I just feel that the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a couple of generations behind the competition, and lacking any clear standout wins compared to the devices mentioned above.

That said, here’s the good from my first week:

	

“App Handles” has been a game-changer and might be my favorite evolution of foldable multitasking since “Open Canvas” on the OnePlus Open.

The Pixel software experience as a whole is top-notch, and I so dearly want to use it on my main foldable.

Having built-in Qi2 charging is so nice after a year with a Fold 7 with a slightly clunky metal ring on the back.

Google’s durability claims are holding up well so far, I’ve yet to get so much as a scuff on the ceramic display.

Tensor G6 is a pretty big upgrade for the foldable as, despite being in the midst of North Carolina’s “Hell’s Front Porch” season of the year, this is the first Google foldable I haven’t felt is prone to overheating.

But there are a couple of factors really holding me back here.

First, there’s the hardware itself. Google is objectively two years behind the competition in regards to overall fit and finish. While I’m perfectly fine with the thickness of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, it’s hard to ignore how much better Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 series phones feel in your hand. Even the wider Fold 8 at 9.7mm – less than .5mm thinner than the Pixel – just feels much better in the hand. Google’s slightly blocky design isn’t just doing it any favors. The Motorola Razr Fold also feels better despite being the same 10.1mm thickness.

The differing thicknesses of the two halves is also just a little weird. I’m not too perturbed by the little ridge you get as a result, but this is just so unusual in the foldable world, at least to this degree.

I could also throw in moderate complaints around the cameras and the display crease, but neither of those really bother me personally.

The biggest complaint so far has been battery life, and it might be a serious problem.

Pixel 11 Pro Fold battery life thus far has been, in a word, bad. The 4,700~ mAh battery just doesn’t hold a candle to any other modern foldable. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 isn’t too far ahead, but the efficiency of its Snapdragon chip combined with the smaller displays goes a long way in making that phone actually last a day, whereas Google’s device does not. And that’s not an exaggeration. Without getting into the weeds of screen-on time – this is not a review – I’ve had multiple days where  I’ve had to plug this phone in at 7pm because it was running into battery saver mode. I’m hoping that this improves as the phone learns my usage habits, but it is not off to a good start. On the bright side, “Extreme Charging Mode” lives up to its name, and does provide some speedy charging compared to past generations, but it certainly doesn’t make up the difference that a good battery would bring.

The only good news? The battery life seems to be getting better by the day.

I’ll have more to say on Pixel 11 Pro Fold in our full review, but first impressions have not been particularly good. It’s probably not helping that I had to swap out my initial review unit due to what seems to be a slight hinge defect (a tiny popping sound when opening the hinge). Nothing else to share on that at this point, but I’ll be curious to see if that happens on any retail units.

Is there anything else you want to know about Google’s latest foldable? Drop a comment below and I’ll do my best to address it in the full review next week.

title: Yes, the Pixelsnap magnets on Pixel 11 are stronger this year
snippet: Pixelsnap is one of the best things added to Pixel phones in a number of years, but it wasn’t quite a perfect first attempt. Luckily, this year those pesky magnets are a little stronger and more reliable on the Pixel 11 series.
fullText:
Pixelsnap is one of the best things added to Pixel phones in a number of years, but it wasn’t quite a perfect first attempt. Luckily, this year those pesky magnets are a little stronger and more reliable on the Pixel 11 series.

In my testing, the magnets this year are just below the strength of the Magsafe connection on an iPhone. Things will connect more securely to the back of your phone, so you’re less likely to knock things off or encounter issues with any other accessories you might want to pair with the Pixel 11.

It’s hard to quantify without trying it out for yourself. You can sort of see in the quick demo below how there is a little extra force needed to pry the Pixelsnap kickstand from the back of the Pixel 11 over the Pixel 10. It takes less pressure from a single finger on the Pixel 10, whereas you need to actively try to remove it on the Pixel 11.

The magnets just have a little more grip, and it’s improved if the accessory you’re connecting has strong magnets already. I wouldn’t say the connection is quite as strong as when using the magnets on an iPhone, but it’s a lot closer:

	

We’re still sort of waiting for basically every Android OEM to jump on board with the Qi2 magnetic connection for flagships. So far, only Google, HMD (Nokia to you and me), and Motorola, with the Edge 70 Max, have bothered to add magnets to the back of devices. Most other brands, namely Samsung, have decided to rely on cases to bring the functionality. It’s a lazy implementation, but I guess it’s one that works.

That has sort of left Google to forge ahead and really make Pixelsnap work. I don’t understand why brands aren’t actively trying to implement “Magsafe” as many OEMs love copying Apple at any other time, so why avoid an easy win? My gripes aside, I’m glad that the magnets are stronger on the Pixel 11, because this means less reliance on having a case if you prefer to actually “feel” your phone day-to-day

title: Google Photos might add map view to Ask Photos search
snippet: An unreleased version of Google Photos appears to include a photo map we haven’t seen on the Ask Photos search page, yet.
fullText:
An unreleased version of Google Photos appears to include a photo map we haven’t seen on the Ask Photos search page, yet.

Image maps were popularized by Snapchat years ago, when location hotspots would show you where users were taking photos or videos in your area, or any area, really. Google later caught on and added an image map to Google Photos, but it isn’t a front-and-center feature for Pixel or Android users.

In an APK dive, it appears an unreleased version of Google Photos will bring a new image map tool to the Ask Photos section of the app (via Android Authority). Ask Photos is Google’s AI-powered search that currently surfaces images to match whatever query you throw at it.

In its current state, searching for a town or country will result in a grid of photos in that location. Google Photos version 7.89.0.966319819 reportedly adds a map section, so those images appear spread out across real locations. Photos with metadata that match the search query will appear as bubbles on a map of that area.

	

The existing function in Google’s public release of the Photos app will show a similar view, formatted as a global heat map. That view sits in the Collections section under Places. You can choose a suggested location, or you can explore the wider area to find photos from certain places.

This private build doesn’t appear polished like the existing heatmap in Collections. It’s also unclear if this feature will still work when Ask Photos is turned off, as Google recently rolled out the option to disable its AI search and revert back to a classic search experience.

There’s no telling whether Google will release this feature soon, or ever, since it was found in a private version of the photo app. A visual map would be a great tool to have, and where it sits now is sort of hidden away.

title: Pixel Thermometer gets new gradient icon on its way out
snippet: After three generations, Google dropped the built-in thermometer from the Pixel 11 Pro. However, like other first-party apps, the Pixel Thermometer app has a new icon.
fullText:
After three generations, Google dropped the built-in thermometer from the Pixel 11 Pro. However, like other first-party apps, the Pixel Thermometer app has a new icon.

The basic design is unchanged, but the thermometer is now blue instead of white, while the mercury uses a darker shade of blue and the background is now white. 

There are no obvious changes inside the app, and that isn’t particularly surprising. Google just added the new icon for Pixel consistency, with this probably being the last major update to Thermometer outside of bug fixes. Hardware support will presumably be available for years to come.

Google, unfortunately, never added a Quick Settings Tile for Pixel Thermometer, but access from the Google Health app is appreciated.

	

This year’s HiLight replacement does have the upside of being included on the Pro Fold model. 

Version 1.0.947990598 of Pixel Thermometer is rolling out via the Play Store. It’s not yet widely available.

title: ‘Moto Snap’ magnetic wireless charger leaks, hopefully as a sign of more Qi2 to come [Gallery]
snippet: Qi2 magnetic wireless charging is finally making some headway in the Android world, with Motorola recently having launched its first smartphone with built-in magnets. Now, a leaked “Moto Snap” wireless charger has surfaced, hopefully hinting at more Qi2 in Motorola’s lineup going forward.
fullText:
Qi2 magnetic wireless charging is finally making some headway in the Android world, with Motorola recently having launched its first smartphone with built-in magnets. Now, a leaked “Moto Snap” wireless charger has surfaced, hopefully hinting at more Qi2 in Motorola’s lineup going forward.

Rewinding, the first Motorola device with built-in Qi2 magnets is the Motorola Edge 70 Max, a device that arrived seemingly out of nowhere with the rarely-seen functionality. The phone supports Qi2 25W charging speeds and has the magnets inside of the actual device, not offloaded to a case like on Samsung’s Galaxy phones. It joined a pretty exclusive club that, outside of this one device, is basically just Google’s Pixel 10 and now Pixel 11 series.

But it’s still an outlier in Motorola’s lineup, though it seems like that might be changing.

Evan Blass took to Twitter/X – the real account, since the old one was hijacked – with images of a magnetic wireless charging apparently called “Moto Snap.” Pixel branding similarities aside, the Motorola logo-clad charger looks to have a braided cable, a purple accent color, and a metal chassis around the back of the charger as well as around the USB-C plug.

	

While this could simply be an official charger for the Motorola Edge 70 Max, it could easily be a sign that Motorola is gearing up to bring Qi2 magnetic wireless charging to more devices in its lineup going forward. I, for one, hope that ends up being the case, but with most of Moto’s lineup being in the budget camp and without wireless charging anyway, it’s hard to know for sure how much impact this change could bring.
